BRANIFF HISTORY TODAY - On this day, Monday, November 12, 1973, Braniff International took up residence in new terminal facilities at two of its major airports in the United States. In Newark, Braniff moved into a different terminal and at John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York, the airline moved into a new terminal with United Airlines.

Braniff's move to the new facilities, which were considerably bigger than the old terminals, was precipitated by the company's significant growth and the resulting increase in flights at both terminals, but specifically at Kennedy Airport. The Kennedy Terminal was more than twice the size of the old Northwest/Northeast Terminal that Braniff had occupied since it opened on November 18, 1962. At the time of the grand opening of the $10 million USD facility, it was one of the most modern airline terminals in the United States but was quickly outgrown by Braniff.

Braniff's New York Kennedy service continued to grow at a fast pace and by the time the carrier moved into the Northside Wing of the United Airlines Terminal it was operating 83 flights every week to major cities in Tennessee, Oklahoma, Arkansas, and Texas. In addition to flights to Washington DC, Kennedy also enjoyed service to Latin America via Washington DC, and Miami, Florida. Braniff also served New York LaGuardia and Newark airport with service to other major US cities.

The new terminal, besides being big, offered Braniff the security of its own gate space, which numbered four. Passengers enjoyed an upper level for arrivals and a lower level for departures and Braniff International Council members were treated to a much larger lounge facility than was available at the Northwest/Northeast Terminal. Square footage of the new terminal was 34,300 square feet for passenger handling and over 8000 square feet of office space behind the Front Ticket Office, which was located on the departure or lower level. Outside on the ramp, an impressive 281,180 square feet of tarmac space was provided for aircraft servicing.

Braniff's new terminals at both Kennedy and Newark featured elegant new interiors by the company's industrial design firm, Harper and George of New York City. The remodeled interiors were similar to the stylish new Dallas/Ft. Worth Regional Airport terminal that began scheduled airline operations in January 1974. Saddle-style lounge seating by John Mascheroni featured warm brown Naugahyde designed by Uniroyal, with each seat individually mounted on rounded polished and chromed arms. Rich carpeting rounded out the look that gave the facility a sleek and modern look.

Besides the luxurious new interiors, the terminals featured all of the classic amenities including curbside check-in and automatic baggage handling. The walk between curbside and the gate was minimal further adding to the high degree of passenger comfort and convenience at both Newark and New York Kennedy airports.

Photo: Braniff International Boeing 727-291 Trijet registered as N408BN is on short final at John F. Kennedy International Airport in October 1978. Ship N298BN is painted in the 1967 Alexander Girard/Harper and George Red Solid Color Scheme with White Engines, Wings and Tail with Alexander Girard Sky Font and BI Tail Logo in Black.

I went to a porch festival in Florida last week, an awesome event, with a variety of great bands playing all over numerous blocks in Springfield.  
Unfortunately, they had to have the gratuitous drag show and one of our group wanted to watch it.  I'd never been to one, so I was a bit curious myself.  Well, the event was as expected: fake women pretending to sing overplayed songs ("I Will Survive", for example), constantly asking for tips, frequently educating the crowd about their cause, constantly seeking praise for their performance, involving young spectators at numerous times as they claimed "it's all about the kids", clumsily gyrating suggestively with gaudy costumes and heavy paintjobs on the face.
The crowd did its' part on cue, appearing to be impressed and supportive, woohooing when the dudes revealed their "sexy" under layers and when they spread their digits wider, coughing up tips for the tip jar.  
Whatever.  I couldn't care less about what excites grown up people at this point.  The reality for me though is that if these clowns had actually displayed some talent beyond being representatives of "the cause", I might have added a dollar to the jar myself, but that wasn't the case.  They weren't remotely passable as attractive "women" nor was there any attempt to actually sing beyond synching their lips (when they weren't grandstanding).  Every other singer at the porch fest was offering soulful attempts at singing and/or playing music, but these clowns, simply due to their political/social status, begged louder but only offered a bare minimum effort in return and yet still drew a bigger crowd than the other bands.  
Sad.  I was glad to move on...

text:
The Piper: His Powers, Erik, and the Hamelin Connection

I wanted to spend a little more time on the Piper because there are several things happening with him in Grimm Fairy Tales #50 that are easy to run together. He interferes with Erik, he steals power from the Casket of Provenance, and he gets that power back to the Dark One. Those actions help set up the attack that follows, but they also leave Sela with a problem that continues after the battle is over.

Spoilers for Grimm Fairy Tales #49–51.

Erik's return is already a big deal for Sela before the Piper shows up. In #49, he's connected to memories she has lost, including their relationship and the fact that she was pregnant. She has questions about her own life that she hasn't been able to answer. Then the issue ends with Erik apparently serving the Dark One, and #50 picks up with him attacking Shang and the defenders.

Sela is trying to understand why someone she loves is doing this. Erik says the Dark One commands him, but when he goes to strike her, he hesitates. His hand shakes, and he drops the sword. The Piper comments that true love is the thing he never seems able to overcome, then plays his instrument. Erik collapses.

I think that hesitation is important to any discussion of the Piper's power. There is resistance happening before he steps in. Erik's feelings for Sela interrupt the attack, and the Piper recognizes the problem immediately. We see a person struggling against what is happening to him, followed by the Piper using music to end that moment of resistance. That gives us a much clearer example of his influence than simply calling him a mind controller and moving on.

It also gives us a limit. His own comment acknowledges that he has trouble overcoming this connection. I wouldn't turn that into a rule that anybody in love is automatically immune to him, because Erik still ends up incapacitated. But the scene does show that the control isn't effortless or unbreakable in every circumstance. Sela reaches Erik enough to stop the sword, even though she can't stop what happens next.

When she demands an explanation, the Piper tells her Erik will never wake again. By #51, we get more information from Kozak, the healer. He says Erik's soul is no longer in his body. Other healers surround Erik and enclose him in a glass coffin to protect the body in case his soul can return. Blake later reasons that finding and freeing the soul could allow that return.

So there is a specific supernatural consequence here. Describing Erik as merely asleep would leave out what the next issue actually tells us. At the same time, these pages don't show the Piper putting the soul into a named container or tell us where he has sent it. We know the condition Erik is left in, and we know what the people trying to help him believe they need to do.

The theft is another part of the sequence that deserves its own explanation. The Piper draws power out of the Casket of Provenance into a scepter. Thane recognizes what he's doing and tries to stop him, but he escapes through a portal. When he returns to the Dark One, his master calls him Anslied and praises him. The comic identifies both his name and the purpose behind the raid.

That scepter matters because the defenders explain that its stolen power can be used only once more. The portal access in this scene depends on a resource he has taken. It would be a stretch to credit him with unlimited travel between realms based on this encounter. He succeeds by getting inside, using the disruption around Erik, taking the energy, and leaving before the defenders can recover it.

The musical part has a real-world comparison, although the comic takes it well beyond anything demonstrated in research. Music can affect emotion, attention, and movement. The National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health describes research in which synchronizing movement to a rhythmic sound may help people with Parkinson's disease walk better. Its overview also notes possible benefits for anxiety and pain, while making clear that many findings are preliminary or mixed.

That's a useful starting point because sound really can influence what we feel and how we move. Think about keeping pace with a beat or hearing a song associated with someone you haven't seen in years. There is a familiar experience underneath the fantasy. But coordinating a movement with a rhythm doesn't demonstrate that a musician can force someone to attack a loved one. Nothing in that research explains removing a soul, either. The Piper's instrument is operating through the supernatural rules of this setting.

The older Pied Piper story is worth looking at alongside this. In Robert Browning's version of The Pied Piper of Hamelin, the Piper offers to remove the rats for a thousand guilders. He does the job, the town's leaders refuse the agreed payment, and he returns to lead away the children. The mountain opens, they follow him inside, and the entrance closes behind them.

One detail I like in that poem is the account from the child left behind. He remembers the music promising a wonderful place, even a cure for his disability. From his perspective, he has missed out on something good. That makes the enchantment more unsettling than a crowd being physically dragged away. The people following the Piper experience a reason to keep following.

Zenescope uses that recognizable connection between music and control for a different conflict. In the issues here, the Piper is carrying out the Dark One's plan, and Erik's resistance lets us see that the person underneath the influence still matters. By the time Anslied leaves, he has delivered the resource his master needs and left the defenders trying to recover someone whose body is still in front of them. Following that through into the glass coffin explains why his brief appearance has consequences well beyond the fight itself.

text:
WHAT IF ONE DAY YOU WAKE UP AND CANNOT ACCESS YOUR OWN MONEY? CASH IS FREEDOM. A CASHLESS DIGITAL WORLD IS A DANGEROUS WORLD. 

WHY THE WORLD MUST NEVER ABANDON CASH.

I have been absolutely livid with @_PVRCinemas at Select City Walk for refusing to accept cash. I hope someone seriously contemplates bringing a PIL challenging the government over the greater issue— its growing obsession with pushing India towards a digital-only economy.

Why really is the government so determined to accelerate the transition to a completely digital economy? What power are they seeking over ordinary citizens? 

The power to wake up one morning and switch off someone’s digital wallet, paralysing their ability to participate in the economy?

Why should any shopping establishment have the right to refuse perfectly valid Indian currency? Cash is India’s legal tender. Its acceptance must be a fundamental right of every citizen and an obligation of every establishment serving the public. Digital payments, cheques, cards and even cryptocurrencies can be additional choices. But cash cannot be treated as an optional convenience that businesses can simply discard. I believe establishments refusing cash should face heavy penalties. More importantly, India needs an explicit legal guarantee of the right to pay in cash.

Digital payments are convenient, but they carry a rarely discussed risk: losing access to your own money with a single click.

Payment platforms such as PayPal, Paytm and PhonePe, can block transactions, restrict access and suspend accounts or services through their automated risk systems. With cybercrimes on the rise, innocent Indians also often experience frozen bank accounts, blocked UPI transactions and suspended payment services. Like in India, in UK, and other countries freezes and closures have left customers unable to access their money. In 2022, during Canada’s Freedom Convoy protests, emergency powers led institutions to freeze at least 257 financial products, including bank accounts & credit cards. 

Private stablecoin issuers can already freeze certain holdings. Bitcoin and similar cryptocurrencies present a different problem. Unlike stablecoins designed to hold a relatively fixed value against the dollar, they can rise or collapse rapidly, making them unreliable for everyday purchasing power. They may offer alternative ownership, but they are no substitute for dependable money whose value does not change overnight.

When money exists only as a digital entry, access depends on an institution allowing you to use it. Privacy, freedom of spending and protection against arbitrary restrictions must be built in and protected by law. 

Cash offers independence from any intermediary. Notes and coins can be exchanged directly. No bank can remotely freeze them, no platform can block the transaction, and no server failure can erase them. Cash works during power cuts, internet outages and cyberattacks. It protects privacy, serves the unbanked and lets people participate without a digital trail of every purchase. Central banks including the Bank of England, the European Central Bank and Sweden’s Riksbank continue to recognise cash’s importance for financial inclusion, resilience and individual freedom.

Governments must make preserving cash a deliberate priority. ATMs & branches must remain accessible, retailers must accept cash till an acceptable limit, and the circulation infrastructure must be protected. India must not let enthusiasm for digital payments eliminate cash from everyday life. The right to use physical currency deserves explicit legal protection.

Digital payments offer speed. Convenience must never cost freedom. A society in which every transaction depends on institutional permission is one in which economic independence can be switched off.

Cash must remain alive, not because we oppose the future, but because we must protect our freedom within it.

text:
The day settles into its quiet evening rhythm, leaving behind the bustle of hours spent and tasks completed. It is in this stillness that a simple, recurring grace takes root—much like tending to a single bloom. A rose does not rush its unfolding; it simply offers its presence, steady and fragrant, anchoring the garden against the fading light. In the same way, small, daily reminders of love, faith, and gratitude gently steady the spirit, inviting the heart to remain anchored in peace rather than drifting into the worries of tomorrow.
 🌹🌹"Above all else, guard your heart, for everything you do flows from it."🌹🌹
— Proverbs 4:23
🌹🌹 "Be still, and know that I am God."🌹🌹
— Psalm 46:10

A Good Night Sonnet
When twilight folds the weary world in grey,
And shadows lengthen where the daylight crept,
A single rose reminds the heart to stay,
And keep the quiet promises it kept.
No storm of thought can shake the rooted stem,
Nor steal the grace that lingers in the air;
The evening stars ignite their gentle gem,
To watch above the soul in silent prayer.
So let the burdens of the hour release,
And lay your heavy cares beside the bed,
For mercy wraps the quiet night in peace,
And guards the pillow where you rest your head.
Sleep safe and deep beneath the heaven’s height,
And wake renewed within the morning light

Sleep peacefully

I asked my bot to reply to your questions..
Those are the right questions, and the $180bn Suffren figure doesn’t answer them.

On yard capacity: France is finishing six Suffrens for its own navy, then Cherbourg has to take on the next ballistic-missile boats and a new aircraft carrier. Twelve extra SSNs for Australia would compete with that, and the submission never shows how the work would be sequenced. A private “unsolicited offer” isn’t the same as France publicly committing the yards — it’s the same industrial squeeze AUKUS already has with the US and UK.

On adapting the design: if the RAN keeps French weapons and combat systems, the cost is interoperability with the US and UK. If it Australianises them, that’s another Attack-class-scale redesign. Neither is in a through-life number with no contingency.

On LEU refuelling: a French-style core is typically refuelled about every ten years. That’s only a short docking if Australia can do the nuclear work here. If the boats have to go to France, you lose transit and yard time, repeatedly, across a 12-boat fleet. The proponents’ “three weeks during scheduled maintenance” claim doesn’t cost either that transit or the facilities to do it in Australia.

text:
[ ECONOMIC STATECRAFT & SUPPLY CHAIN RESHORING ]

• INCIDENT VECTOR: The Canadian government has threatened immediate legal action against Stellantis to claw back substantial taxpayer subsidies. The dispute ignited after the automaker agreed to sell its idled Brampton, Ontario assembly facility to Canadian armored vehicle manufacturer Roshel, effectively abandoning its domestic production commitments.

• TACTICAL ASSESSMENT: The conflict is rooted in a 2022 agreement where Ottawa committed up to $529 million to subsidize the retooling of the Brampton and Windsor plants for next-generation Jeep Compass production. Stellantis, having already drawn $222 million of those funds, canceled the Brampton upgrades in 2025 and announced a shift of Compass manufacturing to Belvidere, Illinois. Industry reports attribute this relocation directly to the Trump administration's trade war and the discarding of the USMCA framework. Stellantis has offered to voluntarily return only $24 million—the portion it claims is strictly tied to the Brampton site—provoking outrage from the Unifor union, which represents over 2,000 displaced workers and has authorized potential strike action in retaliation.

• MACRO IMPLICATION: This confrontation exemplifies the rapid, localized fracturing of the historically integrated North American automotive supply chain under the pressure of U.S. protectionist trade policies. Furthermore, it exposes the severe legal and political vulnerabilities inherent in state-sponsored corporate subsidy programs; as multinational corporations abruptly realign their manufacturing footprints to navigate shifting geopolitical tariff regimes, host nations are left forcing complex litigation to recover sunk sovereign capital.

text:
In the winter of 1777, while George Washington's army was starving at Valley Forge, a group of officers and politicians were quietly working to get him fired. The plot fell apart because a young officer got drunk in a tavern and couldn't keep his mouth shut.

That fall had been a disaster for Washington. He'd lost the battles of Brandywine and Germantown. The British had taken Philadelphia, the American capital, and Congress had fled.

Meanwhile, up in New York, General Horatio Gates had just won the biggest American victory of the war. At Saratoga, he forced an entire British army to surrender. Overnight, Gates was the hero of the Revolution.

People started asking an obvious question. If Gates could win, why couldn't Washington?

One of the loudest voices was Thomas Conway, an Irish-born officer who'd served in the French army and came to America looking for rank and glory. He thought Washington was in over his head, and he said so, in a letter to Gates. In it he wrote that heaven must have been determined to save America, because a weak general and bad advisers would have ruined it.

Nobody was supposed to see that letter.

But Gates had a young aide named James Wilkinson. On his way to deliver news of Saratoga to Congress, Wilkinson stopped at a tavern in Reading, Pennsylvania, had a lot to drink, and started repeating what was in Conway's letter to an aide of another general. That aide passed it along to his boss, Lord Stirling. Stirling passed it straight to Washington.

Washington didn't rant or rage. He sent Conway a short note quoting the line back to him and nothing else. It was his way of saying, I know.

Gates panicked. Instead of admitting anything, he accused Washington's staff, including a young Alexander Hamilton, of stealing his private letters. He even sent copies of his complaint to Congress, which only made things worse.

And Congress was not exactly on Washington's side. That winter it put Gates in charge of the new Board of War, which in theory gave him power over Washington. It also promoted Conway to major general and made him inspector general of the army, over Washington's strong objections. Some members of Congress whispered openly about replacing the commander in chief.

The Board of War even dreamed up an invasion of Canada, led by the young Marquis de Lafayette with Conway as his second in command. It looked a lot like an attempt to pull Lafayette, one of Washington's most loyal officers, away from him. When Lafayette got to Albany, there were barely any troops and no supplies. The invasion never happened.

By spring, the whole thing was collapsing. Washington's officers rallied around him. Lafayette made it clear he wouldn't serve against him. Congress started backing away.

Conway tried a power move. He offered to resign, assuming Congress would beg him to stay. Congress accepted.

Then it got personal. A Pennsylvania general named John Cadwalader, one of Washington's loyal friends, challenged Conway to a duel over what he'd said about Washington. On July 4, 1778, Cadwalader shot Conway in the face. The bullet went in through his mouth.

Cadwalader supposedly said he'd stopped Conway's lying tongue.

Thinking he was dying, Conway wrote an apology to Washington, calling him a great and good man and saying he was sorry for anything he'd done against him. Then he survived. He went back to France and never returned.

Gates got his chance at command again in 1780. He led an American army at the Battle of Camden in South Carolina and was crushed. As his army collapsed, Gates rode away from the battlefield, covering roughly 60 miles before stopping. His reputation never recovered.

And James Wilkinson, the drunk aide who blew the whole thing open, went on to become the senior officer of the U.S. Army and a paid spy for Spain.

It's called the Conway Cabal, and almost nobody learns about it.

text:
⚠️ CANDACE OWENS REJECTED GEORGE FLOYD AS A MARTYR — BUT MALCOLM X HAD A VERY DIFFERENT MESSAGE ABOUT RACIAL INJUSTICE.

NARRATOR: On June 3, 2020, Candace Owens posted a Facebook video she called a confession.

CANDACE OWENS: I do not support George Floyd and the media depiction of him as a martyr for Black America. I hope his family gets justice for the way he died, but I won't accept the narrative that this is the best the Black community has to offer. It's become fashionable to turn criminals into heroes overnight.

NARRATOR: The video was viewed nearly 100 million times. Two days later, President Trump retweeted a clip of Owens criticizing Floyd's portrayal as a martyr.

Decades earlier, Malcolm X had warned about how Black Americans were discouraged from learning about their history.

MALCOLM X (1962): Twenty million Black people who don't even know the history of their ancestors. Why? Because he took it away from them. And if they're trying to tell them how thoroughly and completely they've been robbed, he says you're teaching hate.

NARRATOR: In 2019, Owens testified before the House Judiciary Committee, calling the Southern strategy a myth. Historians challenged her claim, and PolitiFact rated it false.

Malcolm X, however, rejected both major political parties.

MALCOLM X (1964): I'm one of the 22 million Black victims of the Democrats. One of the 22 million Black victims of the Republicans and one of the 22 million Black victims of Americanism.

And when I speak, I don't speak as a Democrat or a Republican. I speak as a victim of America's so-called democracy. You and I have never seen democracy. All we've seen is hypocrisy.

NARRATOR: That November, Owens told Fox News host Laura Ingraham, "I do not remember when I was growing up having all of these race issues."

But the Connecticut NAACP president who had helped her family after she received racist threats as a teenager said they were saddened and disappointed in her.

At her Blexit rally in Los Angeles in January 2019, Owens explained her message.

CANDACE OWENS: This is our official declaration of independence from the left. We are separating ourselves from the victim narrative. We've earned a piece of the American dream. We don't have to cry anymore. We don't have to be upset. We don't have to throw a pity party for ourselves.

NARRATOR: But Malcolm X had described a very different experience of America.

MALCOLM X: We don't see any American dream. We've experienced only the American nightmare.

NARRATOR: And Malcolm had another warning. In November 1963, speaking about the March on Washington, he argued that its original message had been taken over and weakened.

MALCOLM X: They joined it. They didn't integrate it, they infiltrated it. They took it over. And as they took it over, it lost its militancy. They ceased to be angry. They ceased to be hot. They ceased to be uncompromising. It became a picnic, a circus.

NARRATOR: A picnic. A circus. Hold on to that word.

text:
I was an aircraft maintenance officer back in the mid-1980s to early-1990s. 

I blame Gen. Merrill “Tony” McPeak. 

As Chief of Staff (1990–1994) he instituted the Objective Wing reorganization effectively rolling back the reforms led by Gen. Wilbur L. “Bill” Creech as Commander of Tactical Air Command (1978–1984).

Creech spearheaded the Combat Oriented Maintenance Organization (COMO), formalized in TAC Regulation 66-5 around 1978–1979. 

Under COMO, dedicated AMUs were teamed with specific flying squadrons for identity, scheduling, and sortie production, but remained organizationally under Aircraft Generation Squadrons within the DCM complex. 

This made the maintenance organizations structural peers of the flying squadrons/ops side, with both reporting up to the wing commander. It emphasized balancing “fly and fight” with professional “fix” expertise, decentralization of authority where appropriate, and peacetime organization that mirrored wartime needs. 

With some of the MC rates I’ve been hearing, it sounds like the USAF has regressed back to the sorry state we were in after the Vietnam War. Note what Gen. Creech’s changes achieved - and how quickly:

Results were dramatic: mission-capable rates for tactical fighters rose substantially (e.g., from the mid-50s percent range toward the mid-to-high 80s), sortie production increased markedly (often cited in the range of double-digit annual gains and large cumulative improvements by the early 1980s), accident rates fell, and pilot flying hours improved.

I separated from the USAF when Gen McPeak was making his changes (including those goofy uniform changes). 

Apparently CSAF Gen. Michael Ryan began rolling back some of McPeak’s changes starting in late 1999. 

Then CSAF Gen. T. Michael Moseley tried a partial rollback to McPeak’s nonsense in the 2007-2008 time frame but then he and the Secretary of the Air Force were forced to resign in mid-2008 over nuclear stewardship issues, and the full realignment did not take hold service-wide.

The post 2000s structure sounds pretty similar to what I was used to back in the mid 1980s to early 1990s but our interactions with the Air Force Supply System were similar to what this article describes how the Navy’s aircraft maintenance and supply systems are doing things. 

Ping ponging back and forth has been unwise. 

In particular, the changes introduced by McPeak were exacerbated by a RIF occurring at the same time his changes were rolling in. The USAF was targeting a reduction of 7,500 officers but young pilots in tankers, airlift, and bombers were excluded from both the RIF and the from the corresponding separation incentives that were being offered to meet reduction targets. 

Many of these “banked” pilots ended up filling those aircraft maintenance seats newly located back under the flying squadrons in lieu of keeping experienced aircraft maintenance officers in those roles. I often wonder how many we lost to that reduction effort. I was one of them. 

All that said, I am quite curious why the Air Force is struggling so much now. Did our supply system suffer the same king of ping pong changes the aircraft maintenance community was put through?

Did the Air Force accelerate outsourcing more of the aircraft maintenance and supply system roles to civilian control? That was another big change that was happening around the early 90s.

Alphabet’s stake in Anthropic expands

The value of Alphabet’s stake in the artificial intelligence start-up Anthropic has soared to around $US124 billion ($178 billion), making it one of the most lucrative bets in the company’s history.The Google parent disclosed in a filing on Thursday (Friday AEST) that the value of its investments in unidentified private companies totalled roughly $US124.3 billion as of June 30. The filing noted that this value is “primarily” driven by one investment, which is a reference to Alphabet’s stake in Anthropic, according to a person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be identified because the information is not public. The company said it recorded about $US77 billion in unrealised gains from its private investments in the second quarter, without providing further details in the filing. Google has emerged as one of Anthropic’s biggest backers over the past several years. The technology giant first invested $US3 billion in the start-up starting in 2023. Earlier this year, it agreed to invest as much as $US40 billion more, consisting of $US10 billion upfront and a potential $US30 billion in additional funding tied to operational and financial milestones through 2030.Alphabet’s filing on Thursday showed the remaining commitment has fallen to $US20 billion as of June 30 from $US30 billion at the end of the first quarter, suggesting that Google invested another $US10 billion in the start-up last quarter. Rio Tinto dodges merger bullet

Rio Tinto has dodged two 'bullets' due to Glencore's rejection of a merger proposal: a possible BHP takeover bid and a dangerous acquisition. BHP looked closely at whether to bid for Rio Tinto if the latter announced a merger with Glencore. The two companies would make excellent merger partners; amongst others things, their staff and senior people have similar cultures, they are co-operating on future Australian iron ore projects and they are copper joint venture partners in Chile and the US. Meanwhile, there are significance cultural differences between Rio Tinto and Glencore; there is little doubt that Rio Tinto's CEO Simon Trott would have had doubts about a merger once he understood these cultural differences. (RMS)

News/Snapshot

Australian Mining

Global Commodity Rankings

Australia holds some of the world's largest reserves and is a leading producer of several key minerals.

#1 Producer: Iron Ore, Bauxite, Lithium, Rutile, and Zircon.

#1 Reserves: Iron Ore, Gold, Lead, Nickel, Rutile, Uranium, and Zinc.

#2 Producer: Gold, Alumina, and Manganese.

Key Mining Hubs & Major Projects

Western Australia: The nation's "engine room," producing 98% of Australia's iron ore and 60% of its gold. Major sites include the Pilbara (iron ore) and the Super Pit in Kalgoorlie (gold).

Queensland: A global leader in metallurgical coal (Bowen Basin) and silver/lead production (Cannington mine).

South Australia: Home to Olympic Dam, which contains the world's largest single uranium deposit and significant copper and gold reserves.

Major Players

The sector is dominated by several multinational giants and significant domestic players:

BHP: Often ranked as Australia's most valuable company; major interests in iron ore, copper, and coal.

Rio Tinto: A world leader in iron ore (Pilbara) and aluminum.

Fortescue (FMG): Primarily focused on iron ore and rapidly expanding into green energy.

Hancock Prospecting: Australia's largest private mining company, led by Gina Rinehart, the nation's wealthiest person.

South32: Spun out of BHP; manages a diversified portfolio including manganese, silver, and nickel.

2026 Trends & Developments

Critical Minerals Push: The government has introduced a $23 billion package to support domestic processing and manufacturing of critical minerals to reduce global reliance on single-country supply chains.

Uranium Rally: Prices exceeding US$100/lb have sparked renewed interest in Australian prospects like the Kalkaroo project.

M&A Activity: Major merger talks continue between giants like Rio Tinto and Glencore as they seek to consolidate copper exposure for the EV market.

Workforce Challenges: The Minerals Council of Australia is currently calling for migration reforms to address a significant "skills crunch" in the sector.

Alphabet’s stake in Anthropic expands

The value of Alphabet’s stake in the artificial intelligence start-up Anthropic has soared to around $US124 billion ($178 billion), making it one of the most lucrative bets in the company’s history.The Google parent disclosed in a filing on Thursday (Friday AEST) that the value of its investments in unidentified private companies totalled roughly $US124.3 billion as of June 30. The filing noted that this value is “primarily” driven by one investment, which is a reference to Alphabet’s stake in Anthropic, according to a person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be identified because the information is not public. The company said it recorded about $US77 billion in unrealised gains from its private investments in the second quarter, without providing further details in the filing. Google has emerged as one of Anthropic’s biggest backers over the past several years. The technology giant first invested $US3 billion in the start-up starting in 2023. Earlier this year, it agreed to invest as much as $US40 billion more, consisting of $US10 billion upfront and a potential $US30 billion in additional funding tied to operational and financial milestones through 2030.Alphabet’s filing on Thursday showed the remaining commitment has fallen to $US20 billion as of June 30 from $US30 billion at the end of the first quarter, suggesting that Google invested another $US10 billion in the start-up last quarter. Rio Tinto dodges merger bullet

Rio Tinto has dodged two 'bullets' due to Glencore's rejection of a merger proposal: a possible BHP takeover bid and a dangerous acquisition. BHP looked closely at whether to bid for Rio Tinto if the latter announced a merger with Glencore. The two companies would make excellent merger partners; amongst others things, their staff and senior people have similar cultures, they are co-operating on future Australian iron ore projects and they are copper joint venture partners in Chile and the US. Meanwhile, there are significance cultural differences between Rio Tinto and Glencore; there is little doubt that Rio Tinto's CEO Simon Trott would have had doubts about a merger once he understood these cultural differences. News/Snapshot

Australian Mining

Global Commodity Rankings

Australia holds some of the world's largest reserves and is a leading producer of several key minerals.

#1 Producer: Iron Ore, Bauxite, Lithium, Rutile, and Zircon.

#1 Reserves: Iron Ore, Gold, Lead, Nickel, Rutile, Uranium, and Zinc.

#2 Producer: Gold, Alumina, and Manganese.

Key Mining Hubs & Major Projects

Western Australia: The nation's "engine room," producing 98% of Australia's iron ore and 60% of its gold. Major sites include the Pilbara (iron ore) and the Super Pit in Kalgoorlie (gold).

Queensland: A global leader in metallurgical coal (Bowen Basin) and silver/lead production (Cannington mine).

South Australia: Home to Olympic Dam, which contains the world's largest single uranium deposit and significant copper and gold reserves.

Major Players

The sector is dominated by several multinational giants and significant domestic players:

BHP: Often ranked as Australia's most valuable company; major interests in iron ore, copper, and coal.

Rio Tinto: A world leader in iron ore (Pilbara) and aluminum.

Fortescue (FMG): Primarily focused on iron ore and rapidly expanding into green energy.

Hancock Prospecting: Australia's largest private mining company, led by Gina Rinehart, the nation's wealthiest person.

South32: Spun out of BHP; manages a diversified portfolio including manganese, silver, and nickel.

2026 Trends & Developments

Critical Minerals Push: The government has introduced a $23 billion package to support domestic processing and manufacturing of critical minerals to reduce global reliance on single-country supply chains.

Uranium Rally: Prices exceeding US$100/lb have sparked renewed interest in Australian prospects like the Kalkaroo project.

M&A Activity: Major merger talks continue between giants like Rio Tinto and Glencore as they seek to consolidate copper exposure for the EV market.

Workforce Challenges: The Minerals Council of Australia is currently calling for migration reforms to address a significant "skills crunch" in the sector.

text:
Less than a day after Jensen Huang stepped down, Elon Musk has publicly reached out to him three times.
 
Let’s lay out the facts first.
 
1. On November 8, Sequoia Capital partner Maguire posted that Jensen Huang is one of the greatest entrepreneurs of his generation and irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership. Musk retweeted with just two words: I agree.
2. Investor Gavin Baker argued that Jensen Huang’s fate should wait for an investigation and a shareholder vote. Musk replied: Indeed.
3. Today, finance account ZeroHedge called out directly: Elon, hire Jensen. Musk responded personally: That would be an honour.
4. Musk happens to have a massive project in need of a leader: Terafab, the chip factory jointly built by Tesla and SpaceX. Its first phase, valued at $16.8 billion, is already under construction in Texas. On November 6, investor Baron estimated in a face-to-face conversation that the total cost could hit $1 trillion, and Musk largely agreed. The target is 1 million wafers per month by 2032.
5. NVIDIA’s resignation announcement and SEC filing this morning made no mention whatsoever of non-compete clauses, severance packages, or an advisory role.
 
With the facts on the table, let’s walk through the implications.
 
First, the role is a perfect match. What Terafab lacks is not capital, but someone who can take chips from design to mass production and command the operation. Among the handful of people worldwide qualified for this, Jensen Huang is the top candidate — he built the GPU ecosystem from the ground up. Musk’s three public replies speak for themselves; he has made his stance abundantly clear.
 
Second, and most critical: How will the two stocks react if Jensen Huang’s appointment is officially announced?
 
SpaceX (SPCX) will move first, with greater upside elasticity than Tesla. Terafab is nominally a joint venture, yet the core computing narrative belongs mainly to SpaceX. Its AI revenue hit $7.6 billion in Q3, rising more than ninefold year over year, and its orbital data centres are heavily reliant on in-house silicon. Jensen Huang coming on board would be equivalent to bringing in a chief architect for this whole vision. We are already seeing hints in today’s market: SPCX is up 2.7%, while Tesla is largely flat.
 
The magnitude of the rally hinges on the title: If he takes the full-time helm of Terafab, both stocks will rise, led by SPCX. If it is only an advisory role, prices will most likely spike then fade — markets are used to celebrity endorsements. NVIDIA is the mirror image. Broadcom gained 5.2% today, already pricing in the “Jensen Huang exit” scenario. If he joins a rival, that triggers a second wave of selling. NVIDIA would lose far more than an executive; it would lose customer confidence in its product roadmap.
 
Now for the caveats. Terafab’s first test chips are not expected until mid-2027, with mass production even further out. Any rally on an announcement is driven purely by expectations, which will later need to be validated by engineering milestones. Moreover, with Tesla valued at $1.5 trillion and SpaceX at $1.94 trillion, one individual can only move the share price so much. If merger talks between the two firms remain unresolved, the market may price merger dynamics first, rather than Jensen Huang’s hiring.
 
So here is the sequence to watch: First, whether NVIDIA’s board enforces a non-compete agreement. Second, what title Musk offers him. Third, only then, the stock reaction. This question cannot be avoided on the earnings call on the 17th.

text:
e. Call & Letter

Dictating Deal Terms – Pricing, Duration & Structure:

To give an idea of how favorable the multi-year demand backdrop currently is, deal size and duration both continued to rise despite NBIS introducing new ways to add short-term capacity. They’re dictating terms and notching ongoing megawatt pricing power. For context, last quarter, NBIS disclosed pricing per megawatt jumped from a little over $10M at the time of the spin-off to $22.5M on new deals. This quarter, that again ticked higher to $25M+.

On one end, as briefly mentioned, NBIS is introducing various market models to offer short-term compute. This helps them take full advantage of the vast supply/demand mismatch, often fetching over $40M per megawatt for these more temporary deals. They’re now letting customers bid for blocks of guaranteed capacity and renting out idle chips at spot rates without large commitments or long-term lock-ins. NBIS has enticing flexibility to make this capacity available when it’s able to, and quickly pull it when reserved demand requires them to do so.

• These two methods complement 3-6 month cluster commitment offerings.

Along with on-demand and short-term clusters, these give customers more ways in the door and give Nebius a live read on demand. Early results are encouraging. Reserve auctions closed 15%+ above the minimum price. Both winners were brand-new customers, and the first has already grown its contract value 10x.

• They see many short-term and spot-capacity users graduate into 1-3 year contracts, which is their bread and butter.
• They’re also seeing plenty of pay-per-token customers on shared servers moving up to reserve larger dedicated compute clusters.
• Remember when leadership told us last quarter that it was holding back capacity to fetch better terms? It worked. In early September, it released a new batch of capacity with higher prices, longer commitments and more cash required upfront.
• Longer term, the plan is to run all of this through a single trading platform that automatically toggles pricing and terms for all customers.

Nebius is also enjoying stronger 5-year contract demand for Nebius AI Cloud (not just dedicated deals with mega-caps). These deals are long, large and typically prepaid all at once. Customers lock in today’s rates during a time when GPU prices continue to soar. Nebius gets better visibility and a sub-2-year payback period.

Capacity – Footprint Updates:

Q3 was Nebius’s biggest quarter ever for adding active capacity. Four new sites across the U.S. and Europe started producing revenue, and New Jersey got more tranches in Q3 and into November. More is coming in Q4, including new colocation phases in the U.S., Europe and Israel. It’s at 4+ GW of contracted power today and still expects 5 GW by year-end. As a reminder, contracted power is not operating capacity. It’s secured access to electricity. The buildings, cooling, networking and chips still have to show up before a customer can use any of it.

• Missouri, 2 Finland sites and Alabama are expected to add operational capacity in 2027. These will ramp to 3+ GW by sometime in 2030. Pennsylvania is also under construction and should begin contributing after that.

Capacity – Geographic Expansion:

In terms of geographic footprint expansion, Asia-Pacific is going well about 6 months after launching. Customer contracts have been signed across Korea, Japan, India, Australia and Singapore and they’ve hired managers in Korea and Japan to spur more growth. Its first two facilities in the region will be colocation projects in India. Both are expected to start operating in 2027, which is when regional revenue should start to scale.

Moving into more parts of the globe is vital for NBIS’s value proposition. On one hand, governments want to run their AI infrastructure locally to help with tight data controls and easier security. NBIS can provide that, with localized go-to-market across Europe (and now APAC) that lawmakers and core suppliers like Nvidia find valuable. Speaking of Nvidia, they also get to use NBIS to cut through project red tape and expedite regulatory procedures with their more local knowledge. Every country handles data residency, chip export rules and permitting differently. It’s annoying, hectic and inconsistent. Nvidia obviously wants its chips everywhere, and it’s much easier to get there through local, independent cloud partners that already have the sites, power and approvals than to do it alone. That’s part of why Nvidia invests in companies like Nebius and hands them new hardware early. NBIS is happy to be the soldier, considering how much money they expect to make from these AI factories.

• Palantir naming it a preferred cloud partner for its sovereign AI customers is more good evidence. Palantir will pair its Foundry platform with Token Factory and open models to serve those customers.

Capacity – Mix Shift to Owned:

So demand is insatiable, pricing is rising… and Nebius still cut its revenue guide. Why? The capacity didn’t arrive on time. A number of colocation sites are now slated for delivery in the first half of 2027. According to leadership, this is purely timing-related. Nothing was canceled. They proactively communicated this with customers and expect the delays to be short-lived. In August, DataOne, a key New Jersey facility partner, told NBIS the original generator plan wouldn’t work, forcing a switch to cleaner, behind-the-meter Bloom Energy fuel cells. DataOne’s temporary generators were supposed to bridge the gap while Bloom ramped, but it wound them down faster than expected. That gap caused the delay. Again… high degree of execution risk here.

• NBIS plans to use Bloom at its other sites too.

All of this is even more strongly motivating NBIS to prioritize owned facilities over colocations. This is how they pocket a larger piece of the profit pie. This is how they control delivery schedules, with all owned NBIS facilities currently on time. This format also grants more flexibility to scale up capacity or slow down expansion if the backdrop softens for whatever reason. It does mean a lot more CapEx to get projects online, but once that’s incurred, they get all of these benefits in addition to higher-margin business. Nebius also designs its own racks and storage, and leadership expects those costs to keep falling as more capacity comes from owned sites. As seen below, NBIS plans to rapidly shift to this format going forward, and it already has “all power and components secured” for its 2027 demand plan. And yes… that includes Nvidia’s next-gen hardware. Supply of Vera CPUs, Vera Rubin GPUs and Groq chips is confirmed for 2027, with testing and benchmarking now done.

More on Strong Customers:

Nebius has $40B+ in committed revenue from investment-grade customers, led by Microsoft and Meta. Microsoft signed a contract worth $17.4B to $19.4B in September 2025. Meta signed for $3B that November and added up to $27B more this March ($12B committed, plus up to $15B for capacity Nebius doesn’t sell to others first).

Why are these backstops so much more comforting than one from OpenAI or Anthropic? Because of who’s writing the check. Microsoft and Meta are two of the most profitable companies on the planet, with pristine credit ratings. The AI labs are growing at an incredible pace, but they’re still far more dependent on external capital to honor multi-year compute contracts. If funding markets tighten, that’s a problem for whoever built capacity for them. Lenders see the difference too. It’s why Nebius can borrow against these contracts at SOFR + 2.50%. That’s exactly what it did in July with a $775M facility, which is the first under what leadership calls a “repeatable framework.” Other hyperscaler-backed GPU loans price similarly (SOFR + 2.25% for both CoreWeave’s Meta-backed facility and IREN’s Microsoft-backed one), while CoreWeave’s 2026 loans backed by AI labs and smaller customers priced at SOFR + 4.50% to 5.50%. At the same time, this also invites concentration risk. Two customers make up most of the backlog. And as our Amazon review covered, hyperscalers earn much lower margins renting from neoclouds than using their own sites. They’re here because they’re short on capacity. When that shortage ends, renewals are no guarantee. The good news? These are 5-year contracts and new TCV is increasingly coming from AI natives and enterprise platforms like Databricks. The base is diversifying.

More on Depreciation & Payback Period:

Ignoring prepayments and considering all costs, expected payback on comparable 1-3 year deals shortened from 22 months to 19 months Q/Q. That’s so important. GPUs cost a fortune and depreciate far more quickly than other assets like the data center buildings. These being useful for 60 months means NBIS has 41 months of profits to collect. That 41 months is worth north of $85M of revenue per megawatt at current contract pricing… with most of that revenue flowing down to net income. Anything this company can do to shrink payback periods by even a single month is worth roughly $2M in added profit per megawatt, and stretching useful lives has the same impact.

In fairness, there’s a counterargument. Old chips are holding value because compute is scarce. If supply catches up with demand, the oldest and least power-efficient chips lose pricing power first. And if power becomes the bottleneck, newer chips that produce more tokens per watt can justify swapping old ones out early. I wouldn’t pencil in 7 or 8 years. But 5 looks safe.

Platform Innovation – Inference (Token Factory), Post-Training & Agent Execution:

As mentioned, run rate here is approaching multi-hundred-million-dollar levels while contract value rose 17x Q/Q with compelling profitability. Margins are notably favorable compared to other inference providers due to NBIS's direct chip ownership. To keep nurturing the momentum, it purchased EigenAI to increase tokens-per-chip throughput while also buying Inferize last month to fix the “cold start” problem (slow model loading when demand spikes). That will allow chip utilization rates to rise further and NBIS performance dynamics to improve too.

• Kimi K3, Meta Muse Spark Open and others were available the day they came out.
• Artificial Analysis benchmarks put Token Factory in the top tier for performance, latency and quality on the latest DeepSeek, Kimi and GLM models.
• Per leadership, open-source model adoption has accelerated in recent months. As an agnostic place to run any model, they prefer fragmentation and the complexity that coincides with it. They can provide more value in this environment.
• For context, OpenRouter said open-weight models made up 72% of its weekly token volume in September. It first crossed 50% in February.

Next is post-training. Some quick reminders. Training is building a model from scratch. Inference is using that model to conduct work. Post-training is ongoing upgrades to existing models to make them better. Examples include fine-tuning it on a company’s own data, and teaching it through trial and error. To avoid model lock-in, customers can easily transfer that progress to a different model if they find a cheaper option. And importantly, on NBIS, customers can do all of this while running their inference engines and accessing a full suite of software in one single place. It’s a routine sale too, as the infrastructure (training clusters and Token Factory) is already there. Applied Compute and Cursive both post-trained custom models on Nebius AI Cloud, then picked Token Factory for inference.

Finally, like we’ve talked about in other AI infrastructure reviews, agent execution requires a lot of CPU-based compute too. GPUs are incredibly powerful, but they need clear instruction and orchestration, and that’s where CPUs come into play. So Nebius is adding CPU capacity next to its GPUs, including those early Vera CPU deployments. CPU-rich work generally means higher margins too, and it opens up a wide array of potential enterprise agent services to enrich margins and returns. This is why Tavily is so important. Giving agents the search tools needed to fetch timely information and insight is a big part of ensuring outputs are high-quality just like CPU-based presence is.

More Notes:

• Regulation: Nebius doesn’t expect midterms to affect its greenfield or colocation sites, Pennsylvania included. It has sites live or under construction in roughly half a dozen states (Texas isn’t one). And per leadership, data center pushback is coming from both sides of the aisle… not just one party.
• Avride (autonomous vehicles): Avride now has 250 vehicles on the road and wants 350 by the end of the year. It has logged more than 2M autonomous miles and over 100K robotaxi trips. Its Dallas coverage area is 3x larger, and fully driverless service should start by June 2027. On the delivery side, its robots now make more than 6,500 deliveries per day, over 3x more than a year ago.
• Toloka (AI data; equity stake): Revenue doubled Q/Q and it launched a post-training offering.
• ClickHouse (database; equity stake): No update beyond its January raise at a roughly $15B valuation.

James Talarico, the new senator-elect from Texas, is already reaching out and saying he is willing to work with Trump on getting things done, even after all the back-and-forth during the campaign. He talked about helping build something like an LBJ-style legacy if both sides can actually move legislation, which is a pretty direct offer given how sharp the attacks were a few months ago. Talarico has his own list of priorities and knows he will need the White House on board for any of them to go anywhere, so the olive branch makes sense from his side.

I’ve watched enough of these post-election shifts to know that the tone can change once someone has the seat. Trump spent a lot of time going after him by name, yet here is the same person saying the insults can be set aside if there is a chance to pass bills. Whether that holds up once the actual votes start or turns into the usual gridlock is another question. A lot of people will be looking to see if any of this cooperation actually happens or if both sides fall back into the familiar pattern once the cameras move on.

text:
SmartApeSG ClickFix traffic from Nov 12, 2026 walks victims through a fake CAPTCHA, an HTA download, and a roughly 74 MB zip that side-loads a DLL to install CNCmachineRMS RAT. LevelBlue Spider Labs tracks the same chain as BabaDeda.

- The lure: SmartApeSG traffic from cashewminaret[.]org serves a fake CAPTCHA/verification page. The requests are hxxps://cashewminaret[.]org/identity/reset-layout.js, hxxps://cashewminaret[.]org/identity/middleware-build?oSGDPy5P and hxxps://cashewminaret[.]org/identity/gateway-dom.js?18e76625db12fb1d. The page injects ClickFix text that the victim is told to paste into a Windows Run window. The user launches the first stage themselves, so there is no exploit and no attachment to catch.

- Stage 1: the pasted command pulls an HTML-text file from hxxps://orchardandbarite[.]com/spa (40,301 bytes, SHA-256 2eb387df728fc6f5dd2dcffaf1883cbf8c5e0c489f6cb38021d67f856ee669d0). It lands as C:\Users\[username]\AppData\Local\NHEWS.hta. The report describes it as an HTA that retrieves and installs the zip archive for the RAT.

- Stage 2: the HTA fetches hxxps://orchardandbarite[.]com/gross, a zip of 73,912,559 bytes (SHA-256 101e9ac653ccd341e36fae84a5c6920dff47a41822e87db4c72e36da4830d707). It is saved as C:\Users\[username]\AppData\Local\Microsoft\Windows\packwindata\packwindata.pdf. That is a zip archive with a .pdf extension, so an extension/content mismatch is a quick triage cue. The package is built for DLL side-loading of CNCmachineRMS RAT.

- Post-infection: the infected host talks to 87.199.205[.]61 on port 443. The report labels the traffic as encoded C2 for CNCmachineRMS RAT over TCP, not as plain web traffic. The report's references also point to LevelBlue's write-up of CNCmachineRMS as an undocumented RAT at the end of a BabaDeda chain, plus a Netresec post on the CNCMachineRMS C2 protocol.

- Evidence on offer: the report publishes an IOC text file, a full pcap of the infection (about 103 MB) and the malware files (about 74 MB). The zips are password-protected, and the site has a new password scheme explained on its about page. The pcap is useful for building network detections against the encoded C2 and the staged downloads.

Practitioner takeaway: if a host touched the fake CAPTCHA infrastructure, check C:\Users\[username]\AppData\Local for NHEWS.hta and the Microsoft\Windows\packwindata folder for a large file named packwindata.pdf that is really a zip. Preserve both before cleanup, and review what executed alongside them to find the side-loaded DLL host. On the network side, hunt for connections to orchardandbarite[.]com, cashewminaret[.]org and 87.199.205[.]61:443, then scope the user session that pasted the command into Run. IOCs are in the report's text file, and the pcap and sample zips are there for detection testing.

🚨 JMU CLAIMS CONFERENCE MOVE REACHED 2.31 BILLION PEOPLE — NEARLY 30% OF PLANET EARTH

Apparently, James Madison University has conquered the world. Nobody bothered to tell the rest of us.

During Thursday’s Board of Visitors athletics committee meeting, JMU Athletic Director Matt Roan reportedly claimed the announcement of the Dukes’ move to the American Conference generated an audience of 2.31 BILLION people in its first week, with an estimated media advertising value of $21.4 million.

That’s roughly one out of every 3.5 human beings on Earth.

▪️ CONFERENCE MOVE: JMU announced October 12 that it will leave the Sun Belt for the American Conference no later than July 1, 2028.

▪️ 17 SPORTS: All but field hockey will compete in the American.

▪️ FINANCING: JMU says private donors and corporate partners will cover conference exit and entry fees, without tuition or state taxpayer funding.

▪️ THE BIG QUESTION: Does 2.31 billion represent actual unique individuals, cumulative media impressions or potential audience exposure?

Those are dramatically different measurements.

The $21.4 million figure is also an estimated advertising equivalent, not revenue deposited into JMU’s bank account.

The conference move offers opportunities for increased television exposure, higher distributions and greater visibility.

But claiming an audience approaching one-third of humanity deserves an explanation of the methodology.

JMU’s next challenge may be considerably more difficult than reaching 2.31 billion people: convincing its own students to stay until the fourth quarter of football games.

text:
AT 16, BRIAN BANKS WAS ONE OF AMERICA’S MOST PROMISING FOOTBALL PLAYERS. ONE FALSE ACCUSATION DESTROYED EVERYTHING.

He was a star high school linebacker with a full scholarship offer from USC. Head coach Pete Carroll had personally called to recruit him.

His future looked almost guaranteed.

Then one afternoon, everything changed.

Brian kissed a female classmate at school. What he believed was a consensual encounter turned into an accusation of rape and kidnapping.

She claimed he had dragged her into a stairwell.

He was arrested.

The DNA evidence didn’t support her story, but that wasn’t enough to save him.

His mother sold their house and car to afford his legal defense. Brian couldn’t make bail and spent an entire year behind bars awaiting trial.

At just 17, his lawyer gave him two options: accept a plea deal or risk spending 41 years in prison.

Terrified of losing the rest of his life, he pleaded no contest.

The price?

Five years in prison and another five on parole.

He became a registered sex offender, wore a GPS ankle monitor, couldn’t visit schools or parks, and struggled to find anyone willing to employ him.

Meanwhile, the girl and her mother sued the school district, claiming it had failed to protect her.

They received $1.5 million.

Then, in 2011, something unbelievable happened.

Brian received a Facebook friend request.

It was the same girl who had accused him.

She wanted to reconnect and supposedly leave the past behind.

But Brian wasn’t interested in pretending nothing had happened.

He contacted a private investigator. Together, they arranged a meeting and secretly recorded the conversation.

She showed up.

And on camera, she admitted the truth.

Brian had never raped or kidnapped her.

But even after admitting she had lied, she refused to tell prosecutors because doing so would mean returning the settlement money.

In May 2012, after a decade of being treated like a criminal, Brian Banks was finally exonerated.

The court hearing took less than a minute.

Ten years of his life had been stolen. His football career, freedom, reputation, and teenage years were gone.

Then his phone rang.

“Brian, I’m looking for a linebacker. You know where I can find one?”

It was Pete Carroll.

The same coach who had recruited him a decade earlier.

At 27, Brian finally got his NFL opportunity, signing with the Atlanta Falcons.

The girl was eventually ordered to repay $2.6 million.

But here’s the question nobody should ignore:

If someone knowingly destroys an innocent person’s life with a lie, should getting caught mean they simply return the money and move on? https://t.co/4f3iwoX0Wu
