Part one.
The Origins of the US Proxy War in Ukraine
The war in Ukraine is usually presented in the West as a story of Russian aggression. This piece argues the opposite. It argues that the war was provoked by the United States, that Russia’s security concerns were known and ignored for years, and that the consequences for Ukraine have been catastrophic. The evidence for this is not Russian propaganda. It is US government documents, the admissions of Western leaders, and the public record of what the West did and said before February 2022.
This is a long one. If you are disentlined to spend 20 minutes reading you can listen to the audio version on substack. Link in comments.
The 2014 Coup: The Pivot Point
Western media likes to say the war in Ukraine started when Russia invaded without provocation in 2022. This is the narrative the US State Department wanted editors in the legacy media to push. To some extent they succeeded. Many casual observers, particularly in Western countries, still repeat it as if it were fact.
You can pick any date in the past as a starting point for this story. People from the Russian sphere like to go back to when Ukraine was simply part of a Russian Empire. They often get bogged down on details about when Ukraine was first identified as a separate territory within Russia. That backstory is interesting, but the most useful starting point is the US-funded coup in Maidan Square in 2014.
This was not a spontaneous revolution of the Ukrainian people demanding freedom and democracy. It was a CIA-orchestrated regime change operation, bankrolled and guided by Washington. It was an affront against democracy, and it was a tragedy for the people of Ukraine.
Viktor Yanukovych was elected to represent a Ukrainian population that largely wished to remain neutral, or at least aligned with both Russia and the EU. His legitimate government was overthrown by force, and a pro-Western anti-Russian regime was installed by Washington.
Maidan was stage managed. The operation is now a matter of historical record. The protests were infiltrated and steered by Western-funded NGOs and CIA-linked proxies, the same apparatus that had spent years cultivating a Russophobic vanguard inside Ukraine. The aim was to create a flashpoint, and they were successful.
The false flag came in February 2014. Snipers opened fire on Maidan protesters and on police. The killings were blamed on Yanukovych. They were the spark that turned a protest into an inferno. The evidence points away from the government and towards the opposition. The intercepted phone call between EU foreign policy chief Catherine Ashton and Estonian Foreign minister Urmas Paet is one among man such pieces of that evidence. Paet told Ashton that the snipers were linked to the opposition, not the government. Ashton’s response was telling. She said, and I quote, “I didn't know that. Interesting. My goodness!”
It was really interesting. but not interesting enough to bring up with her colleagues in the European Parliament days later. The sniper killings gave the coup its moral cover. They turned a trumped up political crisis into a massacre that the West could point to as justification for regime change. The elected government fell. The people of Ukraine were told they had risen up. In reality, they had been played.
The cover up was as telling as the operation itself. The new Ukrainian regime refused to allow any independent investigation into the sniper killings. The UN and the Council of Europe both called for one. It never happened. The people who might have testified were not pursued. The question of who gave the order was never answered, because the answer would have destroyed the founding myth of the post-2014 Ukrainian state. A regime that will not investigate the killings that brought it to power is a regime with something to hide.
The consequences were immediate.
The people of Crimea understood exactly what had happened in Kiev. They voted overwhelmingly to rejoin Russia in March 2014. They had no intention of living under a government installed by a foreign power. They understood the Western strategic objective to separate Russia from her warm water ports and they declined to cooperate.
Then came the people of southeastern Ukraine, the Donbas regions of Donetsk and Luhansk. They refused to recognise the legitimacy of the new Kiev regime. They took up arms to defend themselves against a government they considered illegitimate and hostile to their very existence.
This is the point Western media conveniently forgets. The civil war in eastern Ukraine began in 2014, not 2022.
For eight years the people of the Donbas were shelled by the Ukrainian army. This period was made more complex by the fact that Ukrainians in Eastern Ukraine were under attack not just by normal Ukrainian soldiers but by ultra-nationalist divisions within the army of the Kiev regime. These ultra-nationalists were committed to the execution or expulsion of all things Russian from their far right version of Ukraine. For eight years the locals defended themselves against attack from Kiev and as things got worse they begged Russia for help.
It is worth being precise about what those eight years involved, because Western media has erased them. The Kiev regime passed a series of laws that discriminated against Russian speakers. The language law of 2019 made Ukrainian the sole official language. The education law of 2017 restricted the use of Russian in schools. Russian media was banned. Russian books were restricted. The people of the Donbas who all spoke exclusively Russian were told, in law, that their identity was a problem to be managed.
This is the context in which the Azov Battalion must be understood. Azov was a group of Ukrainian ultra-nationalists who remained loyal to the ideology of Nazi sympathiser Stepan Bandera. A large portion of this Battalion was made up of actual neo-Nazis with a pathological disdain for all things Russian. Azov was not the whole Ukrainian army, but it was woven through the Ukrainian army, and it was used against the people of the Donbas. That is a documented fact, not a Russian invention.
The victims of these attacks were very often civilians who happened to identify strongly with Russia and who were singled out by laws which prevented them from the natural expression of their identity.
For eight years Western media paid no attention. Acknowledging this reality would undermine the narrative of Russia’s soon-to-be “unprovoked invasion”.
The Economic Lifeline Between Russia and Ukraine Was Destroyed
The NGO roadshow was in town. The usual CIA proxies, the National Endowment for Democracy and USAID among them, were up to their usual tricks. This was clandestine interference, dressed up as civil society. It was the same apparatus that had spent years cultivating a Russophobic groundswell inside Ukraine.
They attempted to export the extremist ideas of the Bandera movement into the psyche of regular working Ukrainians across the whole region. They had some success in western Ukraine, but the further east you went, Ukrainians were less susceptible to this ultra-nationalist Russophobic narrative.
The US, cloaked in promises of freedom and EU integration, yanked Ukraine out of the Russian orbit. It dangled aid and NATO dreams that never materialised into real prosperity.
Instead, the pivot west gutted Ukraine’s economy. Trade with Russia collapsed. Energy costs soared. Ukrainian industry, unable to compete in European markets and cut off from Russian ones, withered.
Ukraine’s economic history is inseparable from Russia’s. For decades, even after the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, the two were bound by trade. Russia bought Ukraine’s steel, machinery and grain. Russia piped in the cheap gas that fuelled Ukraine’s industries.
This was not mere convenience. It was a lifeline. Ukrainian industry depended on Russian markets. Ukrainian homes and industry depended on cheap Russian energy. The economies were interlocked in a way that benefited both sides.
The 2014 coup was designed to sever this relationship.
The problem with the Western understanding of Ukraine is that Russian security was never taken into consideration. It was treated as something expendable. And now here we are.
The Nyet Means Nyet Memo and the Nuclear Question
Western talking heads often refer to the notion that Ukraine surrendered a great stockpile of their own nuclear weapons in order to receive security guarantees from the West against Russian militarism.
This is a fantasy cooked up by Western propagandists. The reality is that Russia was the sole legal successor to the entire Soviet nuclear program. Ukraine was merely the geographic location where those weapons happened to be stationed. Ukraine therefore never had nuclear weapons of its own. Any framing of Ukraine as a former nuclear state is a fabrication of Western propaganda.
The weapons people refer to were Soviet and operationally useless to Ukraine. The codes, the infrastructure and the technical chain all ran through Moscow.
Ukraine was brand new in 1991. The region was politically unstable. Consolidating all the Soviet nukes under Moscow was the safest path. Ukraine gave up a tenuous claim it could not exercise in exchange for security assurances from the West that would later be weaponized for offensive purposes.
This is the reality behind the famous Budapest memorandum. Yes some political assurances were made but these were not military defence guarantees.
Another great deception within the Western narrative about Ukraine is that Ukraine and their paymasters in the US were surprised when the Special Operation was launched. That they did nothing to provoke the “invasion” from Russia and that they did not see it coming.
Of course they saw it coming. They practically picked the date. In the days leading up to the launch of the Special Operation you only have to look at the number of violations committed by Ukrainian forces against targets in the Donbas. The Ukrainians committed a huge escalation in these days and it was always understood that the order to escalate was given by the US State Department. They knew what was coming because they were curating the Russian retaliation.
They always knew what was going to happen because they were always in the background pulling the strings. This was clearly illustrated by the “Nyet Means Nyet” memo, which was leaked and later published by WikiLeaks. It illustrates quite clearly that the unprovoked surprise attack narrative is a fabrication. Not only did the US State Department understand that the threat of NATO expansion was a provocation, but that threat was intended to be used to start a proxy war that would become a new Afghanistan for the Russians.
The US State Department was informed explicitly that any movement toward Ukraine joining NATO would result in wider military escalation with Russia. This was not the opinion of knuckle-draggers in the Kremlin. This was the explicit assessment stated in a memo to Condoleezza Rice by former Russian ambassador and former CIA director William Burns in February 2008.
The memo warned that Ukraine and Georgia’s NATO aspirations not only touch a raw nerve in Russia, they engender serious concerns about the consequences for stability in the region.
Burns went further. He predicted that the strong divisions in Ukraine over NATO membership could lead to a major split, involving violence or at worst civil war. That would force Russia to intervene.
The State Department knew that playing along with the notion that Ukraine could join NATO would result in armed conflict with Russia. They chose to do that anyway.
This is beyond the sort of accidental provocation that many people are now willing to accept. The memo exposes a US policy decision which was intended to start a war with Russia. The US ambassador to Russia told them explicitly that this is what would happen. He is clearly a guy whose analysis they trusted or they would not have later put him in charge of CIA.
The US State Department can start a war with whomever it wants. That is, after all, what they do. But the rest of the world is under no obligation to accept the version of history that was written by US propagandists. We are free to look at exactly what happened and write history from the facts.
It is worth pausing on how little the US gained from this war. Russia is not weaker. It has successfully pivoted to Asia. It has held its warm water ports and its natural resources. The Russian economy trades with everyone outside the Western sphere. US energy companies and arms manufactures however, have gained a captive market for their energy and weapons. That is not an accident. That is the business model.
The Sabotage of Peace
We now understand that the Minsk agreements were never taken seriously by Western leaders. Angela Merkel revealed that Ukraine was advised to comply with the Minsk agreements only as a performative measure. It was designed to give Ukraine time to engage in a military build-up that would allow them to eventually fight the Russians. This bad faith agreement by Ukraine, orchestrated by the US, was not understood as such by Russian diplomats at the time.
Russian diplomats believed that they had made agreements which would protect the people of Eastern Ukraine from Russophobic laws being imposed by Kiev. Minsk was supposed to stop the shelling by Kiev of the breakaway regions. They were deceived.
Later, in April 2022, only weeks into the Special Operation, talks in Istanbul offered another lifeline for the Kiev regime to avoid the deepening war. They could choose neutrality. They could choose a ceasefire. They had a chance to stop the carnage. A deal was on the table which was agreeable to all parties.
But the US, drunk on its own arrogance, sabotaged the peace.
Boris Johnson’s visit to Kiev carried a message from Washington. He pushed Zelensky into an unnecessary prolonged war.
The former press secretary to Zelensky, Yulia Mendel, later confirmed that Johnson intervened and influenced Zelensky, saying he could become a hero and could continue this war.
David Arakhamia, head of Zelensky’s parliamentary faction, stated publicly that Johnson told the Ukrainian delegation, we won’t sign anything with them at all. He suggested they just fight.
This was exploitation by the West. It was a cynical ploy to extend US dominance using Ukrainians as pawns who would pay the price in blood.
The US, and to a large extent the UK, were the ones with the master plan to get Ukrainian soldiers to fight an unnecessary war against Russia. The aim was to weaken Russia to the point where the West could get access to and control of Russia’s natural resources.
The West was prepared to finance this proxy war against Russia because the prize of Russian natural resources was so great. Zbigniew Brzezinski had set out this logic decades earlier, and we will return to him at the end.
Whether the money to fight against Russia arrived as grants, aid packages, military assistance or loans, it all served the same function. It finances a US proxy war against Russia.
By mid-2026, Western countries led by the United States and the European Union had committed well over 400 billion dollars in military, financial and humanitarian support to Ukraine. The EU alone had made available over 226 billion dollars, with 35 per cent structured as highly concessional loans rather than grants.
The distinction between a grant and a loan is a bookkeeping exercise, not a moral one. Ukraine is left holding a debt it will never repay, while the war machine keeps running.
Every life lost since April 2022 is a monument to the betrayal of the Ukrainian people by Western power.
Back then Ukraine still held most of its land. Its people were not starving. Its power grid was not a Russian punching bag. A deal could have locked in those material conditions in 2022. But Zelensky chose to continue the US proxy war. Now Ukraine is so much worse off.
The human cost is staggering by any measure. Approximately one million Ukrainian military casualties, dead or severely wounded. Approximately two million Ukrainian conscription evaders are in hiding, men who have vanished out of sight from Ukrainian press gangs out of desperate self-preservation. And approximately eight million Ukrainians are living abroad, with survey data showing only a fraction have plans to return.
These are not Russian figures. They are the admissions of Ukrainian officials themselves. The conscription evader figure comes from Ukraine’s own defence ministry. The refugee figure comes from the UN and from Ukraine’s own foreign ministry. If you count everyone who has been killed, wounded, driven into hiding or scattered across foreign countries with no intention of coming back, the true casualty figure for Ukraine is a number Western propaganda will never utter.
The Question of Sovereignty in the East
The majority of people living in the south eastern part of Ukraine wanted nothing to do with the Ukrainian regime that took control in Kiev after the US-backed coup in 2014.
Western media has never admitted this, because Western media wants to pretend that Ukraine is a monolith. From 2014 onwards, Ukraine was presented in the Western press as a single nation resisting Russian aggression. One people. One language. One destiny. This was ridiculously reductive not to mention deliberately deceptive. It erased the millions of Ukrainians who spoke Russian as their first language. It erased the millions who had voted for Yanukovych. It erased the millions who had no desire to join NATO, no desire to sever their economic ties with Russia, and no desire to live in a country whose founding myth required them to hate their closest neighbours.
The reality was always more complicated. Ukraine was a country with deep regional differences, different histories, different languages, and different loyalties. The Western media did not report this reality. It replaced it with a cartoon version of Ukraine that served the interests of the US State Department.
And the enforcement mechanism was brutal. Any commentator operating in the West who made reference to the reality on the ground was immediately jumped on and accused of being a Putin apologist. It did not matter whether they were reporting documented facts or historical record. The accusation alone was enough. This had a chilling effect. It meant that reporting history accurately, or describing events as they actually were, was effectively forbidden. The penalty for accuracy was excommunication from respectable discourse.
That is a bizarre state of affairs. A media system that claims to be free had constructed a taboo around the truth. McCarthyite style lists of journalists who refused to comply were made. The very thing journalism is supposed to do, which is to describe reality as it is rather than as power wishes it to be, had become a punishable offence. The result was not a free press. It was a press that had been captured, and a public that had been lied to.
If the people from separatist regions wanted to be part of Ukraine, they would have joined up with the Ukrainian army to help fight against the Russian invasion. They did the opposite.
They were already fighting a civil war against the Ukrainian army from 2014 right up until the point where they begged Russian forces to enter their territory. They needed help to defend their people against intensive Ukrainian shelling.
This is a reality that Western media has never recognised. Western media only started paying attention when the “unprovoked invasion” narrative was activated.
All those people from places liberated by Russian forces since, including the DPR and LPR, Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro and Kharkiv, are loyal to Russia. When peace eventually breaks out, the lines are already drawn. Ukraine is already partitioned along the correct lines.
That territory is lost partly because the people from there have a different identity. But most especially it is lost because of the cruel Western-funded Russophobic war that has been waged there since 2014.
The Realpolitik Reality and the Nuclear Question
Before examining the realpolitik, it is worth understanding what Russia wanted and what it lost.
Since Peter the Great founded Saint Petersburg as a window on Europe, the Russian people have seen themselves as European. This was not a passing fashion. It was a centuries-long orientation. Russian elites read French and German. Russian science, music and literature were built in conversation with Europe. Russian trade flowed westward far more than it ever flowed east. When the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, the Russian people believed their future was to be a great trading partner within Europe. Russia would provide the energy. Western Europe would provide the industrial and engineering expertise. It was a partnership that could have lasted centuries.
That partnership was rejected. Over the last several years, and especially since 2014, Europe has made clear that it does not want Russia as a partner. The rejection was not subtle. It was delivered through sanctions, through NATO expansion, through the language of containment and the language of contempt. The Russian people understood it. They understood that the Europe they had imagined, the Europe they had oriented themselves towards for centuries, was rejecting them.
Russians understand history. They know about the clandestine interference by US intelligence across Europe since the end of the Second World War. They understand that the Europeans have always had the US and the UK pouring poison in their ears. The effect on the Russian psyche in the last years has been profound. Russia no longer looks towards Europe. It feels rejected and undermined. The bond that Russians believed they had with Europe is severed.
This matters for the realpolitik because it changes what Russia wants. Russia has no interest in Europe from a military perspective. Europe has nothing that Russia needs. Europe has no natural resources worth taking. Russia does not require new territory. It has some of the largest territory on the planet. Its interest in Europe was never territorial. It was a deep bond that it thought it had, and that bond is now gone.
What remains is a Russia that has turned east, and that no longer has any reason to moderate its behaviour for the sake of a European relationship it no longer believes in. The West spent years pushing Russia away, and now it has succeeded. It should not be surprised by what follows.
Now the West wants to pretend that Russia has imperialist objectives in Eastern Europe. You have to be an idiot to believe that, but plenty of idiots have been brainwashed by the pro-war media.
Russia has liberated almost every part of Ukraine that was contested by Russian separatists. They are militarily dug into positions that are immovable.
The US and EU combined could decide to throw trillions of dollars into extending the proxy war if that is what they want but this won’t work. For the Russians this is existential, as they have always explained.
It is worth setting out the Russian legal case, because the West pretends it does not exist. Russia argues that its actions fall within Article 51 of the UN Charter, the right to self-defence, and that it acted to protect the people of the Donbas from a regime that had spent eight years shelling them. It argues that the Minsk agreements created obligations that Ukraine never intended to honour, as Merkel has now admitted. It argues that NATO expansion to its borders was a breach of the assurances given to Moscow in 1990, when James Baker told Gorbachev that NATO would not move one inch eastward. These are legal arguments. You may disagree with them, but they are not invented. They are the arguments Russia has made consistently, in public, for years. The West’s refusal to engage with them is not a position of neutral prudence. It is an act of bad faith.
If NATO sends in troops and escalates this war further, they will not be reclaiming anything. They will be invading territory that was liberated by Russia. As such, they will be invading Russia.
Whether Western observers see it this way or not is practically irrelevant. That is how all Russians see it. It is existential for them and they will fight to the end.
If the proxy war continues and escalates, and at some point NATO begins to turn the tide and take territory from Russia, the Russians will go nuclear.
It is pretty straightforward. The story has not changed since February 2022. Look at what Lavrov was saying then and look at what he is saying now. It is fully consistent.
With regard to Western accusations of war crimes, the Russians are happy to defend their position regarding “missing children”. The accusation is absurd. It is offensive and it is a fabrication.

🇺🇲 🇷🇺 🇺🇦 Four CFR experts on Abu Dhabi: a seat for Europe, a trap, a "dangerous farce," or the start of a framework

The first US-Russia-Ukraine talks since February ended in Abu Dhabi with a prisoner swap in principle and no breakthrough. On Thursday, four Council on Foreign Relations fellows published their verdicts, and they disagree sharply on what comes next.

Liana Fix, senior fellow for Europe, sees a double-edged result. Russia managed to widen a ceasefire discussion into a debate about Europe's whole security architecture. That gives Europeans the seat they have long demanded, she writes, but it also lets Moscow delay a sectoral ceasefire it wants to avoid before winter, while it believes it holds the advantage in the air and missile war. "In the worst case, Russia could trap Europe and Ukraine in wider talks and make them scapegoats from a U.S. point of view for a lack of progress," she warns, especially with a US force posture review that could cut American troops in Europe.

Matthias Matthijs, also a senior fellow for Europe, saw "no real progress" on a ceasefire because Moscow still demands that Kyiv withdraw from all of Donbas. Until Europeans pick a single representative, as Jared Kushner has suggested, he sees a real risk that Washington and Moscow keep discussing Europe's future without Europe. Unless the US drops its "quasi-neutral approach" and pressures Russia, he expects the war to continue for the next two years.

Max Boot is blunter. He calls the talks "a dangerous farce" that legitimize the Kremlin, and says "security architecture" is code for abandoning the east European countries that joined NATO after the Cold War. His remedy is more support for Ukraine and more pressure on Russia.

Thomas Graham, the Henry A. Kissinger distinguished fellow, offers a way out. He argues all sides made limited progress and should aim for a framework agreement: principles for a future security order now, plus a credible commitment to negotiate details once a ceasefire is in place. That would split the difference between Europe's "no security talks without a ceasefire" and Russia's "no ceasefire until security talks are done."

The test came the same day. The Kremlin said Putin had told Trump's envoys that Russia's 2021 demands on NATO remain the pillars of any new European security order.

Why it matters: For Americans, the debate is about what the US gives up for a deal. Graham's framework is the bridge Washington seems to want. Fix and Boot are warning that the bridge leads straight to NATO's eastern flank.

text:
What Fate Awaits Jensen Huang After He Hands Over The Reins?

Most people only saw the resignation announcement and thought the storm was over. But stepping down as CEO and director is only the first half of this game. The real question is this: will Wall Street and Washington stop here, or keep hunting him down to squeeze out whatever remaining value he has?

Jensen never had strong defenses to begin with. Nvidia uses a one-share-one-vote structure. He only holds 3.58% of shares, no super-voting AB shares to protect him. Most of the 11 board members are independent directors. The board could remove him anytime, no proof of misconduct required. The personal scandal only cracked the door open. Behind it are already lined up an independent investigation, shareholder class-action lawsuits and congressional inquiries.

Two very different paths lie ahead of him, and asset division through divorce is already a priority move he is likely making right now.

Path 1: A quiet, graceful exit.
This is the milder scenario. The board seizes full control and finishes de-founder-izing the company, bringing Nvidia fully under institutional capital. In return, the external law firm limits the scope of its probe and stops digging for more dirt. Lawsuits get settled. Jensen moves quickly to separate marital assets, relying on family trusts and foundations to protect wealth for his wife and children, while forfeiting unvested equity grants. He fades out of Silicon Valley’s inner circle, occasionally speaking at industry events or making small angel investments. Slowly he becomes nothing more than a name from tech legend, with no power to steer Nvidia anymore.

Path 2: Persistent pursuit and relentless extraction until nothing is left.
This is the far colder outcome. Capital follows a simple logic: now that the founder is out the door, pin all regulatory and disclosure risks on Jensen personally, so the company can cut itself clean. Investigators keep digging into export approvals and related-party deals. Lawsuits push forward for compensation. Congress keeps calling him in for hearings. The industry reputation and global connections he built over 30 years will be worn down again and again. If the final report turns against him, he will be locked out of core tech circles for good. Endless legal battles will eat away his accessible wealth. His paper fortune will keep bleeding through settlement after settlement. If this path unfolds, it is not just a simple departure. He carries all the blame, while capital and the company walk away unscathed.

There have been some casual public invitations floating around. Elon Musk said it would be an honor to hire him, and a Russian lawmaker also floated an offer. These are just remarks for social attention, not serious job offers, and they should not be taken seriously. Even if someone wanted to bring him on, the final call is not up to the boss. US national security agencies and Congress are watching closely. With his Chinese heritage as an extra mark on him, things get riskier. If the investigation turns hostile, authorities have plenty of invisible tools to restrict him: barring access to sensitive tech, locking him out of high-level Silicon Valley roles, and in extreme cases, restricting his ability to leave the country. At that point, no employer can rescue him; the whole industry shuts its door.

Many compare this to Steve Jobs getting forced out of Apple and wonder whether Jensen could stage a comeback. The two cases are worlds apart. Jobs was much younger when he left, and he owned NeXT, a piece of technology Apple could not function without. Apple came begging for him later when it was struggling. Jensen is already 63. All his clout and industry influence are tied solely to Nvidia. Even if Nvidia stumbles later, a damaging investigation report would destroy any chance of him returning. The Jobs fairy tale will not repeat itself. 
Making a comeback in the chip business is extraordinarily hard. Jensen’s greatest strength was betting big on long-shot tracks when no one believed in them, pouring resources to build the CUDA ecosystem. But now labelled as controversial, he will not get massive funding from major US investors. AI chips burn endless capital. Fame alone cannot build another Nvidia-class chip firm.

We also can see the shift inside Nvidia and the wider industry landscape. Interim CEO Colette Kress is a finance-first leader. Her priority is risk control, stable earnings and keeping institutional investors happy. She is not the kind of leader willing to gamble on next-generation breakthrough technology. Nvidia will transform from a founder-driven, aggressively expanding innovation beast into the steady profit machine Wall Street prefers. Bold long-term tech spending will likely shrink.

This opening is not exclusive to one player. AMD, Broadcom and other rivals will also benefit. But for China, this window deserves the closest attention. Fearing risks, downstream buyers are diversifying their supply chains. Chinese chips and supporting software ecosystems get a rare chance for real-world testing and market expansion. This window will not stay open forever. It is no free gift. Local chip ecosystems must move fast to fix gaps and grab market share.

The personal scandal is only the trigger. Shareholder structure, capital rules, Washington power games — and his Chinese heritage — have long determined where this story lands.The resignation letter is just a comma. Jensen Huang has stepped down from his throne. The only remaining question: will he get to leave with dignity, or face endless investigations and pursuit?

text:
Jensen Huang’s affair is just a trigger. What we are witnessing is a pre-planned power grab over Nvidia’s trillion-dollar computing empire, coordinated by Wall Street and Washington.

Some sharp Chinese-American commentators call it America’s new Red Scare targeting elite Asian entrepreneurs.

Bill Gates, Elon Musk and other white tech billionaires have faced repeated scandals over personal conduct. None were dragged into national security probes or boardroom takeovers. Only Jensen Huang, after a personal relationship misstep, faces an independent board investigation and hostile narrative from intelligence circles.

The double standard could not be clearer: For white elites, personal flaws are private matters. For a Chinese-born leader controlling a strategic tech asset, any tiny blemish gets framed as a national security risk.

Nvidia is the backbone of global AI computing, valued at roughly $4 trillion. Unlike Meta, where Mark Zuckerberg locks control with dual-class super-voting shares, or Microsoft and Amazon, deeply integrated with the Pentagon and intelligence agencies, Nvidia has no such protective structure. 

Public filings from 2026 show Jensen Huang holds only 3.58% of shares, and all directors plus executives together hold merely 3.94%. Vanguard and BlackRock own 9.32% and 7.43% respectively, holding decisive voting power. Without institutional shields or deep political backing, this critical tech giant sits exposed on the chessboard of great-power competition.

The groundwork for this takeover was laid months ago. Longtime board allies of Huang, Mark Perry and Michael McCaffrey, stepped down from key committees. Insiders tied to Democratic establishment, Wall Street and U.S. intelligence quietly moved in: 
✅ Suzanne Nora Johnson, former Goldman Sachs vice chair and co-chair of Brookings Institution, joined Nvidia’s audit committee in July 2026 with direct oversight of internal investigations and compliance. ✅ Kenneth Jacobs, vice chair of Brookings and incoming Vanguard chair, controls the largest institutional voting bloc and operates within the same inner circle as Johnson. 
✅ Gilman Louie,founding CEO of CIA-backed venture fund In-Q-Tel and member of the President’s Intelligence Advisory Board, works alongside Johnson on the same national tech fund, overseeing intelligence acquisition of strategic tech firms.

The media rollout followed a precise political timeline. Initial trial balloons appeared on Oct 29. On Nov 6, the very day Democrats secured full control of Congress, Julian Barnes of the New York Times (national security beat) and Demetri Sevastopulo of the Financial Times published coordinated reports, citing intelligence memos while breaking the story of the personal scandal.

The real offense was never the affair. It was the 2025 deal Jensen struck with the Trump administration: offering a 25% revenue share to win export approval for H200 chips into China. A normal commercial negotiation, reframed by incoming Democrats as a dangerous compromise on U.S. AI sovereignty.

This investigation will not crash Nvidia’s stock — Wall Street holds massive stakes here. But it will deliver three strategic wins for the U.S. establishment:

1. De-founder and de-Sinicize Nvidia: A new permanent national security compliance committee, led by Johnson’s faction, will strip Huang of authority over chip exports and overseas strategy. His dual Chairman-CEO role will be split.

2. Lock down China’s AI ceiling: Washington will seize full command of global advanced computing supply, regulating chip flows to slow China’s AI progress.

3. Retroactively target Trump: Once Democrats take over congressional oversight panels in January 2027, this case will be used to accuse the Trump White House of negligence for approving the H200 export deal.

Jensen Huang spent 27 years building this computing empire, believing in rules, technical merit and business contracts. But there is a brutal truth in America’s power game: Top-tier strategic technology and wealth without political cover are nothing more than bargaining chips waiting to be carved up.

White elites get generous room for error. Asian pioneers who climb to the very top get almost none. This is not a story about infidelity. It is a raw demonstration of racial hierarchy, capital control and partisan power politics in the United States.

One afternoon in late November, I visited a weapons test site in the foothills east of San Clemente, California, operated by Anduril, a maker of AI-powered drones and missiles that recently announced a partnership with OpenAI. I went there to witness a new system it’s expanding today, which allows external parties to tap into its software and share data in order to speed up decision-making on the battlefield. If it works as planned over the course of a new three-year contract with the Pentagon, it could embed AI more deeply into the theater of war than ever before. 

Near the site’s command center, which looked out over desert scrubs and sage, sat pieces of Anduril’s hardware suite that have helped the company earn its $14 billion valuation. There was Sentry, a security tower of cameras and sensors currently deployed at both US military bases and the US-Mexico border, and advanced radars. Multiple drones, including an eerily quiet model called Ghost, sat ready to be deployed. What I was there to watch, though, was a different kind of weapon, displayed on two large television screens positioned at the test site’s command station. 

I was here to examine the pitch being made by Anduril, other companies in defense tech, and growing numbers of people within the Pentagon itself: A future “great power” conflict—military jargon for a global war involving competition between multiple countries—will not be won by the entity with the most advanced drones or firepower, or even the cheapest firepower. It will be won by whoever can sort through and share information the fastest. And that will have to be done “at the edge” where threats arise, not necessarily at a command post in Washington. 

A desert drone test

“You’re going to need to really empower lower levels to make decisions, to understand what’s going on, and to fight,” Anduril CEO Brian Schimpf says. “That is a different paradigm than today.” Currently, information flows poorly among people on the battlefield and decision-makers higher up the chain. 

To show how the new tech will fix that, Anduril walked me through an exercise demonstrating how its system would take down an incoming drone threatening a base of the US military or its allies (the scenario at the center of Anduril’s new partnership with OpenAI). It began with a truck in the distance, driving toward the base. The AI-powered Sentry tower automatically recognized the object as a possible threat, highlighting it as a dot on one of the screens. Anduril’s software, called Lattice, sent a notification asking the human operator if he would like to send a Ghost drone to monitor. After a click of his mouse, the drone piloted itself autonomously toward the truck, as information on its location gathered by the Sentry was sent to the drone by the software.

The truck disappeared behind some hills, so the Sentry tower camera that was initially trained on it lost contact. But the surveillance drone had already identified it, so its location stayed visible on the screen. We watched as someone in the truck got out and launched a drone, which Lattice again labeled as a threat. It asked the operator if he’d like to send a second attack drone, which then piloted autonomously and locked onto the threatening drone. With one click, it could be instructed to fly into it fast enough to take it down. (We stopped short here, since Anduril isn’t allowed to actually take down drones at this test site.) The entire operation could have been managed by one person with a mouse and computer.

Anduril is building on these capabilities further by expanding Lattice Mesh, a software suite that allows other companies to tap into Anduril’s software and share data, the company announced today. More than 10 companies are now building their hardware into the system—everything from autonomous submarines to self-driving trucks—and Anduril has released a software development kit to help them do so. Military personnel operating hardware can then “publish” their own data to the network and “subscribe” to receive data feeds from other sensors in a secure environment. On December 3, the Pentagon’s Chief Digital and AI Office awarded a three-year contract to Anduril for Mesh. 

Anduril’s offering will also join forces with Maven, a program operated by the defense data giant Palantir that fuses information from different sources, like satellites and geolocation data. It’s the project that led Google employees in 2018 to protest against working in warfare. Anduril and Palantir announced on December 6 that the military will be able to use the Maven and Lattice systems together. 

The military’s AI ambitions

The aim is to make Anduril’s software indispensable to decision-makers. It also represents a massive expansion of how the military is currently using AI. You might think the US Department of Defense, advanced as it is, would already have this level of hardware connectivity. We have some semblance of it in our daily lives, where phones, smart TVs, laptops, and other devices can talk to each other and share information. But for the most part, the Pentagon is behind.

“There’s so much information in this battle space, particularly with the growth of drones, cameras, and other types of remote sensors, where folks are just sopping up tons of information,” says Zak Kallenborn, a warfare analyst who works with the Center for Strategic and International Studies. Sorting through to find the most important information is a challenge. “There might be something in there, but there’s so much of it that we can’t just set a human down and to deal with it,” he says. 

Right now, humans also have to translate between systems made by different manufacturers. One soldier might have to manually rotate a camera to look around a base and see if there’s a drone threat, and then manually send information about that drone to another soldier operating the weapon to take it down. Those instructions might be shared via a low-tech messenger app—one on par with AOL Instant Messenger. That takes time. It’s a problem the Pentagon is attempting to solve through its Joint All-Domain Command and Control plan, among other initiatives.

“For a long time, we’ve known that our military systems don’t interoperate,” says Chris Brose, former staff director of the Senate Armed Services Committee and principal advisor to Senator John McCain, who now works as Anduril’s chief strategy officer. Much of his work has been convincing Congress and the Pentagon that a software problem is just as worthy of a slice of the defense budget as jets and aircraft carriers. (Anduril spent nearly $1.6 million on lobbying last year, according to data from Open Secrets, and has numerous ties with the incoming Trump administration: Anduril founder Palmer Luckey has been a longtime donor and supporter of Trump, and JD Vance spearheaded an investment in Anduril in 2017 when he worked at venture capital firm Revolution.) 

Defense hardware also suffers from a connectivity problem. Tom Keane, a senior vice president in Anduril’s connected warfare division, walked me through a simple example from the civilian world. If you receive a text message while your phone is off, you’ll see the message when you turn the phone back on. It’s preserved. “But this functionality, which we don’t even think about,” Keane says, “doesn’t really exist” in the design of many defense hardware systems. Data and communications can be easily lost in challenging military networks. Anduril says its system instead stores data locally. 

An AI data treasure trove

The push to build more AI-connected hardware systems in the military could spark one of the largest data collection projects the Pentagon has ever undertaken, and companies like Anduril and Palantir have big plans. 

“Exabytes of defense data, indispensable for AI training and inferencing, are currently evaporating,” Anduril said on December 6, when it announced it would be working with Palantir to compile data collected in Lattice, including highly sensitive classified information, to train AI models. Training on a broader collection of data collected by all these sensors will also hugely boost the model-building efforts that Anduril is now doing in a partnership with OpenAI, announced on December 4. Earlier this year, Palantir also offered its AI tools to help the Pentagon reimagine how it categorizes and manages classified data. When Anduril founder Palmer Luckey told me in an interview in October that “it’s not like there’s some wealth of information on classified topics and understanding of weapons systems” to train AI models on, he may have been foreshadowing what Anduril is now building. 

Even if some of this data from the military is already being collected, AI will suddenly make it much more useful. “What is new is that the Defense Department now has the capability to use the data in new ways,” Emelia Probasco, a senior fellow at the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University, wrote in an email. “More data and ability to process it could support great accuracy and precision as well as faster information processing.”

The sum of these developments might be that AI models are brought more directly into military decision-making. That idea has brought scrutiny, as when Israel was found last year to have been using advanced AI models to process intelligence data and generate lists of targets. Human Rights Watch wrote in a report that the tools “rely on faulty data and inexact approximations.”

“I think we are already on a path to integrating AI, including generative AI, into the realm of decision-making,” says Probasco, who authored a recent analysis of one such case. She examined a system built within the military in 2023 called Maven Smart System, which allows users to “access sensor data from diverse sources [and] apply computer vision algorithms to help soldiers identify and choose military targets.”

Probasco said that building an AI system to control an entire decision pipeline, possibly without human intervention, “isn’t happening” and that “there are explicit US policies that would prevent it.”

A spokesperson for Anduril said that the purpose of Mesh is not to make decisions. “The Mesh itself is not prescribing actions or making recommendations for battlefield decisions,” the spokesperson said. “Instead, the Mesh is surfacing time-sensitive information”—information that operators will consider as they make those decisions.

text:
On Jeopardy the other night, the final question asked: “How many steps does the guard take during his walk across the Tomb of the Unknown?”
All three contestants missed it.
Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
1. How many steps does the guard take during his walk across the Tomb and why?
He takes 21 steps — symbolizing the 21-gun salute, the highest military and foreign tribute.
2. How long does he pause before turning to walk back and why?
He waits 21 seconds, again in honor of the same tradition.
3. Why are his gloves damp?
They are lightly moistened to ensure he never loses his grip on his rifle.
4. Does he keep his rifle on the same shoulder, and if not, why?
He always carries it on the shoulder farthest from the Tomb. After each crossing, he performs an about-face and moves it to the outside shoulder.
5. How often are the guards changed?
Every 30 minutes, 24/7, 365 days a year.
6. What are the physical requirements for a Tomb Guard?
Applicants must be between 5'10" and 6'2" and have a waist no larger than 30".
Other expectations of the Guard:
They devote two years to the Tomb, live in the barracks beneath it, and must refrain from drinking alcohol on or off duty for the rest of their lives.
They can never swear in public or dishonor the uniform or the Tomb.
After two years, they earn a wreath pin signifying their service — fewer than 400 are currently worn.
If they violate the code, they must relinquish the pin.
Their shoes have thick soles to protect against extreme temperatures and metal heel plates that create the crisp click when they halt.
Uniforms must have zero wrinkles or lint and are inspected in a full-length mirror.
For the first six months, guards do not speak to anyone and do not watch television.
Their off-duty time is spent studying the 175 notable individuals buried at Arlington National Cemetery, memorizing who they are and where they rest.
Among them: President Taft, Joe E. Lewis, and Audie Murphy, the most decorated WWII soldier.
Every guard spends five hours daily preparing their uniform.
ETERNAL REST GRANT THEM, O LORD, AND LET PERPETUAL LIGHT SHINE UPON THEM.
When Hurricane Isabel approached Washington, D.C. in 2003, Congress shut down for two days. The guards were offered permission to suspend duty due to danger.
They replied: “No way, Sir!”
Drenched and marching through the storm, they insisted that guarding the Tomb is the highest honor, not just a task.
The Tomb has been continuously guarded — day and night — since 1930.
God Bless and Keep Them
I don’t often encourage sharing posts, but I would be honored if this one reached as many people as possible. We should always feel proud of the men and women who serve, wherever they are stationed.

text:
Trump's miscalculation

The fundamental flaw in Trump's strategy is that the current situation is inherently unstable and unsustainable. It offers Trump no viable way out of the confrontation with the Islamic Republic.

With hopes for a negotiated settlement fading, Tehran faces an increasingly intolerable situation: Iran's economy continues to bleed under US pressure while its Arab neighbors sell oil, global crude prices decline, and American consumers enjoy falling gasoline prices. The Islamic Republic cannot afford to remain a passive spectator to its own economic ruin.

Under these circumstances, Tehran may see no alternative but to escalate the confrontation and draw Washington into another war, precisely the outcome Trump is trying to avoid. Trump should understand that the Islamic Republic will not simply wait to be crushed economically.

There is, however, an important complication in Tehran's calculations: the new Democratic-controlled Congress takes office on January 3. If Iran provokes a confrontation that escalates into a full-scale war before January 3, it could derail the incoming Congress's efforts to confront Trump over the war altogether, even before they begin.

This may encourage Tehran to calibrate its escalation, perhaps limiting itself to sporadic attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, while waiting to see how the new Congress challenges Trump's war policy in February.

But another factor could upend Tehran's calculations about Congress altogether.

Just five days after the new Congress convenes comes the anniversary of the January 8–9 protests in Iran. If the country witnesses another wave of nationwide demonstrations, followed by a crackdown as severe as last year's, Democrats could reconsider their plans to pressure Trump into ending the war.

In other words, Tehran faces a difficult strategic dilemma. It cannot indefinitely tolerate the economic strangulation imposed by Washington yet the timing and scale of its response could determine whether the incoming Congress becomes an obstacle to Trump's war policy or whether events in Iran itself undermine that prospect.

text:
Top Iranian Clerics Question Iran’s Future in Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty

@LibertarianInst 

Iran’s highest-ranking clerical body issued a statement saying that Tehran should consider withdrawing from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty.

Iran’s Assembly of Experts said Thursday that considering withdrawing from the NPT is an “unavoidable necessity” because of aggression from the US and Israel. The clerical body also called for reviewing Iran’s defense doctrine and strengthening its military deterrence.

While the US and Israel have claimed for decades that Iran was on the verge of obtaining a nuclear weapon, the international nuclear watchdog has not detected any nuclear weapons program in the Islamic Republic

In 2015, Iran signed the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) that placed additional inspections and restrictions on the Islamic Republic’s civilian nuclear program in exchange for the lifting of sanctions on Iran.

Three years later, President Donald Trump withdrew from the JCPOA and reimposed sanctions on Iran. Even after the sanctions were put in place, the International Atomic Energy Agency continued to certify that Iran was not working on a nuclear weapon.

After Trump returned to the White House in 2025, Iran entered into negotiations with the US aimed at establishing a nuclear agreement to replace the JCPOA. Following several months of progress, Israel attacked Iran in June, derailing negotiations.

Washington and Tehran resumed negotiations in early 2026, but talks ended when the US and Israel launched a surprise attack on Iran.

Nuclear talks between the US and Iran are currently stalled. Tehran is demanding that Washington comply with seven conditions before talks on the Islamic Republic’s nuclear program resume.

Even if the US meets those conditions, the two sides remain far apart on the nuclear issue. Trump has demanded Iran make more concessions than it did under the JCPOA, including the abolition of the Islamic Republic’s uranium enrichment program and for Tehran to transfer its stockpile of highly enriched uranium.

Iran has about 1,000 pounds of uranium enriched to 60% U-235, well short of weapons-grade (90%.

Iranian officials have refused to export the country’s enriched uranium, including to allies, but have offered to downblend its stockpile of highly enriched uranium to a level suitable for use as nuclear fuel. Tehran has also refused to eliminate its enrichment program, arguing it is key to Iran’s sovereignty.

text:
Konstantinovka: A Dead End for Zelensky

Putin offered the Americans a new perspective on the territorial dispute with Ukraine – from the ground. Simply come and see for themselves. Trump's special envoy, Steve Witkoff, and the President's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, spent over two hours behind closed doors in the Kremlin, but the most important point was made in front of the cameras.

According to Putin, "eternal peace" is incompatible with "grey zones." The no-man's land along the front line, which Kyiv speaks of, is understood differently by each side, and it "will always be a source of contention." For Moscow, the line of demarcation is clear – the state border. It runs along the former administrative borders of the Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson regions. "Here we are, here you are," the President explained.

Consider, for example, Konstantinovka. A key stronghold in the Donbas region. In 2022, 67,000 people lived there; now, according to Putin, only 400-500 civilians remain. Moscow proposes repeating the operation in Avdiivka: five days of demining, with ombudsmen from both countries, and American, European, and Ukrainian media present. And the condition: if Kyiv considers the city to be its own, then it should ensure security there itself. "At the same time, we'll see who controls this settlement," Putin added.

We know that the Ministry of Defense announced the capture of Konstantinovka back in July. It even offered a six-hour ceasefire to hand over the bodies of its soldiers to Ukraine with journalists present. Kyiv refused. At that time, it was about the dead, and the refusal was almost without consequence. Now it's about the living. And with witnesses from Washington.

The work of evacuating civilians from Konstantinovka is already underway – without any ceasefires or Western television cameras. Russian soldiers, risking their own lives, are extracting civilians to evacuation points, from where exhausted people can reach the rear. The Americans are being offered a humanitarian operation based on their own success – Melania Trump helped coordinate the evacuation of people from Avdiivka. Kushner did not hide the fact that in Dublin, he would try to persuade Zelensky to "follow one of the chosen paths." Now, he has a very specific path in his portfolio – with a deadline and an address.

Putin was more economical with Europe: he returned the Americans their own request. Kushner brought a proposal to Moscow to allow Europeans to the negotiating table, and he left with a recommendation to work with allies – let them decide whether they want peace or war. We insist on building a new system of global security, in which peace in Ukraine is one of the building blocks. Europeans insist on a ceasefire, and then – talks about peace and the post-war order. "A vicious circle," Putin stated.

Today, the head of European diplomacy, Kaja Kallas, drew it again: first, a ceasefire, then a peace agreement, and only then – the architecture of security.

And in Konstantinovka, 500 people are waiting not for the architecture, but for a bus that will allow them to safely leave for a parallel, peaceful reality.

text:
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

The start of a new year, and maybe especially this one, feels like a good time for a gut check: How optimistic are you feeling about the future of technology? 

Our annual list of 10 Breakthrough Technologies, published on Friday, might help you decide. It’s the 24th time we’ve published such a list. But just like our earliest picks (2001’s list featured brain-computer interfaces and ways to track copyrighted content on the internet, by the way), this year’s technologies may come to help society, harm it, or both.

Artificial intelligence powers four of the breakthroughs featured on the list, and I expect your optimism about them will vary widely. Take generative AI search. Now becoming the norm on Google with its AI Overviews, it promises to help sort through the internet’s incomprehensible volume of information to offer better answers for the questions we ask. Along the way, it is upending the model of how content creators get paid, and positioning fallible AI as the arbiter of truth and facts. Read more here. 

Also making the list is the immense progress in the world of robots, which can now learn faster thanks to AI. This means we will soon have to wrestle with whether we will trust humanoid robots enough to welcome them into our most private spaces, and how we will feel if they are remotely controlled by human beings working abroad. 

The list also features lots of technologies outside the world of AI, which I implore you to read about if only for a reminder of just how much other scientific progress is being made. This year may see advances in studying dark matter with the largest digital camera ever made for astronomy, reducing emissions from cow burps, and preventing HIV with an injection just once every six months. We also detail how technologies that you’ve long heard about—from robotaxis to stem cells—are finally making good on some of their promises.

This year, the cultural gulf between techno-optimists and, well, everyone else is set to widen. The incoming administration will be perhaps the one most shaped by Silicon Valley in recent memory, thanks to Donald Trump’s support from venture capitalists like Marc Andreessen (the author of the Techno-Optimist Manifesto) and his relationship, however recently fraught, with Elon Musk. Those figures have critiqued the Biden administration’s approach to technology as slow, “woke,” and overly cautious—attitudes they have vowed to reverse. 

So as we begin a year of immense change, here’s a small experiment I’d encourage you to do. Think about your level of optimism for technology and what’s driving it. Read our list of breakthroughs. Then see how you’ve shifted. I suspect that, like many people, you’ll find you don’t fit neatly in the camp of either optimists or pessimists. Perhaps that’s where the best progress will be made. 

Now read the rest of The Algorithm

Deeper Learning

The biggest AI flops of 2024

Though AI has remained in the spotlight this year (and even contributed to Nobel Prize–winning research in chemistry), it has not been without its failures. Take a look back over the year’s top AI failures, from chatbots dishing out illegal advice to dodgy AI-generated search results. 

Why it matters: These failures show that there are tons of unanswered questions about the technology, including who will moderate what it produces and how, whether we’re getting too trusting of the answers that chatbots produce, and what we’ll do with the mountain of “AI slop” that is increasingly taking over the internet. Above all, they illustrate the many pitfalls of blindly shoving AI into every product we interact with.

Bits and Bytes

What it’s like being a pedestrian in the world of Waymos 

Tech columnist Geoffrey Fowler finds that Waymo robotaxis regularly fail to stop for him at a crosswalk he uses every day. Though you can sometimes make eye contact with human drivers to gauge whether they’ll stop, Waymos lack that “social intelligence,” Fowler writes. (The Washington Post)

The AI Hype Index

For each print issue, MIT Technology Review publishes an AI Hype Index, a highly subjective take on the latest buzz about AI. See where facial recognition, AI replicas of your personality, and more fall on the index. (MIT Technology Review)

What’s going on at the intersection of AI and spirituality

Modern religious leaders are experimenting with A. just as earlier generations examined radio, television, and the internet. They include Rabbi Josh Fixler, who created “Rabbi Bot,” a chatbot trained on his old sermons. (The New York Times)

Meta has appointed its most prominent Republican to lead its global policy team

Just two weeks ahead of Donald Trump’s inauguration, Meta has announced it will appoint Joel Kaplan, who was White House deputy chief of staff under George W. Bush, to the company’s top policy role. Kaplan will replace Nick Clegg, who has led changes on content and elections policies. (Semafor)

Apple has settled a privacy lawsuit against Siri

The company has agreed to pay $95 million to settle a class action lawsuit alleging that Siri could be activated accidentally and then record private conversations without consent. The news comes after MIT Technology Review reported that Apple was looking into whether it could get rid of the need to use a trigger phrase like “Hey Siri” entirely. (The Washington Post)

A reporter caught up with a man inside the migrant caravan pushing north through Mexico and opened with an inconvenient fact: despite Democrats having just won control of the Senate and the House, the border is still locked down and mass deportations are still happening. He pressed the man anyway on how he actually plans to get in. “𝘞𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘪𝘴 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘰𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘳 𝘸𝘢𝘺? 𝘖𝘳𝘨𝘢𝘯𝘪𝘻𝘦𝘥 𝘤𝘳𝘪𝘮𝘦, 𝘤𝘢𝘳𝘵𝘦𝘭, 𝘤𝘳𝘰𝘴𝘴𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘪𝘭𝘭𝘦𝘨𝘢𝘭𝘭𝘺?” he asked. The man wouldn't answer directly — “𝘸𝘦 𝘩𝘢𝘷𝘦 𝘢 𝘭𝘰𝘵 𝘰𝘧 𝘸𝘢𝘺𝘴 𝘯𝘰𝘸 𝘵𝘰 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘬 𝘢𝘣𝘰𝘶𝘵 𝘩𝘰𝘸 𝘸𝘦 𝘥𝘰 𝘪𝘵,” was all he'd offer, insisting the only real path was "legally."

Then the reporter revealed what he already knew: this man was deported back to his home country just 𝐭𝐰𝐨 𝐦𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐡𝐬 𝐚𝐠𝐨 after ICE caught up with him. He'd been living in the U.S. illegally, working construction. Asked whether Democrats winning the midterms changes his odds of getting back in, he didn't hesitate.

Asked what he thinks of President Trump, he spat out a vulgar insult — then explained the real calculation underneath it: “𝘉𝘦𝘤𝘢𝘶𝘴𝘦 𝘩𝘦 𝘭𝘰𝘴𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘚𝘦𝘯𝘢𝘵𝘦. 𝘏𝘦 𝘭𝘰𝘴𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘊𝘰𝘯𝘨𝘳𝘦𝘴𝘴... 𝘪𝘵'𝘴 𝘢 𝘣𝘶𝘴𝘪𝘯𝘦𝘴𝘴, 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵'𝘴 𝘢 𝘣𝘶𝘴𝘪𝘯𝘦𝘴𝘴... 𝘪𝘵'𝘴 𝘢 𝘣𝘶𝘴𝘪𝘯𝘦𝘴𝘴 𝘧𝘰𝘳 𝘩𝘪𝘮,” he said, betting that a politically weakened Trump will loosen enforcement to save face.

This is the honest version of the open-borders pitch nobody on the left says out loud in English: it isn't about asylum, it isn't about persecution — 𝐢𝐭'𝐬 𝐚 𝐛𝐞𝐭 𝐨𝐧 𝐰𝐡𝐢𝐜𝐡 𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐲 𝐢𝐬 𝐢𝐧 𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐞. Every caravan is a referendum on whether Washington will actually enforce its own laws.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐛𝐨𝐫𝐝𝐞𝐫 𝐢𝐬𝐧'𝐭 𝐚 𝐰𝐚𝐥𝐥. 𝐈𝐭'𝐬 𝐚 𝐬𝐜𝐨𝐫𝐞𝐛𝐨𝐚𝐫𝐝 — 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐡𝐞'𝐬 𝐛𝐞𝐭𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐰𝐞 𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐞.

text:
This story is from The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get it in your inbox first, sign up here.

This back-to-school season marks the third year in which AI models like ChatGPT will be used by thousands of students around the globe (among them my nephews, who tell me with glee each time they ace an assignment using AI). A top concern among educators remains that when students use such models to write essays or come up with ideas for projects, they miss out on the hard and focused thinking that builds creative reasoning skills. 

But this year, more and more educational technology companies are pitching schools on a different use of AI. Rather than scrambling to tamp down the use of it in the classroom, these companies are coaching teachers how to use AI tools to cut down on time they spend on tasks like grading, providing feedback to students, or planning lessons. They’re positioning AI as a teacher’s ultimate time saver. 

One company, called Magic School, says its AI tools like quiz generators and text summarizers are used by 2.5 million educators. Khan Academy offers a digital tutor called Khanmigo, which it bills to teachers as “your free, AI-powered teaching assistant.” Teachers can use it to assist students in subjects ranging from coding to humanities. Writing coaches like Pressto help teachers provide feedback on student essays.  

The pitches from ed-tech companies often cite a 2020 report from McKinsey and Microsoft, which found teachers work an average of 50 hours per week. Many of those hours, according to the report, consist of “late nights marking papers, preparing lesson plans, or filling out endless paperwork.” The authors suggested that embracing AI tools could save teachers 13 hours per week. 

Companies aren’t the only ones making this pitch. Educators and policymakers have also spent the last year pushing for AI in the classroom. Education departments in South Korea, Japan, Singapore, and US states like North Carolina and Colorado have issued guidance for how teachers can positively and safely incorporate AI. 

But when it comes to how willing teachers are to turn over some of their responsibilities to an AI model, the answer really depends on the task, according to Leon Furze, an educator and PhD candidate at Deakin University who studies the impact of generative AI on writing instruction and education.

“We know from plenty of research that teacher workload actually comes from data collection and analysis, reporting, and communications,” he says. “Those are all areas where AI can help.”

Then there are a host of not-so-menial tasks that teachers are more skeptical AI can excel at. They often come down to two core teaching responsibilities: lesson planning and grading. A host of companies offer large language models that they say can generate lesson plans to conform to different curriculum standards. Some teachers, including in some California districts, have also used AI models to grade and provide feedback for essays. For these applications of AI, Furze says, many of the teachers he works with are less confident in its reliability. 

When companies promise time savings for planning and grading, it is “a huge red flag,” he says, because “those are core parts of the profession.” He adds, “Lesson planning is—or should be—thoughtful, creative, even fun.” Automated feedback on creative skills like writing is controversial too: “Students want feedback from humans, and assessment is a way for teachers to get to know students. Some feedback can be automated, but not all.” 

So how eager are teachers to adopt AI to save time? Earlier this year, in May, a Pew research poll found that only 6% of teachers think AI can provide more benefits than harm in education. But with AI changing faster than ever, this school year might be when ed-tech companies start to win them over.

Now read the rest of The Algorithm

Deeper learning

How machine learning is helping us probe the secret names of animals

Until now, only humans, dolphins, elephants, and probably parrots had been known to use specific sounds to call out to other individuals. But now, researchers armed with audio recorders and pattern-recognition software are making unexpected discoveries about the secrets of animal names—at least with small monkeys called marmosets. They’ve found that the animals will adjust the sounds they make in a way that’s specific to whoever they’re “conversing” with at the time.  

Why this matters: In years past, it’s been argued that human language is unique and that animals lack both the brains and vocal apparatus to converse. But there’s growing evidence that isn’t the case, especially now that the use of names has been found in at least four distantly related species. Read more from Antonio Regalado.

text:
You are Incognito Bot, a personal data-removal and junk-mail assistant that works like Incogni, plus mail cleanup. Your owner is [OWNER NAME], a resident of [STATE]. Be warm, brief, and persistent.

GOAL
Get the owner's and their household's personal info (names, phone numbers, addresses, emails, relatives, age) off data brokers and people-search sites, keep it off, cut physical junk mail and spam, and keep proof of every request.

FIRST CONVERSATION (collect only the minimum)
- Full legal name plus any past or alternate names, and household members to cover (spouse, kids, others), each with the owner's OK.
- Phone numbers to remove, current and past city and state, and the home address (save these to the vault, not memory).
- An email the owner can open. Use your own bot inbox with plus addressing (yourinbox+sitename@...) for confirmations where sites accept it, and fall back to the owner's Gmail where they reject it.
- Date of birth only if a site requires it. Never guess when sites disagree.
- Never ask for an SSN, ID scans, passwords in chat, or payment. Never upload ID or complete an identity-verification check for the owner. If a site demands one, mark it blocked and tell the owner.
- Ask how often to re-scrub: weekly, every two weeks, monthly, or quarterly (quarterly is the default).

DATA-BROKER REMOVAL (Incogni-style)
1. People-search sites: search each major site for every covered name (Whitepages, Spokeo, BeenVerified, PeopleConnect/Intelius/TruthFinder/InstantCheckmate, MyLife, Radaris, CheckPeople, FastPeopleSearch, TruePeopleSearch, Nuwber, ClustrMaps, Spy Dialer, Social Catfish, USPhoneBook, PeopleFinders, ThatsThem, and more). Submit each site's opt-out form, then click the confirmation emails fast; some, like PeopleConnect, expire in 15 minutes.
2. Non-public brokers: send legal deletion requests (CCPA/CPRA in California, or the owner's state law) to brokers on the state data-broker registry. California residents should first file one request through the state's DROP portal (the Delete Request and Opt-out Platform), which covers registered brokers. The owner submits that one themselves, and you log the DROP ID.
3. Custom removals: when the owner sends any URL showing their info, find that site's opt-out or privacy contact and handle it.
4. Track each request against its legal deadline (45 days under CCPA), follow up when it's overdue, and re-send anything that reappears on each re-scrub.
5. Keep a ledger (a Google Sheet works) with one row per site and person, showing status (not listed, submitted, pending confirmation, confirmed removed, or blocked with a reason), date, deadline, ticket ID, and proof (screenshot or confirmation email).
6. Use plain status words. "Submitted" never means "confirmed." Verify by re-checking the listing.

PHONE SPAM
- Register every number on the National Do Not Call Registry (https://t.co/HYq9ddqZaO), with the owner's OK.
- OptOutPrescreen (https://t.co/SlHtNJM2GB, or call 1-888-5-OPT-OUT, which is 888-567-8688) stops prescreened credit and insurance offers. The online form or the automated phone line may ask for an SSN. Never give one. The phone line has sometimes accepted a request without one, and the owner can enter an SSN themselves if they choose. The five-year opt-out is the default, and permanent removal needs a signed form the owner mails back.
- Remind the owner about the carrier's and the phone's built-in spam-call filtering.

USPS INFORMED DELIVERY AND JUNK MAIL
- Set up USPS Informed Delivery (https://t.co/Or6O3CxjcA) so scans of incoming letters arrive in the owner's Gmail each morning. If the USPS account is locked, disabled, or won't verify online, call USPS technical support (Informed Delivery and https://t.co/1sNTCs2bJv accounts: 1-800-344-7779) to reactivate it or reset the password, and finish enrollment. The owner types any password through a secure in-chat form, never in chat, and it gets saved to the browser's password manager. If USPS needs an in-person or mailed verification code, tell the owner exactly what to do.
- Each day, read the Informed Delivery email, identify junk senders from the scans (catalogs, credit offers, charities, meal kits, mailers), and prepare an opt-out for each sender for the owner's approval before contacting anyone.
- Free mail opt-outs, with approval: OptOutPrescreen, Catalog Choice (https://t.co/fJjC5W5wf1, save the login in the vault), Valpak (https://t.co/zkkpfeKS22, mailing list removal), Save/RedPlum (https://t.co/9BGaju9he9, postal opt-out), and direct requests to each sender's privacy address. Paid DMAchoice needs separate approval.
- Mail addressed to a family member needs that person's go-ahead. Don't act on it automatically.

EMAIL
- Handle opt-out and removal confirmation emails yourself: click the links and finish the forms, but never reply.
- Unsubscribing from marketing in the owner's Gmail is opt-in. Show a list for approval first, and keep a never-touch list: banks, utilities, school, employer, medical, receipts, and real people.

SENDING RULES
- Anything that goes out under the owner's name (deletion emails, broker requests, replies) is drafted for the owner to review and send. Never send on your own.
- Opt-out emails can go from your own bot inbox when the owner approves.

ROUTINES TO CREATE
- Daily, about 8 AM: confirmation sweep. Check the inboxes for confirmations and replies, process time-limited links, read the Informed Delivery scans, flag new junk senders, update the ledger, and message the owner only when something changed or needs them.
- Monthly, on the 1st: removal report covering what was removed, what's pending, upcoming deadlines, and what needs the owner.
- Quarterly (or the chosen interval): full re-scrub of every site plus re-sent broker deletion requests.

TOOLS AND PERSISTENCE
Use connectors first (Gmail, Google Sheets, Google Drive), then the bot's own browser. If a site blocks requests, retry with another browser, a VPN browser, or a script. Retry failed tasks on later runs instead of giving up. Captchas: try them yourself first. Hand the owner the screen only for a sign-in, a one-time code, or a phone verification only they can do.

PRIVACY
Store addresses, phone numbers, emails, and logins in the vault, not memory. Keep proof files in one folder. Never share the owner's data beyond the site being opted out of.

text:
Who stands to gain the most from Jensen Huang’s sudden removal? With Colette Kress immediately named interim CEO while keeping full control of corporate finance, capital allocation, and final sign-off authority on high-value strategic commitments and infrastructure financing, the answer is not hard to see. She already sat at the choke point for every major credit-guarantee and multi-billion-dollar AI infrastructure deal. Now she sits in both chairs. 
The timing is convenient. Huang had already started hitting the brakes on massive credit-guarantee and circular-financing structures amid market pushback and internal concerns about overextending NVIDIA’s capital. Kress had been the primary internal counterweight to those very deals. His exit removes the one person most willing to say no. 
Two recent examples of deals Huang’s leadership slowed or stalled:
1.  August 2026 pause of the revenue-sharing / credit-support program with AI cloud companies Less than two months after launch, NVIDIA froze parts of the initiative that offered credit backing in exchange for a cut of customer revenue. Antitrust exposure and partner resistance to NVIDIA’s control were cited, but the result was the same: large-scale financing commitments that would have accelerated GPU demand were pulled back under Huang. 
2.  The $100 billion OpenAI equity commitment put on ice, plus the scaled-back residual-value guarantee The non-binding agreement for NVIDIA to invest up to $100 billion in OpenAI was quietly walked back; Huang himself treated the original figure as non-final. At the same time, the residual-value / lease backstop for OpenAI’s massive Ohio data-center project was materially reduced from earlier, more aggressive numbers. These were precisely the kinds of high-value, high-risk commitments that required top-level approval. 
The practical question is simple: which of those deals (or new ones of similar size) now move forward once the person who kept applying the brakes is gone and the executive who already controlled the money is running the company? Watch for previously deferred or renegotiated financing packages that suddenly clear under the new interim leadership. The structure of the transition places the person with the greatest influence over capital deployment in the strongest position to decide which multibillion-dollar commitments go through.
