text:
URANIUM: FUEL BUYERS ARE TURNING BULLISH WHILE WALL STREET SELLS

Mike Alkin of Sachem Cove joined Erik Townsend on MacroVoices (Nov. 12) to explain a strange split: uranium prices remain firm, but uranium equities are being sold alongside AI and data-center stocks.

Alkin says the bull market never needed AI. Roughly 440 operating reactors, plus a pipeline of 80 more, already require more economically viable uranium than mines can supply at current prices. He estimates structural deficits of 15–25% or more of demand, with nuclear growth accelerating from roughly 0.5% to 4–5% annually.

So why are uranium stocks trading like AI stocks?

Some junior miners marketed themselves as data-center beneficiaries. Banks included nuclear shares in AI and momentum baskets. Now fears of an AI spending bust trigger selling regardless of uranium fundamentals. Flows overwhelm facts.

Fuel buyers are moving the other way.

Alkin has attended Nuclear Energy Institute conferences since 2018, when buyers dismissed his shortage thesis. At the latest meeting, he said he could barely find a bearish fuel buyer willing to debate him. Yet utilities are contracting for only a little over half their annual requirements, leaning on older contracts and inventories.

They have barely tested the supply market. Alkin expects more than 2 billion pounds to require contracting through 2040. After roughly 15 years of inventory drawdowns, utilities may eventually have to buy more than they consume to rebuild stocks.

Long-term uranium prices have already roughly quadrupled despite weak contracting. Tenders that once attracted 7–12 bids now draw very few. Producers with limited capacity have little incentive to sell cheaply. Meanwhile, Alkin says about 70% of uranium is produced in the East while 70% is consumed in the West.

Mining costs are another part of the shortage.

He cited industry estimates of average uranium production costs rising from $24/lb in 2019 to $38/lb in 2025. Kazatomprom once projected costs near $13–14/lb for 2026; he puts them at $38–45/lb today, or above $55/lb using the old exchange rate. Across the industry, projects have suffered major overruns and production misses.

Small mines producing 0.5–2 million pounds a year are particularly exposed. Delayed production supports the uranium price but can destroy returns for shareholders in the companies that fail to deliver. Alkin argues proven operators deserve a scarcity premium.

He used Cameco as an example. Investors focused on its disappointing quarter, but Alkin highlighted something else: Cameco indicated it was signing contracts at triple-digit uranium prices, above the reported long-term benchmark around $98–99/lb. He estimates Cameco trades at about 8–9x EBITDA after valuing its Westinghouse stake, compared with roughly 31x in 2022. That estimate depends on his valuation assumptions.

Elsewhere in the fuel cycle, conversion pricing has risen from roughly $4 to over $60/kg and enrichment from around $30 to over $200/SWU, according to Alkin. His argument: uranium has not yet experienced the same buyer panic.

For investors, he drew a clear distinction. Physical uranium removes mine-level operating risk. Mining equities offer greater leverage to rising prices but carry serious execution risk. The Sprott Physical Uranium Trust was discussed at roughly an 18% discount to NAV, which can persist or widen.

Erik raised factory-built advanced reactors as a possible additional demand shock. Alkin agreed they could worsen shortages but said his thesis does not depend on them. He cited current contract floors near $70–75/lb and ceilings around $150–160/lb. A rush to secure supply could force a sharper price adjustment, but he gave no timetable.

The contrast: Wall Street is selling uranium miners over AI fears while the fuel buyers themselves are increasingly concerned about available supply.

text:
neobudhist illiterate. Siddhartha Gautama never claimed to be an avatar, a Puranic deity, or a Vedic god. He never was. In many South Indian, Maharashtra, andhra and traditional Vaishnava lists, Balarama (Krishna's elder brother) or Vithoba occupies the ninth spot instead of the Buddha.
Jayadeva’s Gita Govinda was a lyrical, devotional poem rather than a foundational Vedic scripture. By praising the Buddha's compassion (sadaya-hṛdaya), Jayadeva was celebrating the universal principle of non-violence (ahiṃsā) through a poetic lens,Poetic Devotion. Buddha (with two 'd's) is a descriptive title meaning "the Awakened One" or "the Enlightened One," derived from the Sanskrit root budh (to awaken or understand).
In Buddhism: Even within Buddhist scriptures, Siddhartha Gautama is not the only Buddha. Theravada and Mahayana texts list many previous Buddhas (such as Dipankara and Kassapa) who achieved enlightenment in earlier eras, as well as Maitreya, the future Buddha.
In Hinduism: Because Buddha simply describes a state of supreme awareness, Hindu texts like the Mahabharata and the Upanishads occasionally use the word buddha as an adjective to describe any realized sage or enlightened soul, long before the founding of organized Buddhism. in sanatan dharma aham brahamasmi we see god in everything everyone.. all creation.. inclduing budha.. but iam a hindu who does nto hold budha as my god.. and you have freedom to beleive what you want to.. but again budha is claimed to be god by budhsits the very same who claim budha rejected vedas ...you cannot claim both are correct dhimmi. because vedic gods and puranic avatars are representation of same cosmic energies. Strictly speaking, mainstream Buddhism is non-theistic and does not view Siddhartha Gautama as a creator God or a cosmic ruler. Both Theravada and Mahayana philosophies explicitly reject the Vedas and the concept of a supreme deity (Ishvara).
 However, in everyday practice—especially in Mahayana and Vajrayana Buddhism—many followers treat the Buddha and various Bodhisattvas much like gods. They build temples, offer prayers for blessings, and bow before statues in ways that mirror Hindu puja (worship).Vedic and Puranic deities operate within a cosmic order (Rta and Dharma) rooted in the Vedas. Someone who explicitly rejected the Vedas cannot simultaneously be a Vedic deity or a Puranic cosmic energy without creating a direct contradiction.
Modern Buddhist thinkers also agree that trying to merge the two dilutes both paths. For them, elevating the Buddha into a Hindu god—or treating him like a Puranic deity—goes against his core message of self-reliance and his rejection of Vedic authority.
Ultimately, Sanatana Dharma's principle of Aham Brahmasmi allows you to respect an enlightened human teacher as part of creation without ever needing to worship him as a deity or place him alongside Vedic gods.

EXCLUSIVE:

Britain needs to embrace artificial intelligence and invest in data centres because it will offer the country a "productivity revolution" and bolster the wages of ordinary workers, the Chancellor has said

In an interview with The Times John Healey, the chancellor, said that artificial intelligence "is coming whether we like it or not" and that Britain needs to take "maximum advantage" of the opportunities it offers

He said that artificial intelligence has the potential to draw investment to Britain on a "big scale" and argued that Britain needs to develop its own "sovereign" artificial intelligence to bolster economic growth and national security

Healey believes that the improvement in productivity the technology brings will filter through to everyone. On Wednesday he discussed the artificial intelligence "revolution" with Kevin Warsh, the chairman of the US Federal Reserve, during a visit to the UK. Andy Burnham, the prime minister, also briefly attended the meeting.

Healey said: "He [Warsh] believes we're on the edge of a productivity revolution and transformation with AI. 

"We had a good discussion because he sees this as not just potentially bringing benefits to the super-rich and big tech, but already in the US, signs that it is increasing, raising the level of productivity, therefore the value and the wages of many ordinary workers. It may be that we're starting to see some of that in some of the detail of the growth figures today in Britain."

He added: "I think the signs are it's a revolution already underway. The challenge for policy makers and I think the change for investors the challenge for investors and business is how do we make the most of this for Britain, and in doing so reassure people about the steps we can help take against the risks that they quite rightly also feel and see."

Healey said that Britain can learn from the bitter debates over the "free for all" of new data centres in the US by ensuring that they have the support of communities. In the Budget he announced a new data centre “covenant”, which will require owners to invest in local communities, create jobs and protect water supplies in exchange for priority access to the national grid.

He said: “It [artificial intelligence] is coming, whether we like it or not. Many people are already using it, I want to avoid the free-for-all on AI and data centres we’ve seen in the states.

“So where NHS health data is used with AI, I want that data in Britain, not in data centres abroad. Where AI is used for our security, I want that data in Britain, for Britain, not abroad. To do that, we have to develop more data centres. I’m ready to back them if they provide the community benefits and can help build public trust.

“If we haven’t got the independence, we haven’t got some of the control and sovereignty on our AI capacity in the UK, then we will find that we can’t provide the level of confidence, the level of security that I think people are rightly wanting, and we can’t make the most of the big economic opportunities that are there.”

text:
King William of Tallus

I had a pretty low opinion of William when Sela and the others reached Tallus, and I don't think that's an unfair way to read him. They have just helped refugees survive an attack outside his city. They come in offering help against Orcus. William ends up ordering Sela handed over to the enemy and her companions killed.

That's a hell of a response to people who were trying to help you.

What makes him worth talking about is that the story lets us see how he gets to that decision. It doesn't make him a secret mastermind, and it doesn't make the decision acceptable. He's a frightened man who inherited a responsibility he never prepared himself to carry. He wants somebody else to tell him how to survive it.

We get a glimpse of him before all this, enjoying the privileges of being the king's son while his father tries to get him to think about the responsibilities coming with the title. William isn't interested. The dangers his father talks about seem far enough away that he can dismiss them. He knows the comfortable version of the kingdom, so he acts like that's the only version he will ever have to deal with.

Then his father is gone, Orcus is outside the walls, and William is standing in front of a statue asking for help.

That scene stood out to me because of how honest he is when nobody else is there. He admits he isn't equipped for this. He understands his own limitations better than you might expect from the way he carries himself in front of everyone else. The problem is that admitting he isn't ready doesn't give him a plan, and the people in Tallus can't wait for him to become a different person.

Orcus takes advantage of exactly that fear. He offers to spare the children if the city delivers Sela and kills her companions. It's a brutal bargain, especially when some of the people turning against Sela are people she has just helped. William lets the three be detained while he considers what to do.

Druanna argues that they're throwing away their chance of surviving, but even she can't simply promise to fix everything. Her own power is limited. William is surrounded by people who need an answer, and the answer he wants doesn't exist. He can't guarantee that fighting will save the city. He can't guarantee that surrendering Sela will save it either. Orcus is asking him to trust the mercy of the person threatening to slaughter everyone.

There's another detail that makes William's eventual choice worse for me. When he goes back to his father's statue, he hears a voice telling him what he wants to hear. It seems to be his father advising him that surrendering Sela might save the children. But William catches the deception. He knows his father wouldn't have surrendered that way. The scene reveals a speaking rat near the statue, so this isn't actually the father reaching out to guide him.

William recognizes the lie, then goes ahead with the surrender anyway.

That means I can't write him off as someone who was simply tricked into believing he was following his father's advice. He has enough judgment to notice the deception. He still chooses to sacrifice the people who came to help. When Gaia breaks them out, he even orders his guards to kill her. She has to overpower the situation and get them away.

The more interesting part comes afterward, because Tallus still has to be defended. Blake and Bolder haven't forgotten what William did. They help anyway. William asks for their help and returns their weapons, and now he has to work alongside people he was willing to execute a short time earlier. I like that the story doesn't need to erase that history for them to understand the city is full of people who still need saving.

By the time the Shadow Dragon attacks, there isn't a simple military solution left. William says he has no army and no more sentinels. Bolder tells him that he needs to buy them time while they go for a weapon that might work. William asks how he's supposed to do that. The answer is basically that he's the king and he needs to figure it out.

Earlier, that pressure sent him back to the statue looking for somebody else's instructions. This time he goes into the street.

The people there want him to lead them away. He asks them to make a stand for Tallus. They point out that they're ordinary people, not soldiers. And William finally gives them something more than a command from a safe distance: he'll be at the front. He'll draw his sword first. If someone has to die, he's willing to be first there too.

He actually follows through. He leads the attack against the dragon, giving Sela a chance when she's in danger. It doesn't magically make him stronger than the creature. The dragon knocks them aside. But there's a real difference between telling other people to pay the price of saving the kingdom and physically putting himself in the way with them.

And he doesn't disappear from the story once that moment is over. When the dragon falls, Bolder makes a pocket in the earth to keep them from being crushed, and William helps cut them out. After the battle, William starts dealing with what the city actually needs. There are people without homes. He takes responsibility for sheltering them. We finally see him acting like someone who understands that the kingdom is made up of people he has to care for, rather than a position that exists to keep him comfortable.

Then Orcus kills him.

After everything it took to reach that point, William is struck in the chest by an arrow Orcus has enchanted with his own aide's blood. He dies in Gaia's arms. His final words recognize that he was truly a king for only a day. That's a rough ending, because we have just started seeing what he might have become if he'd had more time.

I still wouldn't excuse what William did to Sela, Blake, and Bolder. Those were his decisions, and the story gives us plenty of reason to remember them. But I don't think his death makes the change meaningless either. He helped save people he had been willing to sacrifice. He stood in front of the danger instead of sending someone else into it. And he started taking care of the survivors while he had the chance.

That's why I ended up having more interest in him than I expected. He doesn't get a long, comfortable redemption where everyone can gradually forget the worst thing he did. He has to make those better decisions in the same crisis where he made the terrible ones, with the same people watching him. For a brief stretch, they finally get the king his father had wanted him to be. Then they lose him.

text:
Behind the Science: Gaia / Druanna

Gaia is one of those characters where I think the limitation on her power is more interesting than just saying she can control nature. When Sela reaches Tallus, she meets her as Druanna, the city's high priestess. There's a beautiful garden, she's comfortable in the water, and she knows quite a bit about the people who just walked into her home. You could look at that introduction and assume Sela has finally found somebody powerful enough to solve the whole situation.

Then you find out how much it costs Druanna to help anybody.

The garden matters because she has been growing it and caring for it since she arrived. She tells Sela that it feeds her and that she's strongest there. That gives you a reason for the setting beyond having a nature character surrounded by plants. This is where she's built up something she depends on. When she later saves Sela, Bolder, and Blake from the city that has turned against them, she gets them out with these golden ribbons of energy. They survive. The garden doesn't come through it the same way. Its plants are dead, and she collapses.

I like that the story actually follows through on the expense. We get a rescue, but we also get to see what was spent to make that rescue happen. She hasn't just become tired for a panel and then immediately gone back to doing everything she could before.

Her explanation in issue 60 makes the whole thing a lot clearer. Druanna is Gaia, the woman behind the Mother Nature legend in this universe. When she was young, animals were drawn to her and good weather followed her. A fairy explained that Myst's wind, rain, and trees loved her because of the way she cared for them. They wanted to give something back, and the fairy established a connection that let her use their power.

There's a very specific distinction here that I wouldn't want to gloss over. In Myst, these parts of nature have consciousness and can willingly offer that power. Gaia also explains that she could control nature on Earth, but Earth's elements didn't have that same will. The comic is giving its fantasy realm a quality that our world doesn't share. The trees agreeing to help her belong to the rules of Myst. That isn't evidence that real trees are sitting around making the same kind of decisions.

Originally, that connection let her move between realms and maintain their balance. The Dark One wanted her service, she refused, and he worked out how to cut her off. During the attack, we see the severed head of the fairy who had made the connection possible. Gaia suddenly can't call on her power the way she expects to. The Wolf wounds her, and the Dark One tries to drown her. She's rescued by animals, with a crocodile attacking him and birds carrying her away.

That part is important because her later weakness has a cause. Her abilities weren't always this restricted. She survived a deliberate attempt to remove the thing that made them work.

An ally saved her using the Orb of Olan. It's the orb on her staff, and it gives her a substitute connection to the power she used to reach directly. But that substitute only allows a fraction of what she once had, and it drains the source badly. That's why the garden can be destroyed helping her save three people. The orb gives her access, but it doesn't remove the cost.

If I'm breaking this down from the science side, the useful comparison is the difference between having a source of energy and having a way to use it. Those are separate problems. A device can give you access to something without supplying an endless amount of it. Gaia knows what to do with the power. The orb gives her a way to channel it. The remaining question is whether there's enough available, and whether taking it will destroy whatever is supplying it.

Real ecosystems give us a much more grounded version of that dependence. Plants use sunlight to make food, and feeding relationships move that energy through a food web. Change one part of that web and you can affect organisms well beyond the one you directly touched. [NOAA's explanation of food webs](https://t.co/MY9bgvCdi9) is useful here because it follows those connections rather than treating each plant or animal as an isolated thing. That doesn't make Gaia's staff a scientific device. It does help explain why a nature-powered character should have consequences that reach outside her own body.

There's a physical connection between plants and the atmosphere, too. As the [USGS describes it](https://t.co/AXBZ04uYLz), roots take up water, that water moves through the plant, and leaves release water vapor through their stomata. The plant, the soil, and the air are already participating in the same process. Wind, humidity, temperature, and available moisture affect it. You don't need to give the weather a personality to find a real connection between those parts of the environment.

The comic pushes those relationships into outright magic, especially when Tallus is about to fall. Gaia doesn't have enough power left in the plants, so she asks to use Sela as the source instead. Sela has the opposite problem. She has an enormous amount of power and is afraid that releasing it will destroy everyone around her. Gaia believes she can control it, although she isn't certain the staff can handle the transfer.

That's a much better setup than having either of them suddenly discover a new ability at the last second. Their existing problems fit together. Sela can supply what Gaia is missing. Gaia has the control Sela needs. They try it, and the result is a storm and a flood that tear through the army outside the sealed city. It works, but Sela is exhausted by the end and says she can't keep going.

I wouldn't try to calculate the energy of that storm from a few comic panels. We don't have the measurements, and magic is doing the work the story hasn't defined physically. The interesting thing is that the book still keeps track of where the power is coming from and shows the person supplying it reaching her limit.

There's one more detail in issue 62 that I really appreciated. After the battle, Sela helps her restore the garden. It looks like everything has been put back, but Gaia makes a point of saying the original plants are still lost. The new growth hasn't brought those particular lives back. Even with magic, restoring the place doesn't erase everything that happened there. That's a useful distinction when we talk about damage to a living environment, too: making somewhere green again doesn't mean every loss has been reversed.

That's what makes Gaia worth looking at beyond the Mother Nature name. She can be tremendously useful without being able to solve every problem alone. The way she uses nature changes after she's injured, the tool keeping her alive has restrictions, and helping someone can consume the environment she spent so much time nurturing. She survives Tallus and agrees to help Sela with Erik, but that promise is interrupted when Belinda takes Sela through a portal. Finding Gaia gives Sela a real ally. It doesn't give either of them a way around every cost or every person determined to interfere.

13 NOVEMBER 1839 - THANKFULLY, THE DAY A LINCOLNSHIRE TOWN FINALLY ENDED A TRADITION THAT HAD LASTED FOR CENTURIES!

Imagine walking through the beautiful streets of Stamford, Lincolnshire, only to discover that an angry, terrified bull was being chased through the town by an excited crowd! For centuries, this was an annual spectacle. Every 13th November, on St Brice's Day, the people of Stamford gathered for a custom known as bull running.

It was noisy, dangerous, chaotic and, by the nineteenth century, increasingly controversial. According to local legend, the tradition began during the reign of King John. The story tells of William de Warenne, Earl of Surrey, watching two bulls fighting in a meadow. When one escaped into Stamford, causing uproar in the streets, the Earl supposedly found the spectacle so entertaining that he arranged for it to happen every year!

The tale even claimed that land was granted to the town's butchers on condition that they supplied a bull for the annual event. It's a wonderful example of the elaborate stories that grow around ancient customs. But historians cannot establish that the legend is true.

What is certain is that bull running became an established part of Stamford's local traditions. Crowds would gather to chase and torment the animal through the streets. To supporters, it represented excitement, community spirit and the preservation of an ancient English custom. To critics, it was an appalling display of animal cruelty....And the opposition was growing.

By the 1830s, the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, founded in 1824 and later granted its Royal prefix, was campaigning against practices of this kind. The Stamford bull run became a particular target.

The authorities also had good reason to worry about public disorder. Imagine trying to police narrow streets filled with excited spectators chasing a distressed bull!

In 1837, large numbers of police, soldiers and special constables were deployed in an attempt to stop the event...But the bull run went ahead anyway, despite the authorities' efforts.

Two years later, on 13 November 1839, the final Stamford bull run took place. This time, the authorities succeeded in bringing the spectacle to an early end. The bull was captured, and the custom was finally abandoned.

One important factor was financial: Stamford's inhabitants had been made to bear the cost of repeated military and police interventions. The practice had become increasingly difficult to sustain.
And so ended one of England's strangest and most controversial local traditions. The story offers a fascinating glimpse into changing attitudes during the nineteenth century.

Activities once defended as entertainment and community traditions increasingly faced questions about cruelty, public safety and the treatment of animals. Stamford's beautiful medieval and Georgian streets remain. But thankfully, visitors no longer have to worry about finding a bull charging towards them!

No one of God is perfect. Iand they all sin.

What then shall we say that Abraham, our forefather according to the flesh, has found? For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not before God. For what does the Scripture say? “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness.” Now to the one who works, his wage is not credited as a favor, but as what is due. But to the one who does not work, but believes in Him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is credited as righteousness, just as David also speaks of the blessing on the man to whom God credits righteousness apart from works: 
“Blessed are those whose lawless deeds have been forgiven,
And whose sins have been covered.
“Blessed is the man whose sin the Lord will not take into account.” -Rom4:1-8

God justifies the ungodly.
But what about David?
He says: “ blessed is the man who sin the Lord will not take into account.”
To understand that you must understand what happened at the cross. 
There Jesus took the punishment for all the sins that God was ever going to forgive. 

For while we were still helpless, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly. For one will hardly die for a righteous man; though perhaps for the good man someone would dare even to die. But God demonstrates His own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us. Much more then, having now been justified by His blood, we shall be saved from the wrath of God through Him. For if while we were enemies we were reconciled to God through the death of His Son, much more, having been reconciled, we shall be saved by His life. And not only this, but we also exult in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received the reconciliation. -Rom5:6-11

In the OldT, they had to go every year to make the sacrifice of atonement. But Jesus changed all that because, he one time, sacrifice himself for all the sins of his people. Thus he says those who believe in me receive forgiveness of  sins and everlasting life.  They don’t just receive begins of the sin. They’ve already committed, but they receive forgiveness of all their sins. It doesn’t say we might be saved by his life.

…so much the more also Jesus has become the guarantee of a better covenant. The former priests, on the one hand, existed in greater numbers because they were prevented by death from continuing, but Jesus, on the other hand, because He continues forever, holds His priesthood permanently. Therefore He is able also to save forever those who draw near to God through Him, since He always lives to make intercession for them. 
For it was fitting for us to have such a high priest, holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners and exalted above the heavens; who does not need daily, like those high priests, to offer up sacrifices, first for His own sins and then for the sins of the people, because this He did once for all when He offered up Himself. -Heb7:22-27

The word forever indicates the duration of salvation.

But when Christ appeared as a high priest of the good things to come, He entered through the greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands, that is to say, not of this creation; and not through the blood of goats and calves, but through His own blood, He entered the holy place once for all, having obtained eternal redemption. For if the blood of goats and bulls and the ashes of a heifer sprinkling those who have been defiled sanctify for the cleansing of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered Himself without blemish to God, cleanse your conscience from dead works to serve the living God? 
For this reason He is the mediator of a new covenant, so that, since a death has taken place for the redemption of the transgressions that were committed under the first covenant, those who have been called may receive the promise of the eternal inheritance.-Heb9:11-15

Matetsi Victoria Falls
Matetsi Victoria Falls is a family-owned luxury safari lodge set on a private stretch of the Zambezi River in Zimbabwe, about 40 km upstream from the Victoria Falls (Mosi-oa-Tunya). It sits within the roughly 55,000-hectare (136,000-acre) Matetsi Private Game Reserve, which offers 15 km of exclusive river frontage and is part of the larger Kavango-Zambezi (KAZA) Transfrontier Conservation Area.
The property features 18 contemporary river-facing suites across two intimate camps (including family suites), each with private plunge pools and views over the river, plus the exclusive-use four-bedroom Matetsi River House. Design blends modern African aesthetics with local materials such as wood, stone, and copper. Guests enjoy guided game drives (day and night), walking safaris, boat cruises, fishing, spa treatments, and easy access to Victoria Falls tours, helicopter flights, and other regional activities. The reserve is known for elephant and buffalo herds, predators including lion and leopard, and rich birdlife.

text:
Dear Ones, There comes an hour in the life of a people when the things they have built can no longer conceal what they have become. Their institutions may still bear the venerable names of justice and liberty; their treasures may remain abundant, their monuments magnificent. Yet a civilization can preserve the language of righteousness long after its heart has ceased to understand the words.

And still, Heaven has not forgotten the Earth.

What our Heavenly Father and Mother intended from the beginning was greater than the survival of a fallen world. Their children were born to inherit and cultivate divine life, to grow in intelligence and holiness, and to bring forth works whose beauty springs from love freely chosen. The Fall interrupted that glorious undertaking; it did not originate our divine worth. Beneath the injuries of mortality, an inheritance older than our earthly memories remains. Even when we cannot perceive its fullness, the Eternal has not mistaken us for the darkness through which we travel.

Consider, then, the magnificence of what our Savior came to accomplish. He did not descend merely to pardon the wanderer while leaving him forever estranged from home. His redeeming work reaches the hidden springs of our being, where fear has learned to speak with the authority of truth, where suffering has persuaded the heart to distrust its own capacity for love, and where the habits of a fallen world have come to seem more natural than the divine life for which we were created.

He calls us into something greater.

The coming trials will reveal many things that prosperity has allowed us to overlook. A house may appear sound until the ground beneath it moves. So also the soul may mistake familiar comforts for the peace of God, or the absence of opposition for the possession of faith. Yet God has no need of evil to accomplish goodness. The darkness is not our teacher, nor is destruction the author of our redemption. The Lamb has already shown us another way.

And perhaps one of the greatest revelations of difficult days will concern the person standing beside us.

When fear counsels us to close our hands, will we remember how to give? When the world's assurances grow faint, will we still recognize the infinite worth of someone who has nothing to offer us in return? When another's freedom becomes inconvenient to our own desires, will our love remain worthy of its name?

These are among the quiet foundations upon which Zion must rise.

For the Kingdom cannot be established through power that has not first learned reverence, nor through knowledge that has forgotten mercy. The most splendid city Heaven could prepare would remain impoverished if its inhabitants had not learned to honor the sacred freedom of one another. A heart capable of telling the truth without cruelty, of giving without possessing, of remaining faithful without demanding its reward—such a heart has begun to comprehend the architecture of Heaven.

There is an astonishing generosity in the purposes of God. What He gives, He invites us to receive; what we receive, He invites us to make living within ourselves; and what becomes living within us finds its fulfillment in blessing others. Thus the Kingdom advances, sometimes through works so humble that the world passes them without notice.

A child protected. A stranger welcomed. A wrong relinquished. A wounded conscience restored to hope. A truth spoken with such love that another soul remains free to receive it.

These things will outlast much that presently appears immovable.

The last image got cropped somehow—here is the full version, with a few edits.

I bear witness that these things are true with all my soul.

Remember, the challenges to come will awaken us to the absolute need we have for God in all things and to the sacred work of building His Kingdom within and without. May we prepare with courage, tenderness, and unwavering devotion to our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, remembering that the greatest victories of Heaven are not measured by what we compel, but by what love and truth, freely received, enable us to become.

And may the glory of every good and holy thing return unto our Eternal Father and Mother, through the Lamb who makes all things new.

Glory to Elohim, forever and ever.

THE REPUBLIC'S LAST GIFT
The Birth of Zion and the Restoration of the Unfinished Eden

The Republic began to die while its great seal was still affixed to the laws. Its chambers retained the venerable vocabulary of liberty; the solemn words of earlier generations continued to be pronounced beneath painted ceilings; magistrates rose, assemblies convened, and men whose consciences had grown accustomed to compromise spoke with remarkable fluency of justice. Yet a civilization can preserve the grammar of its founding long after it has forgotten the obligations that gave its language meaning. A constitution remains an extraordinary achievement of human intelligence, though parchment possesses no power to make its custodians honorable. The republicans of an earlier age had wrested from arbitrary dominion a magnificent recognition: the individual conscience has a dignity preceding the state, and legitimate government must acknowledge a freedom it did not create. This inheritance was precious. Its betrayal was therefore immense. Gradually, the rights intended to defend human dignity became instruments through which the powerful secured advantage over the defenseless; commerce learned to conceal predation beneath the elegance of agreement, institutions discovered how to satisfy the letter of a covenant while extinguishing its generosity, and public authority assumed the habits of private appetite. Then came the appointed unraveling. The Republic faded, as the illuminated proclamation foretold, because its exhausted order was yielding to the birth of Zion. Within this providential design, the accumulated consequences of deception would expose the insufficiency of the old arrangements, while Heaven prepared a greater social order among those willing to receive it. The distinction carries profound moral weight. Deception remains the work of estranged wills; the restoration belongs to God. Divine wisdom requires no apprenticeship under evil. The Republic's final inheritance was therefore more splendid than its monuments: the very freedom it had imperfectly defended would become the voluntary foundation of a holier commonwealth. What had been proclaimed as a right would mature into a freely undertaken stewardship. The conscience emancipated from earthly tyranny would discover a still greater liberty—the capacity to bind itself, through love, to the good of another. Thus the passing of the Republic prepared the historical threshold of Zion, whose birth required the living consent of those destined to build it.

To comprehend the magnitude of this transition, the mind must return beyond the Republic, beyond the kingdoms that preceded it, to that ancient beginning in which humanity's education was contemplated beneath the providence of Heavenly Father and Heavenly Mother. Eden was the first undertaking of a greater earthly glory: a place where divine children might grow in knowledge, master the powers entrusted to them, cultivate beauty, and participate in creation through the harmonious exercise of love, truth, and sovereign will. The Fall interrupted that undertaking. Its deception was peculiarly ingenious because it presented estrangement as enlargement, offering knowledge detached from the very divine life that made knowledge fruitful. Here the two trees become an inexhaustible explanation of human history. One nourishes the faculties of the soul in their proper relation; the other cultivates a sophistication capable of defending its errors with extraordinary brilliance. The Republic's later disintegration would disclose the same ancient fracture upon a national scale: intelligence serving acquisition while love went hungry, liberty defending appetite while conscience languished, and institutions growing increasingly elaborate as their moral foundations diminished. Yet the Fall left another mystery, tenderer and more consequential than the history of corruption. The veil that limited mortal awareness was distinct from the fallen distortions that injured the exercise of human freedom. A magnificent book may remain closed with every sentence intact; a forged book may lie open upon the table and teach falsehood to all who read it. The first condition concerns access, the second integrity. So, in the sacred understanding of the soul, much of the divine inheritance remained preserved even while embodied consciousness struggled among the confusions of mortality. One might pass through a crowded street, attend to some ordinary obligation, or rest a thoughtful hand upon a windowsill, while capacities of immeasurable beauty awaited fuller expression in the life already being lived. Such hidden magnitude calls for reverence. The wisest soul can misjudge the hour of another's understanding; the most devoted heart can mistake impatience for fidelity. Heaven guards the sovereignty of its children even in their incompleteness. The restoration of Eden must therefore reach deeper than the replacement of governments. It must reconcile knowledge with holiness, awaken the soul's living inheritance, and bring the eternal capacities of spirit into the daily choices of the physical being.

The means of that restoration is the Atonement of Jesus Christ, whose grandeur unfolds with increasing consequence as the promised Kingdom approaches. Imagine the impoverishment of a theology in which redemption merely cancels the record of a ruined life while leaving its powers of thought, affection, and creation untouched. The Savior's gift reaches into the very conditions from which human wrongdoing continually proceeds. Through sanctification and purification, corrupted habits are brought into the searching presence of divine truth; through redemption and restoration, the injured capacities of the soul receive the possibility of renewed life; through exaltation, human becoming opens toward glories that mortal achievement can scarcely conceive. The foundational teachings place this work within the present life, where its fruits acquire the modest but unmistakable reality of action. A man trained from childhood to equate superiority with power discovers the harder courage of relinquishing an unjust advantage. A woman whose gifts have long been constrained by inherited falsehoods begins to act from the dignity of her own considered judgment. A household accustomed to hostility learns the unfamiliar discipline of speaking truth while leaving another person safe enough to hear it. Each transformation alters the conditions of creation. The four eternal realities—connection, nature, identity, and power—cease to remain propositions contemplated from afar; they enter the body as courage, the mind as clearer discernment, the heart as unfeigned tenderness, and the will as the capacity to bring something genuinely good into existence. Here the reciprocal law reveals its deepest generosity: what is received in holiness seeks fulfillment through giving, and what is offered freely enlarges the life of both giver and recipient. Heavenly Father and Heavenly Mother, united in divine purpose, have endowed their children with faculties capable of participating in this sublime exchange. Love gives truth a dwelling among living beings; truth preserves love from the exquisite dangers of self-deception; the sanctified will brings their concord into deed. The Kingdom's foundations are laid wherever this harmony becomes habitual. Every act of integrity prepares its government. Every reconciliation enlarges its peace. Every gift of understanding that enters the body and becomes service advances the restoration of an Earth intended, from its first morning, for divine progression.

The novel's approaching interval of two and a half to three years was consequently a summons of tremendous seriousness. Its significance lay in the accumulation of duties before the great disturbance, when foresight still possessed the leisure to become mercy. The foretold tribulations would begin; the Republic would pass through its appointed dissolution; inherited structures of commerce, provision, and public confidence would be tested beyond the assumptions upon which ordinary life had depended. The warnings contained in the accounts of plagues and trials spoke of interrupted supplies, impaired travel, upheaval among nations, and circumstances in which the habits of abundance could no longer be mistaken for guarantees of security. Yet the preparation required of Zion's future inhabitants was far richer than the accumulation of necessities. In one house, a woman measured the remaining grain and quietly set aside another portion for someone whose cupboards were nearly bare. In another, a family studied the means of preserving water, warmth, medicine, and communication while inviting a lonely neighbor into the conversation. Elsewhere, men and women whose talents had been squandered in rivalry began learning the neglected arts of cooperation: repairing what was broken, cultivating land, resolving disputes before they became injuries, and recognizing the peculiar strength of persons whom the old society had considered unimportant. The unseen architecture of a new civilization emerged through these acts long before any city possessed its name. Prayer accompanied the labor, becoming more attentive as circumstances grew more exacting. Its purpose extended beyond relief from danger into communion with Heaven—a discipline of listening, discerning, receiving, and acting with an increasingly unified heart and mind. The sacred teachings concerning heavenly ministry invited the faithful to cultivate their spiritual faculties, though wisdom also required them to examine impressions responsibly and honor the agency of every neighbor. Fear alone could gather a crowd. A shared devotion to truth and love could form a people. The approaching storm thus revealed the difference between preserving an individual life and preparing a society capable of sustaining life generously. Those who made room for others in the season of preparation were already rehearsing the laws of Zion. They were learning, while abundance still permitted choice, the obligations that scarcity would expose with unforgiving clarity.

As the old civil order receded, leaders of uncommon moral stature arose within the gathering people. Their emergence answered one of the gravest questions in the entire history of government: how may power become sufficiently strong to establish justice while remaining sufficiently humble to preserve freedom? The world had repeatedly solved the first difficulty by sacrificing the second. Zion demanded their reconciliation. The scriptural promise concerning a mighty servant who would set the house of God in order carried the solemn idea of restoration through divinely accountable stewardship; the historical disputes surrounding that promise also warned against the vanity of self-appointment. Within the novel, the coming leadership would therefore be recognizable through its works before its honors: legitimate inheritances restored, disorder patiently corrected, the vulnerable defended, sacred trusts protected, and laws rendered intelligible to the consciences they were meant to serve. Doctrine and Covenants 121 furnished the indispensable moral discipline. Spiritual influence found its authority through persuasion, longsuffering, gentleness, meekness, and love unfeigned. A leader could speak with formidable clarity, resist wrongdoing with unshaken resolve, and still approach another person's will as ground consecrated against trespass. Consider the extraordinary revolution concealed in that principle. The Republic had expended centuries attempting to restrain domination through external checks upon power. Zion would preserve justice through institutions while cultivating an inward character for which dominion over another soul had become spiritually abhorrent. Its finest statesmanship would join an exacting regard for liberty to a generosity large enough to make liberty beneficial to the weak. Those appointed to heal would honor the dignity of the afflicted; those administering justice would resist the purchase of judgment; those teaching holy things would refuse to convert sacred knowledge into personal supremacy; those entrusted with public leadership would measure achievement by the peace and flourishing of the governed. The ancient corruptions of priestcraft, kingcraft, lawyercraft, and doctorcraft would yield wherever their counterfeit authority was displaced by genuine service. And among the builders would arise minds of astonishing refinement, some long unnoticed by the customary hierarchies of the world, whose gifts would prove indispensable precisely because Zion required capacities the old Republic had scarcely known how to recognize. The Knight's office belonged to this order of fidelity. His courage was illuminated by restraint; his vigilance preserved avenues of freedom; his strength made possible a peace in which another's choice remained entirely her own. Such leadership could endure the scrutiny of Heaven because it had learned to regard another person's uncoerced flourishing as one of its greatest triumphs.

Then Zion began to take tangible form. There were storehouses whose abundance had been gathered for distribution rather than display; places of refuge where an exhausted traveler encountered shelter before being questioned about his importance; gardens and workshops in which skill was taught as an inheritance to be multiplied; councils whose deliberations sought the patient convergence of truth and charity; and homes where the dignity of every child was recognized before accomplishment furnished the world with reasons to admire it. Those who arrived brought differing histories, talents, convictions, and wounds. Their unity demanded the difficult labor of becoming worthy of one another's trust. They learned that equality of worth could coexist with extraordinary differences of capacity, and that consecration became most fruitful when individual gifts retained their full particularity. The beautiful mind was free to inquire; the powerful hand was free to build; the generous heart found new objects for its devotion. No person's excellence required the humiliation of another. This was the beginning of a terrestrial society, the higher earthly condition toward which the restored work had long been directed. Its ancestors were Enoch's city and the Salem of Melchizedek, whose remembered holiness rested upon righteousness, peace, and a communal life in which poverty ceased to be the accepted companion of plenty. In those ancient accounts, the ascent of a people toward Heaven concerned the transformation of an entire social order; the future meeting of Zion above with Zion below promised a still greater reconciliation of celestial and earthly life. Now the Republic's fading possessed its full narrative meaning. Its institutions had protected a portion of humanity's inheritance while leaving much of the soul's social destiny unrealized. Zion gathered what was worthy, redeemed what had been corrupted, and established a more complete civilization through the consecrated freedom of its inhabitants. The city was built in the world that had known collapse, its living foundations laid by hands that had once feared the future. As its people grew in mutual fidelity, their earthly works acquired an increasing correspondence with the life of Heaven. This was the promised birth: an actual gathering, an actual government of righteousness, an actual restoration of communal peace, and a people preparing to receive the fuller glory of God. The ruins of the former order remained a solemn remembrance. The new streets belonged to those who had learned to make freedom fruitful.

Yet the largest historical changes sometimes disclose their meaning most perfectly in an occurrence almost too intimate for history to record. Beyond the councils, the gathering, and the extraordinary labor of restoration, an individual life proceeds through its mortal hours. Morning arrives upon a familiar landscape; obligations await; questions arise whose deepest origins remain unnamed. Somewhere within that unremarkable procession of days, an intelligence of uncommon delicacy and strength may be learning to recognize what has long belonged to its own sacred nature. Its unfolding possesses a dignity that no other soul can hasten into being. Elsewhere, a faithful servant has learned that devotion may require the patient government of his own longing, that knowledge brings responsibilities rather than entitlements, and that the highest office of affection is sometimes to preserve an undisturbed place for another person's freedom. Across distances beyond the ordinary measures of geography, the novel permits a quiet correspondence between remembrance and becoming; its earthly expression awaits the sovereign participation of embodied lives. Such reserve contains its own austere beauty. A flower compelled open would surrender the very process by which its life becomes visible. The soul, whose capacities are infinitely greater, deserves a more exquisite regard. What the Eternal Parents have entrusted to a person must become fully that person's own through truth received, love freely answered, and willing action in the world. Thus the great restoration and the smallest act of tenderness obey a common law. Zion itself is a society whose people have learned to honor in one another the divine freedom through which holiness becomes possible. The Republic passes; the Kingdom rises; Heaven's purpose advances through the Atonement of Christ and the willing stewardship of His children. The appointed leaders build, the gathered people serve, the veiled inheritance acquires embodied expression, and what once seemed divided approaches a greater harmony. At the end of the long travail, when the first clear light rests upon the roofs of Zion, its people behold a city whose peace has already begun to resemble the society of Heaven. No earthly name can encompass the generosity from which such a work proceeds. Its joy returns beyond every throne, every crown, every treasured human achievement—unto Jesus Christ, and unto the Eternal Father and Heavenly Mother, whose love gave existence its glorious possibilities. Glory to Elohim, forever and ever.

https://t.co/CuccvGp4Bo

Peace begins with the ability to listen. Drawing on experiences in suicide prevention and domestic violence services, the author explores how empathy can transform the way we respond to suffering and conflict. Through Marshall Rosenberg’s framework of Nonviolent Communication, the article examines how anger, criticism and judgment often conceal unmet human needs. It argues for listening without rushing to offer advice, correct others or defend ourselves. Extending this idea from personal relationships to political and social life, the author suggests that nonviolence begins in everyday encounters, with the willingness to understand another person before passing judgment.

The states that make up the American Union are mostly in the nature of territories. . . formed for technical administrative purposes. These states did not and could not possess sovereign rights of their own. Because it was the Union that created most of these so-called states.

At the very least it should be mildly disturbing to hear that Hitler and Marx were named among the fans of Lincoln, and it should call into question just how “Republican” in the conservative sense Lincoln truly was. Far from being a sole indictment against Lincoln however, we should call into question the whole origin of the GOP. Are they truly conservative if they look back to Lincoln for inspiration? They were the original party to allow socialists to gained admittance into the U.S. government, which ushered in the progressive era of Roosevelt, Wilson, and FDR. It’s clear that a “renewal” is not the answer for the GOP, but rather a complete start from scratch. Either that or the creation of a third-party that will adhere to the Constitution and stop trampling on the rights of states and people like both parties have been in the habit of doing over the past 150 years. Still, it is the principles of God that will save this nation, the God that Hitler, Marx, and Lincoln rejected, not political parties. It is a battle of humanism vs. Christianity and only revival in the orthodox Christian sense has any hope of restoring the government of the United States.

The Council of Clermont was a mixed synod of ecclesiastics and laymen of the Catholic Church, called by Pope Urban II and held from 17 to 27 November 1095 at Clermont, Auvergne, at the time part of the Duchy of Aquitaine.[1][2]

While the council is known today primarily for the speech Pope Urban gave on the final day, it was primarily a synod focused on implementing the Cluniac reforms, enacting decrees and settling local and regional issues.[3] This also included the extension of the excommunication of Philip I of France for his adulterous remarriage to Bertrade of Montfort and a declaration of renewal of the Truce of God, an attempt on the part of the church to reduce feuding among Frankish nobles.[4]

Pope Urban's speech on 27 November included the call to arms that would result in the First Crusade,[5] and eventually the capture of Jerusalem and the establishment of the Kingdom of Jerusalem. In this, Urban reacted to the request by Byzantine emperor Alexius I Comnenus who had sent envoys to the Council of Piacenza requesting military assistance against the Seljuk Turks.[6] Several accounts of the speech survive; of these, the one by Fulcher of Chartres, who was present at the council, is generally accepted as the most reliable.

text:
HOW DARE YOU ? (Recall the 1,200-year-long Arab slave trade and the 11 million Africans captured by rival tribes and shipped to the Middle East... as well as the British Empire’s part in ending it ?)

Britain was not a coloniser; it was a liberator. The monuments that we have, that we conserve, they are linked with the British. If you look at how the slave trade was ended in Malawi, we owe that to the British.

Moses Mkumpha

 Slavery in East and Central Africa, it is almost forgotten; it is not discussed. We need to tell the world about it. With the Atlantic slave trade, we overlook what role the Oman [sultanate] played in the Middle East. What was their role? When looking at the slave trade, it’s always more focused on the transatlantic. There is a misconception that slavery started at the coast, like the coast of Ghana for example, but the history of slavery did not start there at the coast. It began much closer inland, in African communities where people were captured. What about the African leaders that were involved in slavery? We only talk about coastal slavery, but what about the inland dimension, where the slaves came, their roots, the markets? They lack international awareness.

Dr Oris Malijani

Across Africa, Britain has been called an oppressor and confronted with demands for slavery reparations.But one nation is celebrating the British Empire as a liberator. Malawi suffered from the brutality of Arab slavery, with its people captured by rival tribes and shipped to the Middle East, part of a 1,200-year-long traffic in human commodities that is often overshadowed by Europe’s transatlantic trade.The country wants to tell the world about this forgotten slave trade – and how Britain ran a determined campaign to end it. Malawi’s government is overseeing plans to build a museum dedicated to slavery, preserve mosques and markets linked to the trade, and have them inscribed as World Heritage sites to “send a message” internationally about this neglected chapter of history.Through its department of museums, Malawi will also celebrate the British Empire by conserving ruined forts built by colonial forces to protect Africans from marauding slavers.“Britain was not a coloniser; it was a liberator,” said Moses Mkumpha, who is working on the government-backed project to preserve colonial buildings.“The monuments that we have, that we conserve, they are linked with the British. If you look at how the slave trade was ended in Malawi, we owe that to the British.”Speaking in the capital of Lilongwe, Dr Oris Malijani, the project leader, told The Telegraph that Malawi’s plans would help to correct misperceptions about history, saying: “Slavery in East and Central Africa, it is almost forgotten; it is not discussed.”“We need to tell the world about it,” he said. The trade was once rife in the village of Nkhotakota, where today children cartwheel into the surf and boats rock gently offshore, their hulls filled with nothing more than an innocent bounty of fish. From the 1840s until around five generations ago, vessels sailed to this outpost on Lake Malawi – and many more like it – in search of a far more terrible catch. African slaves were seized by hunting parties, gathered in dusty stockades by the shore, and dispatched as human cargo by the sultanates of Arabia. It was a business described as the “trade of hell” by David Livingstone, the Scottish explorer and missionary, who witnessed it first-hand. This trade was the latest expansion of slavery from the Islamic world, which extended caravan routes across the Sahara, and from trading posts established along the coast of East Africa, like the slave hubs of Mombasa and Zanzibar, controlled by the Omani sultanate. According to the Institute of Commonwealth Studies, around 11 million people were transported from the African interior to the Arab world from around 800 to 1900. Unlike the transatlantic trade, more women were taken than men, mainly for domestic service and sexual slavery. On their journey to the coast to be trafficked, slaves were used as porters to carry large quantities of ivory for added profit. Illicit slave markets persisted in the Arab world well into the 20th century, despite determined efforts by Britain to stamp them out at the cost of much blood and treasure. However, Arab-led Saharan and Indian Ocean slave trades have been largely absent from postcolonial demands for apologies and financial reparations, a movement that has recently gained momentum. The King described the transatlantic trade as a “shameful chapter of history” at a Commonwealth summit earlier this month. Britain has also been facing demands for financial compensation, with some independent reports setting the figure owed at £20tn. Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, has partly bowed to growing pressure from the Caribbean Community and the African Union organisations by offering talks on an official apology and forms of investment and debt relief. The transatlantic trade enslaved 11 million Africans from around 1450 to 1900, created most of the black diaspora in the Americas, and creating much of the current racial politics in the West. Institutions from the Church of England to the British Museum have lamented their financial connections to the transatlantic trade, and historic crimes have been used to justify “decolonising” curricula and removing public statues. However, Britain ultimately worked to suppress this traffic, and to crush slavery around the world wherever the empire found it. Mr Mkumpha said that in contrast to the debate around reparations from wealthy Western countries, the trade shipping African slaves to the Arab world had been neglected. He said: “With the Atlantic slave trade, we overlook what role the Oman [sultanate] played in the Middle East. What was their role? When looking at the slave trade, it’s always more focused on the transatlantic [trade].” On the urging of Livingstone and subsequent missionaries, British forces intervened to curb the eastward trade of African slaves. Livingstone, who journeyed across the land that would become Malawi, described “the Lake slave-trade” going on “at a terrible rate”, in a region filled with slaves and littered with the corpses of those killed in wars or famines. After initial steps to protect Scottish missionaries working against the trade in the region, Britain declared it a protectorate in 1891, under the command of Harry Johnston, who promptly set about using troops and gunboats to dismantle slaving networks. His campaign included the defeat of the self-declared “Sultan” Mlozi in 1895. The leader was executed, with his skull allegedly becoming the trophy of a British officer. Meanwhile, on the coast, in 1896, Britain forced the Sultan of Zanzibar to give up slave-trading after a war lasting 45 minutes. Johnston gave his name to Fort Johnston, now the town of Mangochi, which is one of several historical sites that will be submitted for Unesco status as part of a planned “slave heritage route”. This will include other strongholds built to suppress slavers and cut supplies to Arab traders, including Fort Lister and Fort Mangochi in the south. The recent willingness of the Labour Government to make amends for the transatlantic trade has been noted in Malawi, and it is hoped that Britain will help to conserve symbols of historical pride. Mr Mkumpha said: “We need their help in terms of conserving them.”This could come in the form of straightforward funding, but also technical support from British heritage experts and museums. The museums department, which has limited capacity, will also seek to run research projects with universities that have access to archival material linked to Malawi. While raising the profile of the Arab-led trade and exploring how it was crushed, Malawi will also break new ground by stressing the often-overlooked fact that Africans were largely responsible for enslaving and selling fellow Africans. Dr Malijani explained: “There is a misconception that slavery started at the coast, like the coast of Ghana for example, but the history of slavery did not start there at the coast.“It began much closer inland, in African communities where people were captured. What about the African leaders that were involved in slavery?”In the land that would become Malawi – after British rule as Nyasaland and subsequent independence in 1964 – the African leaders dealing in slaves were typically the Islamised Yao people, who made captives of the Chewa ethnic group. On the beaches of Nkhotakota, modern-day Yao tribesmen mend their nets in the shadow of a crumbling mosque, which was built in the 19th century as part of the slaving outpost owned by Salim bin Abdallah, or “Jumbe”, a Swahili-Arab trader. He promoted both slavery and Islam in the area, sent around 20,000 captives each year to the coast, and founded a dynasty of powerful slavers – all called Jumbe – which was finally defeated by the British in 1894. “The mosque has been here many years, many years,” Ahamad Manich, a village elder, told The Telegraph. “There is no one who can afford to build it up. Maybe government.” As well as the British forts, Malawi’s government plans to conserve, and seek Unesco status, for the mosque, the country’s first. Currently, its history is modestly explained by a sign in English, which flocks of curious children from the area appear unable to understand. Heritage officials are planning to clear and excavate ground around the mosque where there was once a slave pen. It is currently a grassy wasteland used to pasture goats and dry “usipa” fish on wooden tables. Other slave market sites in Karonga, Phalombe, and Mangochi will also form part of Malawi’s Unesco plans, which officials hope will “send a message to the international community”. Nkhotakota itself has been chosen as the home for a planned slavery museum. Slavery sites have become tourist attractions in places such as Ghana, where coastal forts are sites of pilgrimage for some. However, Malawi wants to stress that slaves were transported by Africans in the interior, where traditional village life continues in many places. “We only talk about coastal slavery, but what about the inland dimension, where the slaves came, their roots, the markets?” Dr Malijani said. “They lack international awareness.”Mr Mkumpha and Dr Malijani discuss the preservation of Malawi’s historical sites. It is hoped that Malawi’s project will not only raise awareness of Britain’s role in suppressing the slave trade, but potentially will also lure tourists away from popular game parks such as Nkhotakota wildlife reserve and Liwonde national park. This influx of cash could support poorer communities that were, generations ago, ravaged by the slave trade. Government officials also hope that the project will prevent the Arab traffic in slaves from being overshadowed by a fixation on the European trade. Villages such as Nkhotakota show that it was not only across the waters of the Atlantic that the horrors of slavery were visited on Africa. And soon they will offer a clear reminder of the British Empire’s part in ending the cruelty of human bondage.

Craig Simpson (The Telegraph, November 12, 2026)

👑🦁🌍 PRINCE WILLIAM HONOURS AFRICA’S CONSERVATION HEROES — JOINED BY ZARA TINDALL, DIANA’S NIECES & SPECIAL GUESTS AT THE 2026 TUSK AWARDS! ❤️

Dear Royal Community, ❤️

What an inspiring evening for the Prince of Wales!

On Wednesday, 11 November 2026, Prince William attended the 14th annual Tusk Conservation Awards at Raffles London at The OWO, celebrating extraordinary individuals dedicating their lives to protecting Africa’s wildlife, natural habitats and communities.

As Royal Patron of Tusk since 2005, William has long championed those working on the front lines of conservation.

And this evening was about recognising their courage, sacrifice and remarkable achievements. 🌍

🏆 DANIEL YIANKERE — PROTECTING KENYA’S ENDANGERED RHINOS

Daniel Yiankere, Security Manager at Kenya’s Loisaba Conservancy, received the Tusk Wildlife Ranger Award.

With more than 30 years of experience, Daniel leads over 100 security and wildlife-monitoring personnel.

Since 2017, Loisaba has reported no poaching incidents under his leadership.

He also played an important role in the 2024 reintroduction of 21 critically endangered eastern black rhinos, helping restore a species that had disappeared from the conservancy.

Today, new calves offer hope for the future.

His recognition honours not only his personal dedication but also the bravery of the rangers who risk their lives protecting wildlife. ❤️

🌿 RAABIA HAWA — DEFENDING WILDLIFE AND COASTAL COMMUNITIES

Kenyan conservationist Raabia Hawa received the Tusk Award for Conservation in Africa.

As founder of the Ulinzi Africa Foundation, she leads efforts to protect elephants, endangered coastal topi and vulnerable ecosystems around Kenya’s Tana Delta and Lamu.

Her work goes beyond anti-poaching patrols.

Raabia also challenges illegal fishing, destructive trawling and environmental threats through legal action and community advocacy.

Her determination demonstrates that conservation requires courage, persistence and a willingness to stand up for both wildlife and the communities depending on these landscapes.

Congratulations, Raabia! ❤️

🦁 DR COLLEEN BEGG — THREE DECADES OF EXTRAORDINARY SERVICE

The prestigious Prince William Award for Conservation in Africa was presented to Dr Colleen Begg.

For more than 30 years, Dr Begg has worked to protect large carnivores in Mozambique while helping communities find ways to coexist with wildlife.

She has also championed women’s leadership in conservation, supporting a network of more than 100 women conservation leaders across 24 African countries.

Her lifetime of dedication reminds us that protecting wildlife and empowering communities must go hand in hand.

What a remarkable legacy! 🌸

❤️ TWO CONSERVATION HEROES FINALLY RECEIVE THEIR MOMENT

The evening also recognised two previous award winners who were unable to attend their original ceremony during the COVID-19 pandemic.

🇰🇪 John Kamanga of Kenya, recognised for community-led conservation through the South Rift Association of Landowners.

🇿🇼 Amos Gwema of Zimbabwe, honoured for his dedication to wildlife protection and anti-poaching intelligence.

Six years later, both men were finally able to celebrate their achievements in person.

A particularly meaningful moment of recognition! ❤️

👑 FAMILY SUPPORT FOR PRINCE WILLIAM

William was joined by familiar faces from both sides of his family.

His cousin Zara Tindall, daughter of Princess Anne, attended the ceremony.

Also present were Lady Amelia Spencer and Lady Eliza Spencer, the twin daughters of Earl Spencer and nieces of the late Diana, Princess of Wales.

The sisters are ambassadors for Tusk, making their attendance especially meaningful.

text:
A country cannot rise above the political consciousness of its people because political consciousness is the raw material from which institutions, leaders and policies are made. Leaders are drawn from the society they govern, and they behave according to what that society tolerates, rewards and demands.

1. What political consciousness means

It is the degree to which citizens understand their rights, their duties and the workings of power. It includes knowing that public office is a trust, that public money belongs to the people, that votes carry real weight, and that government owes citizens an account. It is a matter of awareness and also of willingness to act on that awareness.

2. Why a nation's ceiling is set by its people

Leaders are a reflection of the electorate. A people who sell their votes for rice, cash or T-shirts will get leaders who treat office as a return on investment. A people who vote along ethnic or religious lines will get leaders who reward loyalty over competence.

Institutions are only as strong as the pressure placed on them. Courts, electoral commissions, legislatures and anti-corruption agencies do not enforce themselves. Where citizens are indifferent, these bodies drift into capture, and where citizens are vigilant, they are forced to perform.

Policy follows demand. Politicians supply what the public asks for. If the public asks for stomach infrastructure, they get handouts at election time. If the public demands good schools, hospitals and power, politicians must deliver or be removed.

Accountability depends on memory and consequence. A politically conscious people remember broken promises and punish them at the ballot box. An unconscious people forget, forgive cheaply and recycle the same failed figures.

3. Illustrations

Nigeria offers a sobering case. Wealth and talent abound, yet public life is dominated by vote buying, godfatherism, ethnic calculation and a culture of excusing leaders who share one's identity. The failure of governance is, in large part, a failure of citizenship.

Other societies show the reverse. Nations such as South Korea, Botswana and Rwanda made their leaps when citizens insisted on discipline, accountability and results. Post-war Germany and Japan rebuilt through a population that demanded and sustained functioning institutions. Ghana's repeated peaceful turnovers reflect an electorate that has learned to use its vote as a weapon.

4. The obstacles to consciousness

Poverty makes people vulnerable to inducement, because a hungry voter finds a bag of rice more real than a manifesto. Poor education leaves citizens unable to read policy or detect propaganda. Ethnic and religious sentiment is easily manipulated. A compromised media and weak civil society deprive people of honest information. And a long history of disappointment breeds apathy, the belief that nothing will ever change, which is exactly what entrenched interests want.

5. The counter-argument

Some argue that structure matters as much as consciousness: that a rigged electoral system, a captured judiciary or an overwhelming security apparatus can defeat even a vigilant people. This is true in part. But structures are themselves human products, and they change when enough citizens refuse to accept them. Consciousness is therefore the precondition for structural reform, not a substitute for it.

6. The way forward

Civic and political education should begin in schools and continue through religious bodies, community associations and the media. Citizens must reject vote buying and treat their votes as a non-negotiable trust. Voters should judge candidates by record and capacity, not by tribe, faith or generosity. Independent journalism and civil society must be strengthened to keep power under permanent scrutiny. Above all, citizens must participate beyond election day, through attending town halls, monitoring budgets and demanding explanations.

The controversy comes amid a wider federal investigation into Omar’s immigration history and financial affairs. She denies wrongdoing.

If substantiated, the allegations raise serious questions about the use of immigration enforcement and prosecutorial powers for political purposes.

AMERICAN HERO OF THE DAY:

MINNEHAHA COUNTY DEPUTY KATHERINE FRANK, 26, KILLED SERVING A MENTAL HEALTH HOLD

Deputy Katherine Ann Frank of the Minnehaha County Sheriff's Office in Sioux Falls, South Dakota, was 26. One month ago today, on October 12, 2026, she died at Sanford hospital, surrounded by her family. In her final act of service, she became an organ donor.

On October 9, Deputy Frank was one of three deputies serving a mental health hold at a home in Sioux Falls. The suspect, Brandon Oetken, 39, opened fire in the entryway. She was struck at close range. A second deputy returned fire. Oetken faces three counts of attempted first-degree murder of a law enforcement officer.

She was born in Fargo, North Dakota, grew up in Madison, Minnesota, and graduated from Dawson-Boyd High School in 2018. She served with University of Minnesota police from 2018 to 2021, rising to corporal, then spent nearly two years as a correctional officer at the South Dakota State Penitentiary before joining the Minnehaha County Sheriff's Office in June 2024.

Her family describes her as incredibly funny, and as someone who gets along with just about everybody. She is survived by her parents, five siblings, her grandparents, and her boyfriend.

Rest in peace, Katherine.

You were the best America has to offer, and you always will be 🇺🇸
