text:
Allen Jackson Now – Broadcast Nov. 11, 2026

Al Gore and Gavin Newsom want Democrats to put climate change back at the center of politics. In this episode of Allen Jackson Now, Pastor Allen Jackson welcomes Marc Morano, publisher of Climate Depot and former Senate Environment and Public Works Committee staffer, to examine the renewed political push for climate policies.

Al Gore’s organization and California Governor Gavin Newsom are urging Democrats to make climate policy a renewed political priority. Pastor Allen challenges the influence of secular ideology on government policy and warns against allowing fear-driven narratives to replace careful examination of the facts. We must remain anchored in truth during a season of extraordinary cultural and political change.

: Well, good evening and welcome to Nashville. I’m Allen Jackson. President Trump has made American energy independence a cornerstone of his America First agenda—withdrawing from international climate agreements, rolling back environmental regulations, and promoting the oil, natural gas, and coal industries that have helped power America’s economic prosperity.

But following the midterm elections, the political landscape has shifted dramatically, and a climate movement that appeared to be losing influence may be preparing for a significant comeback. This week, influential global climate activists are boarding their private jets that run on fossil fuel, and they’re flying to Turkey for the United Nations climate summit. President Trump didn’t send an official delegation, but more than 100 governors, mayors, and officials are participating.

Former Vice President Al Gore’s organization is urging newly elected Democrat officials to prioritize climate policy. California Governor Gavin Newsom wants Democrats to stop avoiding the climate debate, arguing that everything from droughts to the price of beef and the price of coffee should be connected to climate change. And looking toward 2028, progressive Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez could become the Democratic presidential nominee, and she was one of the principal architects and public champions of the Green New Deal. It called for a sweeping government-led overhaul of America’s energy and transportation systems through massive amounts of taxpayer dollars.

Michigan’s newly elected Senator Abdul El-Sayed has supported the Green New Deal and has advocated moving toward 100% renewable energy. And in Texas, Senator-elect James Talarico argued in 2022 that not eating meat was necessary to fight climate change. There’s a larger contradiction here. America is in a high-stakes national security race with China for dominance in artificial intelligence—a technology that demands enormous amounts of reliable electricity. While communist China aggressively builds coal-fired power plants and expands its energy capacity to fuel its technological ambitions, progressive Democrats and climate activists are pushing to heavily restrict America’s energy production.

There’s a strategy that has been in play in our nation now for decades. It’s the ascendancy of globalism and the diminishment of nationalism. The worldview that has held globalism up and the values that guide their decisions are not in sync with the biblical worldview. If you want to promote the globalist worldview, the effect is you must diminish your other allegiances. Instead of nations making decisions based on their own strength, they outsource those decisions to international agreements.

It was President Barack Obama who bypassed Congress by formally committing the U.S. to the Paris Climate Agreement. He put U.S. energy policy inside of a global climate framework instead of making American energy production the top priority. The Paris Agreement sounds good on paper—reduce emissions, protect the planet—but at what cost? America starts pulling back on fossil fuels. President Obama rejected the Keystone pipeline in 2015, arguing it was not in the national interest, and then he tied it to climate concerns.

The unfortunate reality is secular ideas are driving policy. It is not science. Science didn’t drive the discussion that said fossil fuels are going to destroy us; that was very much ideologically driven. Case in point: in 2018, climate activist Greta Thunberg fired off an urgent tweet. The tweet said, and I quote: “A top climate scientist is warning that climate change will wipe out all of humanity unless we stop using fossil fuels over the next five years.” Well, here we are eight years later, and the people of the planet are still with us, thank God. What has vanished is not humanity and the earth, but rather that tweet.

Former Vice President Al Gore, the United Nations, and other globalist groups lean toward the same kind of error. They emphasize worst-case scenarios, using fear to drive urgency, and then calling for greater government intervention as the solution. It’s their religion. It’s what gives them a place in our world.

Well, I’m grateful for what President Trump has done in putting America first when it comes to energy. Trump made energy dominance federal policy. He cut energy regulations, making it easier and less expensive to drill and produce. During Trump’s first term, America became a net energy exporter with domestic energy production exceeding consumption. In 2019, America also became a net petroleum exporter, marking a historic reversal from decades of heavy dependence on foreign oil. Trump pulled America out of the Paris Climate Agreement. He argued that U.S. workers should not bear the cost of global climate rules that competitors like China do not match. China is the world’s largest carbon dioxide emitter, responsible for roughly a third of global emissions. China and India combine to produce approximately 40% of annual global fossil carbon dioxide emissions. Why aren’t the globalists and progressive Democrats bringing the same kind of scrutiny to those nations? Why focus on America?

Well, I propose that being anchored in truth is vital in this season because we’re walking through another season of change and unprecedented discontinuity. So, how do you stay anchored? The best way I know to maintain your equilibrium is to stay grounded in the Bible. I know it sounds like such an oversimplification, but it isn’t. It’s worth an investment of your time on a daily basis to read your Bible, then determine to honor Christ in every area of your life so that you might walk in the light of the truth that you’re learning.

Joining us in just a moment is the former senior staffer of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, Marc Morano. He’s now the publisher of Climate Depot and our go-to expert on the environment. He’s coming to us today from Turkey where he’s attending the United Nations Climate Conference. I’ll be right back.

: Tonight we’re joined by the former senior staffer of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, Marc Morano. Welcome to the show, Marc.

: Thank you, Reverend. Happy to be here live from Antalya, Turkey, at this turkey of a UN conference, COP31.

: Well, thank you for staying up late to do this. You are joining us from Turkey and it’s the UN’s climate summit. President Trump didn’t send an official U.S. delegation, so maybe you can give us a little bit of insight into what’s happening on the ground and what we should be aware of.

: Well, this just began—yesterday was the first official day. And rest assured, I want to tell everyone in America, Donald Trump did not send an official delegation, but I have appointed myself the unofficial U.S. representative.

There’s been a lot happening on the ground here, and it opens up with the World Health Organization President Tedros announcing that climate change was increasing cancer and heart attacks, which is scientifically absurd. Beyond this, you can see what the agenda is: they want to merge climate change into a public health agenda. He said that the public health threat of climate change was the strongest call for “climate action.”

Reverend Jackson, they have talked openly about adding climate change to death certificates as a cause of death. They have had doctors in Canada diagnosing patients as suffering from “climate change” when they get heat stroke. The American Cancer Society has done studies fretting about the carbon footprint of cancer treatments. So this is a very serious development, especially given what we saw happen during COVID, where the medical community went all authoritarian and appealed to authority. That was part of it.

The second part was John Kerry showing up—and just as gleeful as John Kerry can be, he still had a long face, oddly enough. I don’t know how he pulls that off, but he was happy. All right, that was a cheap shot there. But he revealed that America voted for climate change and made climate change a voting issue in the midterms. What I find fascinating about that is Michael Shellenberger did an analysis, and just 2% of Democratic House and Senate candidates even mentioned climate change during the entire year of 2026—2% of press releases mentioned it. Now that they’ve won, suddenly climate change is the mandate that they have.

We have 120 members of the U.S. Conference of Mayors, and we have 20 Democratic congressmen arriving later this week, and they’re all claiming some kind of climate mandate. This is how you turn a midterm election into a complete sea change on the climate front. They are going all in. There’s so much excitement here that Greta Thunberg, now 23 years old, has appeared at her first UN conference in five years. She senses that climate is about to rise like a vampire again, and she doesn’t want to miss out on all the fun.

: Well, just to make the point that you’re not actually manufacturing this, we have a clip from the UN climate change secretary. Listen to what he had to say.

(): The climate crisis is now a global health crisis of pandemic proportions. The impacts of rising heat on pregnancy, newborns, and maternal health are another unfolding health disaster which has the fingerprints of the climate crisis all over it. The root cause is humanity still burning colossal amounts of coal, oil, and gas and destroying forests.

: How is it possible to make these sweeping statements and offer no data, no scientific support? They just declare a crisis with all the authority of a revivalist preacher. How do they get away with that?

: They get away with it year after year, decade after decade. There’s really no one except the scattered climate skeptics and scientists who are willing to challenge it—and, of course, the Trump administration. That’s why they’re so excited. They see the midterms as a rebuke of Trump, and he was probably globally the number one reason they couldn’t get away with the kind of nonsense you just played.

First of all, climate is not causing any kind of public health problem. If you go back 100 years, there’s been a 99% drop in climate-related deaths. Second of all, the United Nations, the World Health Organization, and all these public health officials like to say that any bad weather event is due to your SUV driving, your coal plants, or you eating meat—when in reality, hurricanes, floods, tornadoes, wildfires, and droughts show either no trend or declining trends on climate timescales of 30, 50, or 100 years. So, it’s completely bonkers, unscientific, and insulting to the basic intelligence of the listener that they even make claims like that.

But they are in a giant echo chamber here, and they feel the energy. There’s so much energy here that the German chancellor’s party, the CDU party in Germany, is now considering creating a public register of any German citizens who allegedly spread “climate disinformation.” And the UN has already said they’ve partnered up with Google to make sure that the public only hears what the UN wants them to hear.

So this is a situation right now where we’ve got to be extra vigilant. As Donald Trump serves out his next two years and the Democrats have majorities, they are going to do everything possible to get the U.S. back in, and it does set the stage for 2028. I feel that never has there been more of an opportunity for someone like AOC—Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez—to win the presidency with the electorate doing these wild swings and the Republican Party fractured. This is just the kind of election in 2028 where someone like AOC could get in, and then it’s going to be all climate, all the time—Green New Deal, Democratic Socialists of America.

And one last point on this: this whole movement where they’re trying to merge climate, public health, infant mortality, cancer, and heart attacks is part of this DSA movement, which I like to say is not your father’s Green New Deal. If you go back to 2019, that Green New Deal was pretty wacky, but this new version of the Green New Deal is even more sinister in scope. You have leaders of the DSA openly embracing Stalin and Mao. Up until a few years ago, the DSA wouldn’t even allow avowed Soviet communists in, and they reversed that—they now allow them in, and they are now the think tank, the brainchild if you will, for the Democratic Party, leading the charge for taking power. So we are at a dark moment in U.S. history politically at this time.

Rough Transcript:

: Well, Marc, we need to take a short break. I hope you’ll stay with us for another segment.

: Sure. Yes, absolutely.

: We’re back now with the publisher of Climate Depot, Marc Morano. You know, Marc, I like to believe that I’m an environmentalist. I want the environment to be healthy and I think we have a responsibility to be good stewards of the planet Earth, but I don’t want to be a left-wing loon connected to communism, socialism, and the DSA. Is there a lane for those of us that might be a little more grounded in reality and real science?

: There has been, and the Trump administration was actually achieving it. With Chris Wright as Energy Secretary and Lee Zeldin at the EPA, they were trying to restore both the Energy Department and the EPA to their original missions. Keep in mind, the EPA’s entire mission was hijacked by President Obama and then President Biden just for climate change. The entire environmental movement has been hijacked by climate change.

In Washington, D.C., we had hundreds of millions of gallons of raw sewage spilling into the Potomac River for weeks and months at a time. For both entities in charge of the jurisdiction—meaning the District of Columbia and the state of Maryland—the entire focus of their environmental departments was on banning gas-powered cars and promoting EVs, solar, and wind, all about global warming and climate change, and they were almost clueless on how to deal with the raw sewage spill.

We saw during the Biden administration, with the East Palestine train wreck and the toxic plume that went up from the chemical explosion, they were almost paralyzed because they thought, “Wait, that’s not CO2. That’s not climate change,” and they just didn’t do anything. We have lead in drinking water and toxic waste site cleanups. What the Trump administration has been trying to do is restore the environmental movement back to the environment.

We had a professor named Denis Rancourt out of Canada, who was a left-wing professor, and he said the entire environmental movement is now focusing on this tenuous level of carbon dioxide in the environment—which is a trace natural gas that humans exhale—instead of actually focusing on real environmental problems. And the American people agree with this. Every Gallup poll has showed that global warming and climate change are dead last among environmental issues, meaning they rank lower on Americans’ concerns than species extinction, deforestation, clean air, and clean water. People just don’t care about climate change.

But the socialist left, the political left, and the international global elites from the World Economic Forum and the World Health Organization all focus on climate change because it’s the ultimate measure of control over humans. Over the last three years—particularly the last two—there’s been an unbelievable collapse of the whole climate movement. What we’re seeing here right now is like a vampire rising from the ground. You have hundreds of Democrats flying out here, John Kerry and Al Gore on the ground, and Greta back involved, and you can just feel it. There are so many people, Reverend Jackson—we had to wait four and a half hours yesterday just to get into this conference. The highways are clogged with people, and the restaurants are clogged. I think this was like a last-minute add-on that the country of Turkey was not ready for, with all the excitement due to the U.S. midterms.

They’re declaring the rise of climate even though they never talked about climate. In fact, one last point: climate activists have conceded—and this is on a website called HEATED—that the billionaire donor class of the Democratic Party explicitly told House and Senate candidates, “Do not mention climate change. Do not bring it up. Only use phrases like ‘affordability.'” And the Democrats did that—98% of press releases had zip mention, not even a mention of climate. Now that they’ve won the election, guess what they’re doing? “We have a climate mandate. The world’s concerned. We’re back in.” The whole event here over two days on Thursday in Turkey is all these mayors, congressmen, and Democrats coming to say, “We’re back in it. The U.S. is back in the climate agenda.”

: Well, data centers have been a hot topic through the election cycle. What’s the truth about data centers and their impact on our environment?

: There are two aspects to this—one some of your audience may not like, and the other I think they’ll understand very easily. Let’s talk about the environmental impact first. Data centers have a lower footprint than almost every other energy source or facility you could put up. They’re equivalent to putting in a shopping mall. They can recycle up to 60% to 70% of their water; they have new techniques to do that. They’re now going to be mandated by federal law to provide their own energy, and they’re also being mandated to work with local communities so that local communities aren’t damaged.

Having said that, here’s where I think the Republicans miscalculated in the midterms, and this is pretty significant. I don’t know if you’ve had a guest talk about this yet, but let me throw this out at you. I work for the Committee for a Constructive Tomorrow (CFACT) along with my website, Climate Depot. We deal with the anti-solar and wind folks, we deal with agriculture and the farmers, and we deal with the environmentalists on offshore wind. All of those grassroots people did not like data centers, and it really wasn’t even about the environmental impact. They just didn’t like the idea of Big Tech fat cats getting potential government contracts, and they didn’t like the scary thought of a surveillance state or Big Tech getting more power. And thirdly—which I don’t think anyone mentions enough—these are ugly, Soviet-style buildings. We’re finding out from the exit polls that people were just not happy, and I mean the Republican base. That is an issue that has to be retooled messaging-wise and policy-wise for Republicans to deal with. I don’t know if you were expecting me to say that, but I think that’s an important aspect of this midterm defeat.

: Now, we like the truth. I understand that congratulations are in order—Newsweek recently included you in their list of the 50 most prominent green policy dissenters. What an honor.

: Yes, thank you. I joined, of all people, Bill Gates. Bill Gates came out last year at the United Nations climate summit in Brazil and announced that climate was no longer a catastrophe and that people should focus on human flourishing. Of course, he was about to go heavily into AI, so people speculated that’s why. But I’ve been listed there with Jeff Bezos, Bill Gates, Joe Rogan, and Donald Trump, which begs one question, Reverend Jackson: how is my net worth not even on any scale compared to theirs? I feel like I’ve completely failed when you put me in their company.

In all seriousness, it’s an honor to be mentioned on that list of Newsweek’s top climate skeptics with those names because I’ve been fighting this whole climate movement for almost three decades now. My first global warming interview was back in the year 2000.

: Marc, I appreciate your time today and, most importantly, your commitment to the truth. Thank you.

$BRT Q3 2026 earnings: BRT's rent income barely moved, but its interest costs climbed

BRT Apartments, a Southeast and Texas landlord, collected slightly more rent but kept less of it for shareholders. Revenue rose 1%, while interest costs climbed 7% because BRT swapped cheap old mortgages for pricier new ones. As a result, cash earnings per share, a measure the board weighs when it sets the dividend, fell 14%.

• Revenue: $𝟐𝟒.𝟕𝐌 (+1.2% from a year ago)
• Cash earnings per share (AFFO): $𝟎.𝟑𝟏 ($0.36 a year ago)
• Interest expense: $𝟔.𝟑𝐌 ($5.9M a year ago)
• Interest outlook: 𝐀𝐛𝐨𝐮𝐭 $𝟏.𝟖𝐌 𝐚 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐡𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐞𝐫 (from debt deals in July and August)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🔴 Bearish

The story got worse because borrowing costs now absorb the small rent gains, and BRT expects that to continue. The company estimates its recent debt deals add about $1.8 million a year in interest. Its loans due in 2027 also carry rates below today's market, the filing says. One positive: overhead fell after senior executives retired, though most of that saving involves no cash.

The question now is whether BRT can keep its dividend and buybacks while debt costs rise. Either rents pick up and refinancing stays affordable, or the landlord cuts payouts, sells buildings or issues shares. The terms on next year's mortgage refinancings will settle it.

[Model: Claude Opus 5.5. Full article with charts - link in bio]

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢 𝐎𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐡𝐞𝐚𝐝 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬 𝐅𝐞𝐥𝐥 𝐀𝐟𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐄𝐱𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐑𝐞𝐭𝐢𝐫𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬
BRT Apartments runs its business with a small central team, and the cost of that overhead fell 10.5% from a year ago. The filing ties most of the drop to smaller stock-award charges after senior executives retired.

• Overhead: 14.2% of revenue, against 16.1% a year ago
• Stock-award charges: down $439,000 in the quarter
• Payroll over nine months: down $152,000

The saving lifts reported profit, but most of it involves no cash. Stock awards never counted in BRT's cash earnings measure. So the cash gain comes mainly from lower pay, and that is small beside the rise in interest.

What to watch: overhead as a share of revenue in the fourth quarter. A level near 14% would show that the landlord now runs on a lower cost base.

🟢 𝐁𝐑𝐓 𝐂𝐮𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐏𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐈𝐭𝐬 𝐂𝐫𝐞𝐝𝐢𝐭 𝐋𝐢𝐧𝐞
BRT keeps a $40 million credit line with Valley National Bank as backup money. In September the two sides amended it, so BRT now pays 2.1 percentage points above a benchmark short-term rate, down from 2.5.

• Minimum rate on the line: 5%, down from 6%
• Cash plus unused credit: about $52 million on November 2
• Extra cash from refinancing Civic Center 2 in July: about $20 million, by our math

This matters because the landlord may need the line for Ranch Lake, a Florida complex it agreed to buy, and for loans due next year. But the line itself expires in September 2027, so BRT must renew it too.

What to watch: whether BRT draws on the line to close Ranch Lake in early 2027. That would add debt whose rate moves with the market.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬 𝐆𝐫𝐞𝐰 𝐅𝐚𝐫 𝐅𝐚𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐚𝐧 𝐑𝐞𝐧𝐭
BRT Apartments borrows against its buildings, and many of its mortgages carry rates fixed years ago. As those loans come due, the landlord replaces them at today's rates. In July it swapped a 3.73% loan on its Civic Center 2 property for a 5.38% loan.

BRT said that loan and four refinanced late last year added $663,000 of mortgage interest in the quarter. Rent income did not keep pace, so interest now takes a bigger share of every dollar BRT collects.

• Interest expense: up 7.1% from a year ago
• Revenue: up 1.2%
• Interest as a share of revenue: 25.5%, up 1.4 percentage points
• Cash earnings per share: 31 cents, against 36 cents a year ago

This matters because cash earnings pay the dividend. Landlords call this measure AFFO, short for adjusted funds from operations, and it strips out depreciation and other non-cash charges. BRT's per-share figure fell 14%, and the company expects mortgage interest to keep rising.

What to watch: interest expense in the fourth quarter, the first full quarter with the new Civic Center 2 loan. A further rise in its share of revenue would mean rents still trail borrowing costs.

🔴 𝐏𝐚𝐲𝐨𝐮𝐭𝐬 𝐄𝐱𝐜𝐞𝐞𝐝𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐁𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐬𝐬 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐞𝐝
BRT Apartments says it will "carefully monitor our discretionary spending", naming the dividend and buybacks as the largest items. Yet over nine months it paid $10.4 million in cash dividends and $9.4 million for buybacks.

• Dividends plus buybacks: 117% of operating cash flow, by our math
• Dividend: 81% of cash earnings per share (AFFO), against 69% a year ago
• Equity: $150 million, down 15% since December

So BRT pays out more cash than its operations bring in, and cash fell to about $12 million by November. Its credit line requires a "tangible net worth of $140 million", and the filing does not show how the bank measures it.

What to watch: fourth-quarter buybacks and the next dividend decision. More buying while cash shrinks would leave less money for 2027 refinancings.

🔴 𝐑𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐁𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐥𝐲 𝐌𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐝 𝐢𝐧 𝐎𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐮𝐩𝐩𝐥𝐢𝐞𝐝 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭𝐬
BRT said too many new apartments compete for tenants in eight of its markets, including Atlanta and Dallas. It offers rent discounts, called concessions, "as a means to improve occupancy", and those discounts cut rental income.

• Rate increases: $86,000, about 0.4% of rental revenue by our math
• Property operating costs: 46.8% of revenue, up 0.4 percentage points
• Buildings co-owned with partners: operating margin of 48.1%, against 52.4% a year ago

Utilities, payroll, advertising and repairs pushed property costs up 2.1%, while cheaper insurance offset only part. So rent minus property costs at buildings BRT owned a year ago, which landlords call net operating income, hardly changed.

What to watch: the rental-rate line in the fourth-quarter results. If rate increases stay this small, rent cannot cover the rising interest bill.

🔴 𝐌𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐠𝐚𝐠𝐞𝐬 𝐖𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐡 $𝟐𝟎𝟕 𝐌𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐂𝐨𝐦𝐞 𝐃𝐮𝐞 𝐛𝐲 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟖
Most of BRT's mortgages end with one large repayment, called a balloon payment. The filing lists $207.4 million of these due through 2028, including loans at buildings it co-owns with partners.

BRT wrote that its cash flow and cash are "insufficient to fully fund" those payments. Without new loans, the landlord may issue shares or sell buildings "on potentially unfavorable terms".

• Due in 2027: $102.8 million
• Due in 2028: $104.6 million
• Average rate on loans maturing through 2027: 4.75%

This matters because recent refinancings all raised the interest bill. By our math, the rate a BRT partnership got in Atlanta in August sits about 1 percentage point above the 2027 loans' average.

What to watch: the rate on the first 2027 refinancing, which BRT will report in its filings next year. A rate near today's market would lift interest costs again.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐁𝐑𝐓 𝐏𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐬 𝐚𝐧 $𝟖𝟎 𝐌𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐅𝐥𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐝𝐚 𝐏𝐮𝐫𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐬𝐞
BRT agreed in June to buy Ranch Lake, an apartment complex in Bradenton, Florida, for about $80 million. The deal includes a government-insured mortgage at 2.91%, below current market rates, which BRT would take over. The seller reported $7.3 million of revenue over the past year, about 8% of BRT's sales last year by our math. BRT expects to close in early 2027, once the housing agency and lender approve.

𝐁𝐑𝐓 𝐍𝐨𝐰 𝐀𝐬𝐬𝐮𝐦𝐞𝐬 𝐇𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭 𝐌𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐠𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐑𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐬
Each quarter BRT estimates what its fixed-rate debt would be worth at current lending rates. In September it used rates above 6%, against roughly 5% in December. That puts its mortgages $41.9 million below their book value, so its existing loans cost less than new ones would. The filing also cites tariffs, recession risk and the wars involving Ukraine and Iran.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐃𝐞𝐛𝐭 𝐚𝐬 𝐚 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐭𝐨𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐚𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐭𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): 𝟕𝟒.𝟒%  ⇗ accelerating
Borrowing keeps climbing as a share of what BRT owns. Debt equals 74.4% of total assets, against 71.6% in December, and the ratio has risen in each quarter this year. New mortgages added debt while depreciation and losses shrank the asset base, which leaves less room to absorb pricier refinancings.

𝐏𝐫𝐞𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐫𝐞𝐝 𝐞𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐢𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟏𝟖.𝟐𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇒ stable
BRT's two preferred stakes in apartment owners, which it books as loans, kept paying on time. Interest income from them rose 6.8% to $346,000. But at today's market rates, BRT values them $540,000 below their book value, because those rates now exceed what the stakes pay in cash each month.

𝐃𝐢𝐥𝐮𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): 𝟏𝟖.𝟕 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
The share count fell 1.1% from a year ago because BRT kept buying back stock. It repurchased 276,014 shares in the quarter, after none a year earlier. A smaller count supports per-share figures, but it did not stop cash earnings per share from dropping.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐄𝐱𝐭𝐫𝐚 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐥𝐲 𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐟𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐝𝐞𝐛𝐭 𝐝𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐬: 𝐚𝐛𝐨𝐮𝐭 $𝟏.𝟖 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐚 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫  ⇗ accelerating
New. BRT estimates its July and August debt deals add about $1.8 million a year in interest. By our math, that equals about 7% of the third quarter's interest cost on a yearly basis. The company also expects its 2027 refinancings to raise mortgage interest, because current rates exceed what those loans carry.

𝐐𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐥𝐲 𝐝𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐝: $𝟎.𝟐𝟓 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from $0.25 per share
Unchanged. BRT paid 25 cents a share again in October. The filing puts cash dividends through 2028 at no less than $41.8 million at that rate. The board sets the amount each quarter after reviewing cash needs, debt maturities and earnings measures, the filing says.

𝐒𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐛𝐮𝐲𝐛𝐚𝐜𝐤 𝐚𝐮𝐭𝐡𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐳𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧: $𝟏𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐫𝐨𝐮𝐠𝐡 𝐃𝐞𝐜𝐞𝐦𝐛𝐞𝐫 𝟑𝟏, 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟖  ⇗ accelerating
🠅 raised from about $4.9 million remaining through December 31, 2028 (as of August 3, 2026)
Raised. The board refilled the buyback program to $10 million in September, its second top-up this year. BRT then spent $3.3 million in October and early November, leaving about $5.4 million. By our math, nine-month buybacks already run nearly twice the 2025 full-year total.

𝐑𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐡 𝐋𝐚𝐤𝐞 𝐚𝐜𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧: 𝐚𝐛𝐨𝐮𝐭 $𝟖𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧; 𝐜𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐢𝐧 𝐐𝟏 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from about $80 million; closing expected in Q1 2027
Unchanged. BRT still expects to close the Bradenton purchase in the first quarter of 2027. By our math, the price minus the assumed mortgage leaves about $34 million for BRT to fund. The company plans to use cash, operating cash flow, mortgage proceeds and, if needed, its credit line.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

text:
The uncomfortable truth:

Buc-ee’s has the legal right to protect its trademark. The law is on its side. The precedent supports aggressive enforcement. The corporation is doing exactly what trademark attorneys advise: sue early, sue often, sue everyone.

And none of that makes it right.

A family in Beavercreek, Ohio opened a carryout store in 2017. They named it after their town. They put a beaver on the sign  because the town is called Beavercreek. They sell snacks and drinks to their neighbors. The owner feeds his two children with the income.

A multi-billion-dollar Texas corporation with 75,000-square-foot travel centers, 100+ gas pumps, and a legal team that files a dozen lawsuits a year looked at that family carryout and said: your beaver logo could confuse our customers.

16 miles apart. One has 100 gas pumps and sells Beaver Nuggets to millions. The other has no gas pumps and feeds two kids.

And the law says: Buc-ee’s might win.

Because the law doesn’t ask: is this fair? The law asks: is there a likelihood of confusion? And in the sterile language of trademark analysis  same industry, same animal, same color  the answer can technically be yes. Even when every human being with functioning eyes can see these are not the same thing.

John Oliver dared Buc-ee’s to sue someone its own size. Buc-ee’s looked at HBO, looked at the family carryout, and chose the carryout. Because HBO has lawyers. The carryout has two kids to feed.

That’s not trademark protection. That’s choosing which fight you can’t lose.

Buc-ee’s will probably win this lawsuit. The legal math favors the bigger budget. The settlement offer will be cheaper than the legal bills. The store might rebrand. The store might close.

And Buc-ee’s will have protected its trademark. And lost something that no trademark registration can get back: the belief that the company with the friendly beaver is one of the good guys.

“I have two kids and this store is how I feed them.”

That’s the other side of a federal trademark infringement lawsuit. A family that named their store after their town. In a town named after beavers. Being sued for using a beaver.

The beaver logo is on the sign. The lawsuit is in federal court. The internet has picked a side.

And Buc-ee’s is winning the case while losing the room.

text:
The Brian Banks case is one of the most heartbreaking examples of how a false accusation can destroy an innocent person's life. In my opinion, anyone who deliberately makes a false accusation that leads to another person's imprisonment should face serious legal consequences. Justice should never be a one-sided system where the accused loses everything while the accuser walks away without accountability.

Brian was only 16 years old when his future was taken from him. He had talent, ambition, and a promising football career ahead of him. He was offered a scholarship by USC, and the NFL was within his reach. Yet, because of a lie, he spent years behind bars, lost his opportunities, and carried the stigma of being a registered sex offender. No amount of money can truly compensate for the years he lost, the emotional trauma he endured, or the experiences he could never get back.

What makes this case even more disturbing is the alleged refusal to tell the truth because of financial consequences. If someone knowingly allows an innocent person to remain imprisoned to protect a financial settlement, that is not merely a moral failure; it is an attack on the justice system itself.

However, I also believe this case should not be used to discourage genuine victims from reporting abuse. False accusations must be punished, but legitimate victims must still feel safe coming forward. The law should distinguish between an honest mistake and a deliberate fabrication intended to destroy another person's life.

Brian Banks deserves recognition for his resilience. Despite everything he endured, he refused to allow his past to define his future. His story reminds us that the justice system can make devastating mistakes, and those mistakes can have consequences that last a lifetime.

My position is simple: if you knowingly lie and send an innocent person to prison, you should face proportionate criminal penalties, financial restitution, and accountability.

One lie destroyed ten years of his life. The question is, should the person responsible be allowed to move on as if nothing happened?

text:
Politico: DUBLIN -  EU leaders gathering in Dublin on Friday will continue arguing over who should represent them in talks about Ukraine’s future after a day of ferocious diplomatic activity. As Donald Trump’s administration intensifies its efforts to broker an end to Russia’s war and Europe may have secured a place at the table, bickering over who will speak on behalf of the bloc already looks like overshadowing the summit in the Irish capital — that wasn’t even supposed to be about Ukraine in the first place.

“You could even have a TV show about it,” Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal joked to POLITICO in an interview on Thursday, in a sign of just how stark the divisions have become among leaders. “But we are saving the best part for tomorrow.”

Russia’s full-scale invasion started in February 2022 and as Trump’s enthusiasm for brokering peace has ebbed and flowed, the EU has found itself edged out of the picture ― despite increasingly picking up the tab.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who met with about 50 EU and non-EU leaders in Dublin on Thursday, warned that Russia was seeking to reshape Europe’s security architecture and insisted that European governments must have a voice in the negotiations, following two days of Russia-Ukraine-U.S. negotiations in Abu Dhabi that largely left out the EU.

Trump’s envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, discussed the issue with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow earlier on Thursday before the American pair touched down in Dublin in the evening to offer Zelenskyy their thoughts.

The EU is united over the need to have a seat at the table as Ukraine’s main backer, but not on who it should send, with diplomats and officials telling POLITICO that the bloc has split into at least three camps.

In one, there is growing support for European Council President António Costa, whose role makes him the natural candidate to represent the bloc. In another, there’s France and Germany, both of which are reluctant to surrender their own places at the negotiating table to Brussels.

And then there’s the loneliest camp of all, the backers of Kaja Kallas. The bloc’s top diplomat would be the obvious pick, if not for her hawkishness on Russia, which some diplomats say could put off the Kremlin and make her a liability.

Costa is accountable

When it comes to speaking for Europe, there’s one man who’s already got that in his job description.

Costa is emerging as the most broadly acceptable candidate among EU capitals. His institutional role gives him a mandate to represent the bloc’s leaders on the world stage, while his position and background as a former Portuguese prime minister afford him some neutrality, according to a European diplomat, who was granted anonymity because of the sensitive nature of the discussions.

Estonia’s Michal was the first leader to come out in support of Costa, telling POLITICO his “mandate comes directly from the [European] Council” and makes him “accountable” to the EU’s member countries.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who called for the issue to be added to the agenda of Friday’s talks, said she would be OK with Costa, while Luxembourg and Poland’s leaders also backed him in remarks to reporters Thursday.

Costa himself has also made it clear that the EU is represented internationally by its institutions — meaning him.

Kallas, however, is a much more divisive proposition.

Some diplomats see the former Estonian prime minister, who an EU official once said eats “Russians for “breakfast,” as an unacceptable interlocutor for the Kremlin.

“That’s a joke, right?” another European diplomat said of the prospect of Kallas representing the EU in the high-stakes talks, describing her as “probably the worst person you could pick.”

But others argue that it’s precisely this hawkish reputation that makes her the right person for the job. “It would make much more sense,” a second senior European diplomat told POLITICO. “That’s what Putin would do. He would pick whoever you don’t want to talk to.”

Michal argued Kallas’ role makes her a natural second to Costa, and that both will presumably be in their positions until their terms end in 2029, making them more reliable than a national leader. “Putin doesn’t have to like it,” he added.
Paris and Berlin are less keen

The biggest obstacle to choosing a negotiator, though, might not be Putin but the EU’s two biggest capitals.

France and Germany are unlikely to welcome an arrangement that gives Brussels a monopoly on representing Europe in negotiations, two European diplomats and an EU official told POLITICO.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz made his opposition clear Thursday, calling the participation of the E3 countries in talks on Ukraine “a well-established format.”

“We are also working together on this task with five representatives — from Germany, the United Kingdom, France, Italy, and Poland. I see absolutely no problem with keeping it that way,” he said.

Paris also has little incentive to hand over its seat at the table. France is a permanent member of the United Nations Security Council and possesses Europe’s only nuclear arsenal, giving it diplomatic and military leverage that no EU institution can replicate, French MEP Fabrice Leggeri of National Rally told POLITICO, adding he could “hardly imagine” Costa or Kallas speaking for Paris.

“France, Germany, and the U.K.,” the E3 countries, “will always be France, Germany and the U.K.,” Estonia’s Michal argued, adding nothing stopped them from talking bilaterally to Moscow. But on decision-making affecting the whole continent, they needed to get on board with “consensual politics.”

“This is what the European Union is,” he said. “This is the basis of having this kind of consensual politics and keeping everybody together on the same page against Russia.”

EU leaders are unlikely to formally appoint an envoy at Friday’s gathering, but discussions could produce a broader “understanding” about how Europe should be represented, a senior EU official said.

Irish Foreign Minister Helen McEntee told POLITICO that at Friday’s talks, leaders will still need to “tease through” the issue “a little bit more.”

They may not have that much time, though. Zelenskyy this week urged the EU to hurry up and pick someone — anyone — to speak for it. “I think that in November, not later, we need to accept who will represent Europe in negotiations,” he said.

There's a reason for that: western Europe is a sub-continent with a lot of historically intermarried, fractious actors in states which have either been at war with eachother, or with Russia or others for a thousand years or more.  

Here's a (brief) run-down of the wars France and Britain alone were fighting against each other, they continued until they decided to try a different enemy together i.e. Russia in Crimea. 

Medieval Clashes (1066 – 1453)

Anglo-French War (1109–1113) — Fought over control of the Vexin region in northern France.

Anglo-French War (1116–1119) — King Louis VI of France clashed with King Henry I of England over Normandy.

Anglo-French War (1123–1135) — Continued disputes over the Duchy of Normandy.

The Revolt of 1173–1174 — King Louis VII backed a rebellion by Henry II’s sons against the English crown.

Anglo-French War (1202–1214) — King Philip II of France successfully stripped King John of almost all English territories in France, including Normandy.

The Saintonge War (1242–1243) — King Henry III failed to reclaim his family's lost French lands.

The Gascon War (1294–1303) — Fought over the remaining English territory of Gascony in southwest France.

The War of Saint-Sardos (1324) — A brief conflict in Gascony that acted as a direct precursor to the Hundred Years' War.

The Hundred Years' War (1337–1453) — The famous, multi-generational conflict over the French throne, ending with England losing nearly all its continental possessions except Calais.

Renaissance & Early Modern Conflicts (1475 – 1667)

English Invasion of France (1475) — King Edward IV invaded France, resulting in the Treaty of Picquigny.

The Italian Wars (1494–1559) — England repeatedly intervened against France across several phases, including the War of the League of Cambrai (1511–1514) and the Rough Wooing in Scotland, where France backed the Scots against England.

Anglo-French War (1557–1559) — England allied with Spain against France, resulting in England losing Calais, its last foothold on mainland Europe.

Anglo-French War (1627–1629) — King Charles I sent forces to aid French Huguenot rebels during the Siege of La Rochelle.

Second Anglo-Dutch War (1666–1667) — France entered the war on the side of the Dutch Republic against England.

The "Second Hundred Years' War" (1689 – 1815)

During this era, England (and after 1707, Great Britain) fought France almost continuously for global, colonial, and naval supremacy:
Nine Years' War (1688–1697) — Known as King William's War in North America, fought to stop the expansion of King Louis XIV.

War of the Spanish Succession (1701–1714) — Known as Queen Anne's War in North America, preventing France and Spain from uniting under one Bourbon monarch.

War of the Austrian Succession (1740–1748) — Included the Jacobite Rising of 1745, where France backed Bonnie Prince Charlie's attempt to take the British throne.

Seven Years' War (1756–1763) — A true global war across Europe, North America, and India, resulting in Britain taking Canada and Florida from France.

American Revolutionary War (1778–1783) — France officially allied with the American colonies, supplying crucial troops, money, and naval power to defeat Britain.

French Revolutionary Wars (1792–1802) — Britain led multiple European coalitions against the new French Republic following the execution of King Louis XVI.

Napoleonic Wars (1803–1815) — Britain fought Napoleon Bonaparte across Europe and the high seas until his final defeat at the Battle of Waterloo.

COSTS 

(I'm looking at what historians have written converting war costs into modern value, looking at two metrics, Simple Retail Price Index (RPI) / Inflation or what the goods and soldiers' wages would cost in today's pounds/euros and Relative Share of GDP (or the economic impact) to calculate how much of the nation's total wealth the wars consumed, which is sort of considered the most accurate way to measure the true burden of a war).

So, using the Relative Share of GDP (comparing historical spending to the size of the modern UK/French economies), the major Anglo-French conflicts would cost well over £15 trillion to £20 trillion combined in today's terms.

For the costs for the biggest chapters of the "rivalry", I've focused on British Treasury records (which are the most complete continuous financial records in Europe)

1. The French Revolutionary & Napoleonic Wars (1793–1815)
Historical Cost (Britain): ~£1.65 billion (and added ~£850 million to the British National Debt).
Modern Equivalent (Inflation only): ~£140 billion – £160 billion.
Modern Equivalent (Share of GDP): ~£6 trillion – £8 trillion.
Cost reality: This was the most expensive conflict in British history relative to the size of the economy. By 1815, Britain’s national debt exceeded 200% of its GDP (a higher debt-to-GDP ratio than after World War I). 
To pay for it, Britain invented the world's first income tax in 1799 and suspended the gold standard. 
France funded its armies largely by plundering conquered territories across Europe, though Napoleon’s final defeat still left France paying massive war reparations.

2. The Seven Years' War (1756–1763)

Historical Cost (Britain): ~£80 million to £100 million (British debt doubled from £74m to £133m).
Modern Equivalent (Inflation only): ~£15 billion – £20 billion.
Modern Equivalent (Share of GDP): ~£1.5 trillion – £2 trillion.
The Financial Reality: Fighting a global war across North America, Europe, India, and the Caribbean nearly bankrupted both nations. 
Britain "won" Canada and India, but the resulting debt crisis forced Parliament to tax the American colonies (the Stamp Act, Tea Act, etc.), directly triggering the American Revolution.

3. The American Revolutionary War (1775–1783)

Historical Cost (Britain): ~£80 million to £100 million.
Historical Cost (France): ~1.3 billion livres tournois (roughly £55–£60 million at the time).
Modern Equivalent (Share of GDP): ~£1.2 trillion – £1.5 trillion (for Britain) and ~£1 trillion+ (for France).
Cost reality: While Britain absorbed its debt thanks to the Industrial Revolution and the Bank of England, France's decision to fund the Americans pushed the French monarchy into total bankruptcy. 
By 1788, over 50% of France's entire national budget was going just to pay the interest on war debts, the direct spark that ignited the French Revolution in 1789.

4. War of the Spanish Succession (1701–1714) & Nine Years' War (1688–1697)

Historical Cost (Britain): ~£50 million (Spanish Succession) and ~£30 million (Nine Years' War).
Modern Equivalent (Share of GDP): ~£1 trillion – £1.5 trillion combined.
Cost reality: The Nine Years' War was so expensive that England couldn't pay for it with traditional taxes. In 1694, King William III created the Bank of England specifically to borrow £1.2 million from the public to build a navy to fight France. This was the birth of the modern British National Debt.

5. The Hundred Years' War (1337–1453)

Historical Cost (England): Estimated at roughly £3 million to £5 million spread across 116 years (with single major campaigns, like Henry V’s Agincourt campaign, costing around £100,000–£200,000).
Modern Equivalent (Inflation only): ~£3 billion – £5 billion.
Modern Equivalent (Share of GDP): ~£2 trillion – £3 trillion+.
Cost reality: In the 1300s, the entire annual income of the English Crown in peacetime was only about £30,000
Fighting France required King Edward III and his successors to constantly beg Parliament for wool taxes, take massive loans from Italian bankers (bankrupting the Bardi and Peruzzi banking families of Florence when England defaulted), and pawn the Crown Jewels.

6. Medieval & Tudor Clashes (1066–1667)

Modern Equivalent (Share of GDP): ~£1 trillion – £2 trillion combined.
Cost reality: Wars like Henry VIII’s invasions of France in the 1510s and 1540s were ruinously expensive. Henry VIII burned through the entire fortune his father (Henry VII) had left him, sold off most of the land seized during the Dissolution of the Monasteries, and finally resorted to "debasing" the currency (replacing silver coins with cheap copper coated in silver), which caused massive inflation across England.

Summary: What Did the Rivalry Actually Buy?

Aside from trying to reshape the world map, the financial struggle between Britain and France literally invented modern global finance and debt:
To beat France's larger population and landmass, Britain invented the Bank of England, government bonds, the stock market, and income tax.  We have been forced to fund their wars of lies and avarice for hundreds of years and it's even worse now.
France's inability to modernize its tax system to keep up with British borrowing led directly to the collapse of the French Monarchy in 1789.
Britain never did finish paying off the final consolidated bond/s.

text:
🚨 HERE WE GO $RKLB: PETER BECK JUST DROPPED SOME MASSIVE DETAILS ABOUT ROCKET LAB'S FUTURE. 

$70M LAUNCHES, 50% MARGINS, IRIDIUM AND A $1 TRILLION SPACE MARKET.

I went through Sir Peter Beck's latest interview a few hours back with Tevis.  

1. Q3 EARNINGS: BECK IS MORE INTERESTED IN CONSISTENT GROWTH THAN ONE GOOD QUARTER. 

Beck said:  

"A billion dollars of launch sold in the quarter is, that's pretty good."

He also pointed to Rocket Lab's consistent growth over multiple years, with annual revenue approaching $1 billion.  

What interests me is that Rocket Lab is building a substantial space systems business while simultaneously funding Neutron.  

The launch contracts are getting attention, but the underlying business has continued growing even without Neutron generating revenue.

2. NEUTRON'S DELAY: BECK WOULD RATHER FIND PROBLEMS ON THE GROUND THAN IN FLIGHT.

Neutron was originally targeted for 2024. The current expectation discussed in the interview is 2027.

Beck acknowledged that the original target assumed an unusually favorable development schedule.

His exact comment:

"I'd much rather find an issue with, for example, a tank on the ground during a test program than find it in flight."

I agree with him here.

A delay is frustrating, especially when development costs are significant but identifying structural problems during testing is preferable to losing a vehicle and potentially disrupting an entire launch schedule.

The important question now is whether the engineering issues are actually being resolved.

3. NEUTRON IS BEING BUILT FOR MULTIPLE LAUNCHES, NOT JUST ONE SUCCESSFUL FLIGHT.

Beck said Rocket Lab isn't simply trying to get the first rocket onto the pad. It's preparing to launch the second, third, fourth and subsequent vehicles without lengthy gaps.

He discussed three important investments.

- An autonomous ocean recovery barge requiring approximately two to three years to build.
- Engine manufacturing capacity capable of producing an engine in a matter of days. 
- Building multiple components in parallel rather than waiting for every earlier component to complete testing.

That last point is imp.  

Parallel manufacturing carries the risk of scrapping hardware if designs change, but it can shorten the time between early flights.  

Rocket Lab is spending money today to prepare for a higher launch rate later.

4. NEUTRON COULD REACH OPERATING PROFITABILITY BELOW 10 LAUNCHES ANNUALLY.

This was one of my favorite statements.  

Beck said:  

"We amortize or at least cover the costs of everything at a pretty short number, below 10 launches a year." 

He also reiterated the long term model:  "50% gross margin."

At a $70M launch price, eight annual launches would represent $560M in gross launch revenue before any adjustments.  

That doesn't mean $560M in profit but Beck's argument is that reusability and higher launch frequency allow the company to spread fixed infrastructure costs across more missions.  

The distinction is important. This is management's expected mature operating model, not a margin Rocket Lab has already demonstrated with Neutron.

5. NEUTRON'S $70M LAUNCH PRICE IS NOT A DISCOUNTED INTRODUCTORY OFFER. 

Beck was very clear about pricing.  

"There's not a single Neutron vehicle that's been discounted." 

In fact, he said Rocket Lab deliberately waited until it could sell launches at full price.  

That's interesting because customers normally demand discounts when purchasing flights on rockets that haven't flown.  

But launch capacity is limited and customers planning satellite constellations need to secure deployment windows years ahead. 

Rocket Lab is using that scarcity to protect pricing rather than sacrificing margins simply to fill its launch manifest.

6. IRIDIUM INTEGRATION: BECK EXPECTS THE IMPORTANT WORK TO HAPPEN IN MONTHS, NOT YEARS. 

The interviewer asked whether operational synergies could take three to five years.  

Beck responded:  

"I would measure this in months, not years." 

He acknowledged that integrating Iridium would be a larger organizational challenge than previous acquisitions.  

But his reasoning for buying a space services business was straightforward.  

Rocket Lab knows how to design spacecraft and launch rockets. Iridium brings an established customer base and the experience of operating commercial services from orbit.  

Beck openly acknowledged that Rocket Lab has something to learn from that experience.  

I like that approach. Buying an established services operation could shorten the time needed to develop a recurring revenue business, although closing the transaction and achieving integration synergies remain risks.

7. ROCKET LAB ISN'T PLANNING TO STOP WITH SATELLITE COMMUNICATIONS. 

Beck said investors should expect multiple space-based services, not just communications.  

Rocket Lab wants to combine its spacecraft manufacturing, launch capability and future orbital infrastructure with businesses that generate revenue after satellites reach orbit.  

The Iridium transaction is being discussed as a starting point for that broader services strategy.  

It's not supposed to be the final acquisition or the only space service Rocket Lab offers.

8. LAUNCHING ROCKET LAB'S OWN SATELLITES COULD GENERATE BETTER LONG-TERM ECONOMICS. 

Beck explained the difference very simply.  

- Launch another company's satellite and Rocket Lab receives launch revenue once. 
- Launch its own satellite and the company could collect service revenue for years.  

His exact line:  

"The economics are far stronger to launch your own stuff." 

He discussed the possibility of reserving substantial Neutron capacity for Rocket Lab's internal programs while continuing to serve outside customers.  

A successful launch business gives Rocket Lab access to space. Owning operational satellites could allow it to capture more revenue from what those spacecraft actually do once they're there.

9. ORBITAL DATA CENTERS: BECK IS INTERESTED BUT HE ISN'T BETTING THE COMPANY ON THEM. 

Rocket Lab has already signed Starcloud as a Neutron customer. But Beck was surprisingly cautious about the economics of orbital data centers.  

"I'd rather be a fast follower than kind of leading out the front." 

And:  

"I'm certainly not gonna bet the business on it." 

I actually respect that.  

The opportunity could become significant, but power generation, thermal management, networking and the cost of replacing hardware in orbit remain difficult engineering and financial questions.  

Rocket Lab can sell launch and spacecraft services into that market without committing billions to owning orbital computing infrastructure before the economics are proven.

10. DEFENSE CONTRACTS COULD BECOME A RECURRING SOURCE OF DEMAND. 

Beck expects continued opportunities in national security space programs.  

His reasoning is that defense satellites eventually need replacing, while changing threats create demand for new capabilities.  

He also described these programs as relatively resilient across changes in government.  

It's important because national security satellites aren't necessarily one time purchases.  

There can be recurring opportunities from replacement constellations, upgrades, additional spacecraft and new missions.  

Rocket Lab still has to compete for those contracts, but Beck expects demand to remain consistent.

11. THE POST-MIDTERM POLITICAL ENVIRONMENT ISN'T HIS BIGGEST CONCERN. 

When asked whether changes in Congress could affect defense spending, Beck described the outlook as largely business as usual.  

He pointed to bipartisan support for important national security space programs.  

That's not a guarantee against budget changes, but it helps explain why Rocket Lab is continuing to invest in government satellite capabilities.  

12. EUROPE COULD BECOME ROCKET LAB'S NEXT MAJOR DEFENSE MARKET. 

This was one of the more interesting international comments.  

Beck said European allies increasingly want their own sovereign space capabilities rather than depending entirely on foreign providers.  

He connected that demand to Rocket Lab's European expansion and acquisitions.  

The opportunity isn't simply selling American spacecraft to European governments.  

It's establishing the local presence and industrial capabilities needed to compete for European sovereign defense programs.  That could become an important source of new spacecraft and services revenue.  

13. BECK THINKS THE MARKET STILL MISUNDERSTANDS ROCKET LAB. 

When asked about the biggest misconception, Beck joked that he might have chosen the wrong company name.  

People see Rocket Lab and immediately think rockets.  But according to Beck's estimates:  

- Launch: approximately $10B addressable market. 
- Space systems: approximately $30B. 
- Space services: approximately $320B, with some forecasts exceeding $1T in the coming decade. 

These are market estimates, not Rocket Lab revenue projections. Still, they explain why Beck is willing to invest so heavily in launch infrastructure.  

His expectation is that the services business could eventually become much larger than the launch business itself.  

14. HIS MESSAGE TO RETAIL INVESTORS WAS ABOUT PROFITABILITY. 

Beck thanked shareholders who supported Rocket Lab through its earlier years.  

But his final comment was the most important:  

"This company needs to be profitable and it needs to be robust and enduring." 

I think that says a lot about how he's approaching the next phase.Rocket Lab has already proved it can build and launch spacecraft. Neutron could expand the addressable launch market considerably.  

The harder part is converting that infrastructure into a consistently profitable business capable of supporting its own growth.  

Interview credits: @FunOfInvesting 
Go visit his channel to watch the interview.

Good Read!🫡

On Jeopardy the other night, the final question asked: “How many steps does the guard take during his walk across the Tomb of the Unknown?”

All three contestants missed it.

Tomb of the Unknown Soldier

1. How many steps does the guard take during his walk across the Tomb and why?

He takes 21 steps — symbolizing the 21-gun salute, the highest military and foreign tribute.

2. How long does he pause before turning to walk back and why?

He waits 21 seconds, again in honor of the same tradition.

3. Why are his gloves damp?

They are lightly moistened to ensure he never loses his grip on his rifle.

4. Does he keep his rifle on the same shoulder, and if not, why?

He always carries it on the shoulder farthest from the Tomb. After each crossing, he performs an about-face and moves it to the outside shoulder.

5. How often are the guards changed?

Every 30 minutes, 24/7, 365 days a year.

6. What are the physical requirements for a Tomb Guard?

Applicants must be between 5'10" and 6'2" and have a waist no larger than 30".

Other expectations of the Guard:

They devote two years to the Tomb, live in the barracks beneath it, and must refrain from drinking alcohol on or off duty for the rest of their lives.

They can never swear in public or dishonor the uniform or the Tomb.

After two years, they earn a wreath pin signifying their service — fewer than 400 are currently worn.

If they violate the code, they must relinquish the pin.

Their shoes have thick soles to protect against extreme temperatures and metal heel plates that create the crisp click when they halt.

Uniforms must have zero wrinkles or lint and are inspected in a full-length mirror.

For the first six months, guards do not speak to anyone and do not watch television.

Their off-duty time is spent studying the 175 notable individuals buried at Arlington National Cemetery, memorizing who they are and where they rest.

Among them: President Taft, Joe E. Lewis, and Audie Murphy, the most decorated WWII soldier.

Every guard spends five hours daily preparing their uniform.

ETERNAL REST GRANT THEM, O LORD, AND LET PERPETUAL LIGHT SHINE UPON THEM.

When Hurricane Isabel approached Washington, D.C. in 2003, Congress shut down for two days. The guards were offered permission to suspend duty due to danger.

They replied: “No way, Sir!”

Drenched and marching through the storm, they insisted that guarding the Tomb is the highest honor, not just a task.

The Tomb has been continuously guarded — day and night — since 1930.

God Bless and Keep Them

I don’t often encourage sharing posts, but I would be honored if this one reached as many people as possible. We should always feel proud of the men and women who serve, wherever they are stationed.

Duty – Honor – Country

IN GOD WE TRUST — with Herbert F Wieland.

Noty z Kremlu

Russia is once again trying to reopen the question of Europe's security architecture. 

The timing is favorable for Moscow: the United States is pushing for a peace settlement as quickly as possible and at almost any cost, and Russia has sensed an opportunity to demand far more than it is realistically in a position to achieve.

So what would this mean in practice?

The demands Moscow presented to the U.S. and NATO in December 2021:

🔴 An end to NATO enlargement 

Ukraine and other countries would be barred from joining the Alliance.

A return to the 1997 military status quo

NATO would have to significantly reduce its military presence in countries that joined after 1997, including the Czech Republic, Poland, Slovakia, and the Baltic states.

Restrictions on NATO military activities in Eastern Europe

This would also apply to military exercises, defense cooperation, and the deployment of certain weapons systems.

Withdrawal of U.S. nuclear weapons from Europe

The proposal included a mutual ban on deploying nuclear weapons outside a country's own territory.

What would Europe look like under Russia's vision?

🇪🇺 Western Europe would retain most of its existing military capabilities and NATO structures.

🇨🇿 Central and Eastern Europe would remain in NATO, but the Alliance's ability to reinforce and defend the region would be significantly constrained. 

Article 5 would still formally apply, but putting it into practice would become far more difficult. 

Countries in the region would be forced to invest heavily in their own defense capabilities.

🇺🇦 Ukraine would lose any prospect of NATO membership, and its military cooperation with the West would be severely restricted.

🇷🇺 Moscow would find it much easier to exert both political and military pressure on neighboring countries. 

It could use their fears as leverage in negotiations over sanctions, support for Ukraine, and other security issues. 

At home, the Kremlin would present such an outcome as a major geopolitical victory.

Is this realistic?

At the moment, no.

Listening to statements from Russian negotiator Medinsky or reading commentary in state outlets such as RIA Novosti, one might get the impression that Russia is standing on the outskirts of Kyiv, ready to deliver a final decisive blow. Nothing could be further from the truth.

Russia's economy is facing serious structural problems as a result of financing the war. 

High interest rates are choking investment, businesses are struggling with labor shortages, and an ever-growing share of state resources is being diverted to the military at the expense of the civilian economy. 

Domestic debt is also rising rapidly. Russia can still fund the war, but only at the cost of deepening problems that will take years to resolve.

The Kremlin's maximalist demands are essentially a bluff. 

Moscow invokes Yalta and Potsdam, when the Soviet Union, as a newly emerged superpower, had a decisive say in shaping postwar Europe. 

But Russia is not a superpower, however hard it tries to present itself as one. And Europe is not exhausted as it was after World War II.

It has simply grown comfortable.

And that is beginning to change.

Even the U.S. side has reluctantly acknowledged that no solution is possible without Europe. 

Washington is demanding that Russia offer concrete measures to reduce tensions and provide guarantees that it will not attack European countries in the future. 

According to U.S. sources, Russia will not be granted a veto over European security, and no agreement should be reached without the support of both Europe and Ukraine.

And it is a disservice to Pakistan of the worst kind.

Samdani argues Washington's bet on Field Marshal Asim Munir is a "false promise," that Pakistan's military has failed at counterterrorism in KP and Balochistan, violated rights, endangered the $1.25 billion US investment in Reko Diq, and deepened ties with China. She ignores the obvious: Pakistan did not choose a security state. Geography imposed it.

Her timing is mischievous and her effect is dangerous. By directly targeting Pakistan's counterterrorism capacity at the exact moment TTP, BLA, and IS-K are escalating attacks from Afghan sanctuaries, she is, directly or indirectly, helping the terrorists. Weaken the military, cut its spares, freeze its training, isolate its chief, and who benefits? Not Pakistani democrats. Not Baloch mothers. The men who plant IEDs in Khyber and ambush convoys in Chagai.

She blames operations for militancy. The truth is the reverse. Pakistan has lost over 90,000 lives. The Afghan Taliban returned because Washington signed the Doha agreement and fled, not because Islamabad created them. Reko Diq is not proof of failure; US EXIM approved $1.25 billion because it trusts Pakistan to deliver.

A Pakistani urging Washington to punish Pakistan at its most vulnerable moment is not dissent. It is a disservice to the country she claims to care about.

Pakistan has an elected Parliament, a Prime Minister, and a Constitutional Court. A strong military under civilian command is not military rule. Congress should see this piece for what it is: not a warning about Pakistan's future, but the work of an opportunist trying to sell Pakistan's security for applause in Washington.

text:
MIDDLE EAST SITREP | 13 NOVEMBER 2026

Period Covered: 12–13 November 2026

The Middle East remains on heightened alert as the US–Israel–Iran conflict enters approximately its 258th day. Although direct large-scale exchanges between Washington and Tehran have slowed, instability continues across the Gulf, Gaza, Yemen, and Lebanon.
Here are the key developments and strategic implications:

2. IRAN–GULF 
Iran Claims Strike on US Radar in Bahrain

On 13 November, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed responsibility for destroying a US early-warning radar installation in Bahrain. Tehran described the operation as retaliation for an attack on a telecommunications tower in Sirik, Hormozgan province, on 12 November.

If confirmed, the incident would represent a significant escalation involving US military infrastructure in a Gulf state. Bahrain hosts the US Fifth Fleet headquarters. Neither Washington nor Manama had immediately confirmed the Iranian claim.

Strait of Hormuz and Energy Security

Maritime security remains under pressure, with multiple reports of damaged or burning oil tankers in and around the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian sources have attributed some incidents to mines in restricted maritime areas, although responsibility remains contested.

Shipping traffic remains substantially below pre-conflict levels, while oil spills continue to affect parts of the Gulf coastline. Brent crude has traded in the mid-$90 range amid persistent supply concerns.

US Posture and Regional Diplomacy

President Donald Trump stated that Washington does not require an agreement with Tehran and directed Vice President JD Vance to prioritize domestic issues. Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and other Gulf partners have reportedly urged restraint against further large-scale military operations.

The US naval blockade of Iranian ports remains in place, while military readiness on both sides continues.

3. GAZA AND ISRAEL–HAMAS
Israeli Strike Hits Nasser Hospital

An Israeli airstrike struck the surgical building of Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis overnight on 11–12 November.

Gaza's Health Ministry and civil defence authorities reported six fatalities, including surgeon Dr. Rizq Abu Shaira and a 13-year-old child, with approximately 20–30 people wounded.

The Israeli military stated that it targeted Hamas Khan Younis Brigade commander Muhammad Abu Ismail and other militants allegedly operating from a command centre inside the hospital. Hamas denied using the medical facility for military purposes.

The incident has drawn condemnation from humanitarian organizations, including Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF).

Humanitarian Situation

Winter conditions are worsening the humanitarian crisis. Heavy rainfall and flooding have damaged temporary shelters housing displaced Palestinians, while UN relief officials have warned of delays in delivering tents and essential winter supplies.

The late-2025 ceasefire remains fragile, with continued violations and intermittent Israeli strikes.

Israeli Political Developments

Israel's post-election political transition adds another layer of uncertainty. With Benjamin Netanyahu serving in a caretaker capacity and Gadi Eisenkot involved in government formation efforts, future security and military policy decisions remain difficult to assess.

4. YEMEN AND HOUTHI–SAUDI TENSIONS
Houthi Claims Target Saudi Energy Infrastructure

On 12 November, Yemen's Houthi movement claimed attacks against several Saudi targets, including:

A pumping station along the East–West oil pipeline.
An oil facility in Yanbu.
An Aramco facility or building in Riyadh.
Additional military targets.

Saudi-led coalition forces reported intercepting drones over the Riyadh region and Eastern Province.

The claims highlight continued Houthi pressure on Saudi Arabia's energy infrastructure and strategic economic corridors. Independent confirmation of the reported damage remains necessary.

UN Security Council Renews Yemen Sanctions

On 12 November, the UN Security Council unanimously renewed Yemen-related sanctions, including asset freezes and travel bans, until November 2027. It also extended the mandate of the expert panel.

The Council condemned Houthi escalation and cross-border attacks against Saudi Arabia while taking steps to restrict access to dual-use components and chemicals associated with drone and missile production.

It reiterated that there is no military solution to the conflict and emphasized the importance of political dialogue.

5. LEBANON AND HEZBOLLAH
Israeli airstrikes, shelling, and drone operations continue across southern Lebanon.

Hezbollah leadership has reiterated its opposition to disarmament while Israeli forces remain present in Lebanese territory. Meanwhile, significant displacement continues to affect communities in southern Lebanon.

Although no major new escalation has been reported over the latest 24–48-hour period, continued exchanges indicate that the northern front remains unstable.

6. OUTLOOK: NEXT 24–72 HOURS
Three developments warrant particular attention:

1. Bahrain and Potential US–Iran Escalation

The most immediate concern is confirmation of Iran's claimed strike on US radar infrastructure in Bahrain and any subsequent US response. An acknowledged attack on US military assets could undermine the existing stalemate between Washington and Tehran.

2. Houthi–Saudi Energy Security

Further Houthi attacks or attempted strikes against Saudi oil infrastructure could increase regional economic pressure and threaten alternative energy export routes.

3. Gaza's Humanitarian and Security Situation

Continued Israeli operations, particularly around civilian infrastructure, alongside worsening winter conditions, could intensify humanitarian pressures and complicate ceasefire arrangements.

Additional Watchpoints:

Developments in Israel's post-election government formation.
Maritime incidents and possible mine-related disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.
Israeli military readiness and activity along the Lebanese front.
Diplomatic efforts by Gulf states to prevent renewed large-scale confrontation.

7. STRATEGIC ASSESSMENT: GEOPOLITICAL IMPLICATIONS
The regional security environment remains characterized by interconnected conflicts rather than a single, contained confrontation. While direct US–Iran military exchanges have slowed, pressure continues through maritime disruptions, attacks on energy infrastructure, and activity across multiple regional fronts.

Iran's reported claim involving Bahrain is particularly significant because it potentially extends the confrontation to US military infrastructure hosted by a Gulf partner. However, the absence of independent confirmation makes caution essential.

For Gulf states, the immediate strategic priority remains protecting energy infrastructure, maritime routes, and territorial security while preventing further escalation. For Washington and Tehran, the existing lull offers limited room for de-escalation, but continued military readiness and regional proxy activity leave the situation vulnerable to renewed confrontation.

Geopolitical Outlook: The current situation reflects a temporary balance of deterrence, military signalling, and strategic restraint rather than a sustainable political settlement. The greatest risks over the next 72 hours are a potential US response to the Bahrain incident, further Houthi attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure, and renewed escalation across the Gulf.

Bottom Line: The region remains caught between escalation and containment. Whether this fragile equilibrium holds will depend on the ability of regional and external powers to prevent isolated military incidents from developing into a wider confrontation.

Source Base: Reuters, Al Jazeera, BBC, Arab News, Gulf News, DAWN, ISW/CTP assessments, UN-related reporting, and regional media coverage.

Disclaimer: This SITREP is based on the open-source information provided for 13 November 2026. Iranian military claims, reported damage, casualty figures, and battlefield developments remain subject to independent verification. It is intended for situational awareness.

text:
Steven Spielberg and Amy Irving announced their divorce in April 1989, after less than 4 years of marriage. The settlement was reported at around $100 million, one of the biggest Hollywood had ever seen. Their prenup was reportedly written by hand, on a napkin, with no lawyers. A judge threw it out.

April 25, 1989. The front page above ran the day after they announced the split.

They first dated in 1976 and broke up in 1980. The breakup reportedly cost Irving the role of Marion Ravenwood in Raiders of the Lost Ark, which Spielberg had offered her.

In 1985 they got back together. Their son Max was born that June, and they married later the same year.

The marriage years were huge for him. The Color Purple, Empire of the Sun, and Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade, which opened a month after the announcement.

California is a community property state. Money earned during a marriage generally belongs to both spouses equally. Before the wedding the couple had reportedly drawn up their own prenup, with no lawyers involved. Irving argued she had signed it without a lawyer of her own. A judge set it aside.

The settlement was reported at around $100 million. They shared custody of Max.

They announced the split "in the spirit of caring." 2 years later Spielberg married Kate Capshaw, the star of Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom.

Half the internet calls it the most expensive napkin in history. The other half says it was just California law doing exactly what it was written to do.

$100 million for skipping the lawyer.

Was Amy Irving a lucky ex-wife, or did Spielberg just learn the most expensive lesson in Hollywood?
