text:
To someone unfamiliar with Fremen culture, Stilgar spitting on Duke Leto’s table looks like an insult. But on Arrakis, it was actually one of the most valuable gifts he could offer.

In Frank Herbert’s original Dune novel, water isn’t simply something you drink when you’re thirsty. It determines survival, wealth, social standing and even how the Fremen understand death.

Arrakis is an extremely hostile desert world where losing even a small amount of moisture can have serious consequences.

The Fremen wear stillsuits that recycle their bodily fluids, reclaiming water that would otherwise be lost through perspiration, breathing and other bodily functions.

They even recover the water from their dead and return it to the community.

So when Stilgar spits on the Duke’s table, he’s deliberately giving away a portion of his own body’s moisture.

He’s offering Leto a gift that carries genuine value in Fremen society.

But notice what happens next.

Duncan Idaho immediately understands the gesture because he has spent time living among the Fremen.

He stops the Atreides soldiers from reacting, thanks Stilgar for the gift and spits on the table himself.

He then quietly explains to Leto that Stilgar’s gesture was a token of respect.

And Leto does something equally important.

Rather than treating the gesture as an insult, he accepts the custom and responds by spitting on the table too.

That moment tells Stilgar something about the Duke. Leto is willing to respect Fremen customs instead of demanding that everyone behave according to Atreides traditions.

The exchange also helps establish a bond between the two communities.

Stilgar subsequently offers Duncan a place among his people, allowing him to maintain his allegiance to House Atreides while becoming Fremen.

There’s an even deeper detail in the book.

When the conversation turns to the dead Fremen warrior, Stilgar declares that the man’s water belongs to the Atreides because he died in their service.

His final words make the significance clear:

The water of the dead man becomes a bond between them.

Think about that.

On a planet where water determines whether an entire community survives, giving someone your own bodily moisture is not a meaningless gesture.

Stilgar wasn’t insulting Duke Leto. He was offering him a part of himself, and on Arrakis, that was worth far more than an ordinary handshake.

text:
During an extremely hot summer in 1965, 4-year-old Roger Lausier’s parents had taken him to the beach in Salem, Massachusetts. He was having a great time. Building sand castles, watching the waves crash into the cliffs, and enjoying the sunshine. At one point, there was a drop-off on one of the hills. He soon found himself in the water. Not knowing how to swim, he tried to cry out, but the water sucked into his lungs. A moment right before he was about to drown, strong arms grabbed him. A woman carried him to shore.

. . . 

In 1965, a woman named Alice Blaise rushed into the water off a Massachusetts beach to save a drowning four-year-old boy.

Nine years later, that same boy would save her husband’s life.

Neither rescue was planned. And the extraordinary connection between them was not discovered until afterward.

The boy was Roger Lausier.

In the summer of 1965, Roger was playing at Salem Willows Beach when he wandered into the water and was caught by a dangerous current.

He was only four years old and unable to save himself.

Alice Blaise, a stranger who happened to be nearby, saw him struggling and went into the water after him.

She brought Roger safely back to shore.

For Alice, it was an act of courage performed in a moment of emergency. For Roger and his family, it meant that a little boy would live to see another birthday.

The years passed.

In 1974, Roger returned to the same Massachusetts beach. He was now 13 years old.

While out on the water with an inflatable raft, he heard a woman desperately calling for help.

Her husband was drowning.

Roger paddled toward the struggling man and managed to keep him afloat until additional help arrived.

The man survived.

His name was Bob Blaise.

What Roger did not know was that Bob’s wife was Alice, the woman who had saved him from drowning nine years earlier.

The astonishing connection reportedly emerged later, when the people involved learned one another’s identities.

The little boy Alice had pulled from the water in 1965 had grown into the teenager who helped save her husband in 1974.

The rescues happened at the same beach, separated by nearly a decade.

There was no arrangement, no promise of repayment, and no reason for Roger to recognize the man he was helping.

He had simply heard someone in trouble and responded.

Alice could not have known that the child she saved would one day be standing between her husband and death.

And Roger could not have known that the stranger he helped was connected to the woman who had once given him a second chance at life.

Two ordinary summer days, nine years apart, became an extraordinary story of how one act of courage can return to touch the very family that first offered it.

text:
NEVER AGAIN
A Proposal for the Dissolution of the Russian Federation Following Military Defeat in Ukraine
POST-WAR INTERNATIONAL SECURITY AND ACCOUNTABILITY PROPOSAL

Proposed for consideration by the United Nations, European governments, NATO members and the international community.

Core principle: Russia's defeat in Ukraine must mark the end of the political and military structure responsible for decades of aggression, territorial expansion and threats against neighbouring nations.

The objective of this proposal is not simply to end one war. It is to establish a post-war settlement intended to prevent the re-emergence of a Russian state capable of threatening the sovereignty and security of Europe and its neighbours.

1. The Case for Fundamental Change

The Russian invasion of Ukraine represents a direct challenge to the principles of national sovereignty, territorial integrity and international peace.

The United Nations General Assembly has formally condemned Russia's aggression and reaffirmed Ukraine's internationally recognised borders.

The international response must therefore extend beyond temporary ceasefires, sanctions and diplomatic assurances.

A settlement that simply removes the current Russian leadership while preserving the same centralised political and military structure risks leaving the underlying security problem unresolved.

The question confronting Europe is whether it can afford to allow the same concentration of power to rebuild and potentially threaten its neighbours again.

2. The Proposed Dissolution of the Russian Federation

The principal objective of this proposal is the termination of the Russian Federation in its existing form.

Following military defeat, a comprehensive post-war settlement should establish the dissolution of the existing federal state and the dismantling of its centralised military and political command structures.

This would be a fundamental consequence of the post-war settlement, not an optional political reform offered to the defeated government.

The settlement should provide for:

The termination of the existing federal government's authority.
The dissolution of its centralised military command.
The termination of its existing imperial administrative structures.
The establishment of internationally supervised transitional administrations.
The creation of separate successor political entities.
International recognition of successor states following an agreed legal and constitutional process.

The objective would be to prevent the recreation of a single centralised power capable of exercising military domination over the former federation's territories and neighbouring countries.

3. The End of Russian Imperial Expansion

The international community must address the historical concentration of political and military authority in Moscow.

The successor political arrangements should prevent the restoration of an imperial system through which the political, economic and military interests of smaller republics and regions are subordinated to a central government.

Particular attention should be given to the constituent republics, including:

Tatarstan
Bashkortostan
Sakha (Yakutia)
Chechnya
Dagestan
Buryatia
Tuva
Kalmykia

Their future political status should be determined within the binding international settlement, with democratic representation, protections for minorities and safeguards against renewed coercion.

4. Nuclear Disarmament and Military Restrictions

The former Russian Federation possesses an enormous nuclear arsenal and substantial conventional military infrastructure.

The dissolution of its existing political structure cannot be considered complete without addressing these capabilities.

The post-war settlement should establish:

Internationally supervised nuclear disarmament.
Secure accounting and custody of nuclear weapons during the transition.
Verified dismantlement of agreed nuclear stockpiles and delivery systems.
International monitoring of nuclear materials.
Restrictions on offensive missile capabilities.
Limits on military forces capable of threatening neighbouring states.
Independent verification and long-term inspection arrangements.

The transition must not create a situation in which nuclear weapons become distributed among unstable or competing successor governments.

5. Accountability for War Crimes

The dissolution of the Russian Federation must not replace individual criminal accountability.

Those responsible for planning, authorising and carrying out internationally recognised crimes must face appropriate legal proceedings.

This includes:

The crime of aggression.
War crimes.
Crimes against humanity.
Unlawful deportation and forced transfer.
Torture and unlawful detention.
Attacks against protected civilian populations and infrastructure.

No individual should receive automatic immunity simply because they previously occupied a position of political or military authority.

International courts and properly constituted tribunals should determine individual responsibility according to applicable law.

6. Reparations for Ukraine

Ukraine must not be expected to finance its own reconstruction following the devastation caused by Russia's aggression.

The post-war settlement should establish a comprehensive compensation programme.

This should include:

Reconstruction of destroyed homes and infrastructure.
Restoration of hospitals, schools and public services.
Compensation for civilian victims.
Support for displaced Ukrainians returning home.
Environmental restoration.
Rehabilitation of damaged agricultural land.
Long-term economic recovery.

Russian state assets should be considered for use in financing reparations through lawful international mechanisms.

The Council of Europe has already established the Register of Damage for Ukraine as part of the international reparations process.

7. Permanent Protection for Europe's Neighbours

The settlement must establish a new European security framework.

Ukraine, Moldova, Georgia, Finland, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland and other neighbouring countries must not be left vulnerable to another period of Russian military expansion.

The framework should include:

Binding non-aggression commitments.
Internationally monitored military restrictions.
Stronger collective defence arrangements.
Protection against foreign military coercion.
International monitoring of successor-state military activity.
Mechanisms for responding to violations.

No country should have to surrender its political independence or foreign policy choices because of threats from a neighbouring power.

8. International Administration and Implementation

The dissolution of a state possessing nuclear weapons, extensive military infrastructure and a population numbering in the hundreds of millions presents extraordinary challenges.

An international implementation authority should therefore oversee the transition.

Its responsibilities should include:

Supervising the termination of existing federal institutions.
Securing nuclear weapons and strategic military infrastructure.
Establishing transitional political administrations.
Overseeing the division of federal assets and liabilities.
Establishing recognised borders and citizenship arrangements.
Preventing armed conflict between successor administrations.
Protecting civilians and ethnic minorities.
Monitoring compliance with military restrictions.
Coordinating reparations and reconstruction obligations.

The settlement would need an internationally agreed legal mandate and enforceable arrangements for implementation.

9. The Principle of Collective Security, Not Collective Punishment

The purpose of this proposal is to dismantle the political and military structures responsible for repeated aggression, not to punish ordinary Russian civilians for the actions of their government.

Russian citizens should not be subjected to indiscriminate violence, forced displacement or collective criminal responsibility.

The consequences should fall upon the defeated state's governing institutions, military structures, responsible individuals and state assets, in accordance with international law.

A lasting settlement must also protect the civilian populations of any successor territories.

10. Final Declaration: Never Again

For too long, Europe's security has been shaped by the possibility that Russia might once again use its military power against its neighbours.

Ukraine has demonstrated the catastrophic human cost of allowing territorial aggression to go unanswered.

A temporary military defeat, a change of leadership or another diplomatic agreement cannot by themselves guarantee that history will not repeat itself.

The international community must confront the structural causes of this insecurity.

This proposal therefore places the dissolution of the existing Russian Federation at the centre of a punitive post-war settlement.

Its objective is to end the centralised political and military system responsible for aggression, ensure accountability, compensate its victims and establish a security framework that prevents the restoration of the same imperial military power.

The people of Ukraine deserve justice. Europe's neighbouring nations deserve security. Future generations deserve a continent in which borders are respected, and independence is not conditional upon the goodwill of a powerful neighbour.

The end of the war must mean more than the end of the fighting. It must mean the end of the system that made the aggression possible.

Never again should a European nation have to live in fear of invasion from Moscow.

Supporting international legal foundations

United Nations Charter, Article 2(4): Prohibition on the threat or use of force against another state's territorial integrity or political independence.

UN General Assembly Resolution ES-11/1: Condemnation of Russia's aggression against Ukraine.

Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court: Legal framework covering war crimes, crimes against humanity, genocide and the crime of aggression.

UN General Assembly Resolution ES-11/5: Framework concerning remedies and reparations for aggression against Ukraine.

Council of Europe's Register of Damage for Ukraine: Existing international mechanism for recording damage and compensation claims.

text:
IF I WERE YOU, reading this week that an AI crash is coming, I would ask one question before selling anything with AI in its name: a crash in what?

The Economist's cover shows the letters AI crumbling, and its leader is titled "Why you should expect an AI crash", with the qualification that it need not be a financial cataclysm. A Federal Reserve vice chair lists a large correction in equities among the risks if AI returns disappoint. Axios calls it the industry's week from hell. Nvidia has lost its founder and nearly a third of its value in five weeks.

I do not expect a collapse of AI. That is a narrower claim than it sounds, and a different one from this week's covers. Every technological revolution meets the same two characters: the enthusiast who believes every price is justified and the pessimist who mistakes a falling price for the end of an industry. AI now has plenty of both. Here is the record, from filings, surveys and market data, then the argument, then the part of the bear case I think is right. Facts are stated as facts. The interpretation is mine and is labelled as such.

FOUR THINGS HIDING IN ONE WORD

When someone predicts a collapse, I want to know which balance sheet or which behaviour they mean.

One: a collapse in valuations, what investors will pay for the earnings. A wonderful business can be a poor investment at the wrong price.

Two: a collapse in a financing model. A company with an impressive product can still run out of cash if its commitments grow faster than its ability to fund them.

Three: an infrastructure bust. Capacity built in the wrong place, at the wrong price, ahead of demand, or without the power to run it.

Four: a collapse in adoption. Customers stop using the technology because it is too expensive, too unreliable or not useful enough.

The first is not a forecast: for the leading stock it has already happened. The second and third are real risks and I will not talk them down. The fourth is the only one that would end the AI economy, and it is the one for which I can find no evidence. The first three can happen without the fourth, and a financial crash can be deep and painful while the technology keeps spreading. My thesis is a judgment about adoption. It is not a promise about anyone's return.

THE WEEK

On Thursday 12 November Jensen Huang resigned as president, chief executive and director of Nvidia, effective immediately, after 33 years. He had acknowledged an extramarital affair; the woman, according to press reports citing American intelligence, is suspected of being a Chinese asset, and a second relationship, with an executive who reported to him, was reported on Wednesday night. Nvidia had said it was examining whether he had been "the target of a foreign intelligence effort". A suspicion is not a finding, and I will treat it as a suspicion.

Colette Kress, chief financial officer since 2013, is interim chief executive and remains chief financial officer. Harvey Jones becomes the first chair the board has ever had. There is no named successor.

The shares fell as much as 14%, to $148.80, and closed at $166.19, down 4.3%. On 6 October they had closed at $239.24. That is 30.5% in five weeks and, on my arithmetic, about $1.75 trillion of market value.

VALUATIONS: ALREADY CUT

The 30.5% is three legs, not one. From 6 October to 4 November, before either shock, Nvidia lost 16%, in weeks when Alphabet and Microsoft declined to raise their capital-spending forecasts. Around the midterms it lost 7%. In the week of the scandal, 11%. About half of the fall came before the election, a fifth with it and a third this week. The scandal is the loudest leg. It is not the largest.

Look at the day itself. On the session in which the central figure of the AI trade resigned, the Nasdaq lost 0.4% and closed 4.3% above its level of a week earlier. AMD rose 5.9% and Broadcom 5.5%, while CoreWeave and other clouds that depend on Nvidia's chips fell hard. Money did not leave artificial intelligence. It changed supplier. Nvidia itself closed within a dollar of the day's high on about 748 million shares, roughly seven times its October average. Somebody bought what was sold.

Look at what the analysts did. Bernstein cut Nvidia to Market Perform and halved its target from $400 to $200, and left its earnings forecasts where they were. At least ten analysts turned more cautious in the week, by FactSet's count as reported by CNBC. What was cut was the multiple: about 14 times the next twelve months' expected earnings on TIKR's consensus, a five-year low, against a five-year average of about 36.

The arithmetic is simple. Take the $12.10 a share analysts expect over the next twelve months. At 36 times that is $436. At 14 times it is $169, roughly where the stock closed. One analyst, Dan Ives, had estimated that Nvidia would be worth 25% to 30% less without Huang; applied to the $186.64 of the Friday before the scandal, that is $131 to $140. On that view the founder discount is less than half taken, and I would not tell anyone the bottom is in. But if earnings estimates fell 30% at an unchanged multiple the price would be about $119, and that, a fall in the business rather than in its price, is what nobody has yet written into a forecast.

The earlier leg tells the same story. On 5 November, two days after the midterms, the Nasdaq fell 5.5%, the Philadelphia Semiconductor index about 12%, its worst day since March 2020, and roughly $2.5 trillion of market value went in a session. The trigger was not an earnings miss. Democrats had swept Congress and taken the governorships of Texas, Ohio and Georgia, and most of 41 local ballot measures on data centres had gone against the builders. That is a permitting question, and a serious one. It is not a demand question.

Cisco, the Nvidia of the last cycle, traded at well over 100 times earnings in March 2000, and the Nasdaq then lost 78% by October 2002. Nvidia trades at 14. A stock at 14 times can fall further. It cannot fall the way a stock at 100 times falls unless the earnings go.

DEMAND: WHAT DID NOT FALL

Nvidia reported $96.2 billion of revenue for its July quarter, up from $46.7 billion a year earlier, and guided to $108 billion, give or take 2%, for the quarter it reports on Tuesday.

Amazon Web Services grew 39% in the third quarter to $46 billion, Microsoft's Azure 48% to $33.2 billion, Google Cloud 103% to $30.7 billion, a figure that includes sales of Google's own chips: $110 billion in three months. A year earlier the three were growing 20%, 40% and 34%. AWS alone reports a backlog of about $578 billion.

The four largest builders guide to $720 to $740 billion of capital spending this year, with more than $1 trillion expected next year. The only cut of the season, Microsoft's from $175 to $170 billion, was attributed by the company to delayed deliveries, with customer demand still above supply. A cut caused by a shortage is the opposite of a demand problem.

ADOPTION: RISING, AT A FALLING PRICE

That is demand measured at the suppliers. The harder question is the end customer.

In McKinsey's 2026 global survey, published in August, nearly nine in ten respondents said their organisations regularly use AI in at least one business function, and the share scaling it across the enterprise rose from 38% to 44%. Four in five said it had improved their own productivity, and six in ten expect their organisations to spend more on AI over the next year. The survey covered 1,719 respondents in 97 countries. It records what respondents report and is not a census.

The same survey contains the number optimists skip. Only 37% attribute any EBIT impact to AI, unchanged from 2025, and about 6% attribute to it 5% or more of EBIT. Use has spread faster than profit. An employee can save an hour while the income statement does not move, because the workflow around that hour was never redesigned. For a chief financial officer the question is not how many people have access to a tool. It is what happens to cost, speed, quality, revenue and risk once the tool is part of the process. A successful pilot is a promising start. It is not yet a consolidated income statement.

Now a second dataset. Ramp, which tracks the spending of more than 85,000 American businesses, reports that 56.8% of them paid for AI in October, 13 points more than a year earlier. Yet spending on AI tokens grew just 1.5% across August and September combined, after 42% in July. In the four weeks to 23 October token volume rose 37% while token spend rose 9%, which implies a price per token about a fifth lower in a month. Ramp's economist attributes the slowdown mainly to price cuts and to customers learning to control their usage, not to weaker demand. Two more details belong in an honest account. The median business paying for AI spends about $16 per employee a month, while the top 1% spend about $10,000: adoption is broad and still shallow. And about 1% of businesses account for roughly 80% of what OpenAI and Anthropic earn from Ramp's customers. These are Ramp's customers, not the labs' total sales, and a few months are not a trend.

Read together, the two say something the word "crash" hides. Companies are using more AI and paying less for each unit of it. That is not a collapse in adoption. It is a collapse in price, and a falling price is a transfer: from the companies that sell intelligence to the companies that use it. This is where I part company with this week's covers. What is deflating is the price of AI, of its shares and of its tokens. What is not deflating is its use.

FINANCING: WHERE THE BEARS ARE RIGHT

The internet was real too. Being right about the technology protected no one who bought the Nasdaq in March 2000. The internet did not ask permission from a stock index to change the economy, and AI will not either. But neither owes investors a positive return. What turned that repricing into a collapse was not a shortage of users. It was the financing.

Michelle Bowman, the Fed's vice chair for supervision, said on 10 November that AI-related debt is on track to exceed $800 billion this year, and that leases, contract commitments and residual-value guarantees could add more than three times that: by arithmetic, more than $2.4 trillion of obligations, most of them absent from the balance sheets investors read. She described suppliers and hyperscalers taking stakes in their own customers as creating "the appearance of circular financing". She also attributed roughly a quarter of the excess over the Fed's inflation target to AI-related price pressures. A boom strong enough to show up in inflation is not short of demand. It is also one the central bank cannot easily rescue with lower rates.

Anthropic's amended prospectus shows third-quarter revenue of $16.96 billion, twelve times a year earlier, beside $895.4 billion of purchase and lease commitments, about thirteen times its annualised third-quarter revenue. Quarter-on-quarter growth slowed from 144% to 47%, and an operating profit of $974 million became an operating loss of $567 million, largely because $5 billion of compute was bought on expensive short-term contracts. Put Ramp's falling token price next to those commitments and you have the financing question in one line: revenue per unit is falling while the bill was signed for a world of 144%.

Nvidia is not only a seller of chips. Its July-quarter filing shows $99 billion of equity investments in its own ecosystem, $25 billion more committed, and guarantees of up to $108.5 billion, of which $105 billion backs a single data-centre campus leased to an OpenAI affiliate. Kress told analysts in August that demand from the AI labs for which Nvidia expects to use its own balance sheet should be roughly a quarter of its business next year. In the same month it signed memorandums with capital providers meant to mobilise more than $500 billion of third-party money for AI infrastructure, and IFR counted more than $530 billion of commitments of all kinds at the company.

The supplier finances the customer so that the customer can buy from the supplier. Such transactions can have a legitimate commercial purpose, and their existence does not prove that sales are fictitious or that the sector is a Ponzi scheme. But an analyst should ask whether the demand would survive on similar terms without the financing. How much revenue comes from independent end customers? How concentrated is it? Can customers renew when the introductory budget disappears? Those are questions about durability and concentration, not accusations.

INFRASTRUCTURE: THE PHYSICAL LIMIT

Microsoft said roughly three quarters of the $45.2 billion of capital expenditure it reported for the September quarter, a figure that includes finance leases, went to short-lived assets, mainly CPUs and GPUs, up from about two thirds a quarter earlier. Chips that age in a few years are being financed across the industry with bonds that mature in decades. The word AI does not make a GPU exempt from economics.

And the buildings need power. The International Energy Agency projects that electricity consumption by data centres will roughly double, from about 485 terawatt-hours in 2025 to about 950 in 2030, with AI-focused facilities tripling. That is a projection for all data centres, not a measurement of AI. A global total also hides the local problem: a grid connection that arrives late, a county that votes no, as most of those 41 ballots did. In the next phase, access to reliable power could matter as much as access to capital.

So there is a credible scenario in which this goes badly wrong, and it does not require anyone to stop using AI. Enterprises prove reluctant to pay enough for production use. Token prices keep falling faster than costs. Power delays several large projects. Overcapacity compresses prices just as financing becomes more expensive. Leveraged developers miss obligations and the losses spread to lenders and infrastructure owners. That would be a genuine financial crisis in parts of AI, not a change in sentiment. My belief that adoption continues is not an argument against that possibility. It is a judgment that useful applications would continue through it.

WHERE THE SCANDAL MEETS THE SYSTEM

This is my reading, not a reported fact. Huang's importance to the AI economy was never only the product roadmap. He was the person across the table in those deals: the stakes, the guarantees, the capacity promises that let suppliers and developers build ahead of orders. Key-man risk at Nvidia is a credit question before it is an engineering one. The chips for 2027 are already designed. What is not designed is who signs the next $105 billion guarantee, and on what terms.

The interim answer is a governance oddity. The executive who knows every one of those commitments best is now chief executive and chief financial officer at once. For customers and lenders that is continuity. For a board supervising $108.5 billion of guarantees, it is one person in two chairs that exist to check each other.

And there is a governance fact that predates the scandal. Until Thursday Nvidia's board had never had a chair. Its chief executive had, by Bernstein's count, about 60 direct reports and, by the Wall Street Journal's account, no belief in succession planning. He held 3.61% of the company, by Reuters's count. He did not control Nvidia by votes. He controlled it by being indispensable, and the board let a $4 trillion company depend on that. The governance discount was always there. The market had no reason to price it until this week.

One fact limits the China channel everyone expects: Nvidia's $108 billion guidance already assumes no data-centre compute revenue from China. The cost of this affair will be measured in trust, in Washington where the company needs licences and in boardrooms where it needs counterparties.

THE CHEAPER SHOVEL

Nvidia's gross margin was 75% last quarter. A leaderless Nvidia facing AMD, Broadcom and Google's in-house chips is a supplier with less power over customers whose combined capital budgets exceed $700 billion a year. If that power erodes, the loss falls on Nvidia's shareholders and the gain goes to the buyers of compute. One level up, the same thing is already happening to tokens. I am not forecasting where prices go. I am saying who benefits when they fall. A cheaper shovel is bad news for the shovel maker. It is not bad news for the mine. Some of the biggest beneficiaries of this cycle may be businesses that use AI rather than sell it.

NEXT WEEK'S EXAM

On Tuesday 17 November Nvidia reports its third quarter, the first without Huang. For years the division of labour on those calls was simple: the finance chief read the numbers and the founder sold the future. Now one person has to do both. Three answers matter more than the revenue line: whether guidance for the January quarter still rises, whether the guarantees and lab financings stand on the terms already signed, and whether the board gives a date for a permanent appointment.

Anthropic has set a range of $70 to $78 for 825 million shares, up to about $64 billion, with a further $26 billion of private investment alongside from Google, Nvidia and others, for a valuation of roughly $1.4 trillion, below what had been expected earlier in the year. Pricing is due on Wednesday 18 November and trading on Thursday 19 November. Axios reports annualised revenue of $81 billion in October and commitments of nearly $901 billion. Notice who is in the private placement: a supplier. Of the 825 million shares, about 801 million are new shares sold by the company: the money funds compute bills, not exits, which means the public is being asked to pay for the build-out before the return on it is known. SpaceX rose after its record June listing and then fell below its offer price within weeks. A strong first day will prove little. A pulled deal would prove a great deal, because it would narrow the equity window on which the financing chain now leans.

FOUR OBJECTIONS, ANSWERED

"This is the dot-com bubble again." The valuation is not: 14 times against more than 100. The utilisation is not: builders short of capacity against dark fibre. The financing might be, which is why I spend more time on debt than on demand.

"The demand is circular." At the margin, visibly. At the core, three cloud providers collected $110 billion in a quarter and more than half of Ramp's businesses pay for AI out of their own budgets. Circular financing inflates the pace. It did not invent the product.

"The Democrats will stop the data centres." No moratorium has been enacted. If one becomes law, that is a supply shock: it delays revenue, strands some of the capital raised this year and raises the value of capacity already built. It would hurt builders and chip volumes. It would not mean people stopped wanting the service.

"Adoption without profit is a fad." It may be an early stage. Only 37% see EBIT impact and that share did not move in a year: if it has not moved in another, I will worry. But customers who are not yet earning from AI are also paying less per unit of it, which is not how a fad ends. It is how a technology becomes ordinary.

WHO CAPTURES, WHO PAYS

AMD and Broadcom captured, on the day, part of the premium that left Nvidia. Hyperscalers capture bargaining power over their supplier. Users of AI capture the falling price of intelligence. A buyer of Nvidia at 14 times earnings captures a price that assumes the founder was the business.

The index holder pays: every pension and passive fund whose Nvidia holding is worth 30% less than five weeks ago, without anyone having taken a decision. Model developers pay if price competition outruns their commitments. Suppliers who built on a handshake pay if the handshake is renegotiated. Lenders pay if a developer cannot refinance. And gold settled on Thursday at a 52-week low of $3,889.40; by the Journal's account, investors are selling winners to cover losses in technology. When the hedge is sold to fund the losing trade, leverage is being unwound somewhere.

NO COLLAPSE DOES NOT MEAN NO COST

A repricing is not painless because it is not a collapse. About $1.75 trillion has left one stock in five weeks, and that stock sits in most index funds and pensions. Bowman's own warning ran through this channel: lower share prices weaken household spending and dearer credit hits housing and small business, with no need for a single data centre to be cancelled. Saying there is no collapse of AI is a statement about the technology and its users. It is not a promise about your portfolio.

WHAT WOULD PROVE ME WRONG

I would abandon the adoption thesis if, across several reporting periods, independent paying demand stagnated or reversed: Ramp's 56.8% falling, production use dropping when trials and subsidies end, a sustained inability to show net economic value. I would call it a crash of the whole system if two or more of the large builders cut 2027 capital plans for lack of demand rather than lack of chips or permits, if Nvidia's orders shrank rather than its multiple, or if the Anthropic listing failed and the debt market for data centres closed behind it. None of these has happened. Every one of them could.

WHAT I WOULD MONITOR

Nvidia on 17 November and Anthropic on 18 and 19 November. The succession, and whether the finance role is separated from the chief executive's. The 2027 capital-expenditure guides in late January, and the reason given for any change. Ramp's monthly index: paid adoption, token volume and token spend, read separately. Asset write-downs, capacity utilisation and customer concentration in the next filings. Spreads on AI-related debt. The first data-centre bills in Texas, Ohio and Georgia.

The criterion is measurable. If earnings estimates and paid adoption hold through those tests while multiples and token prices stay low, November 2026 was a repricing: painful, overdue in places, survivable. If they start to fall, I was wrong, and The Economist was early rather than late.

Markets have a useful habit of asking for evidence eventually. They also have a less useful habit of waiting until after the money has been spent.

If I were you, I would not confuse the fall of a man with the fall of a market, or the fall of a price with the fall of a business. A crash needs customers to leave. So far, only a chief executive has.

I do not expect the end of AI. I expect the end of the idea that an AI story is enough.

text:
Fourteen-year-old eighth-grade cheerleader Jorgia Walls from Lawrenceville, Georgia, won first place as a solo squad of one at the annual Gwinnett Football League (GFL) Cheer Off after all seven of her teammates dropped out earlier in the season...

Jorgia started the season with seven teammates at Peachtree Ridge, but all of them eventually quit. Her coach offered to move her to a younger seventh-grade squad, but Jorgia chose to finish her final GFL season on her own. Performing her solo routine in front of a packed arena, she won over the crowd and took home first place. 

. . . 

By the time 14-year-old Jorgia Walls arrived at her final cheerleading competition, every other girl on her team had quit. Seven teammates were gone. She had spent months preparing, and now she would have to perform alone in front of 1,500 people.

Jorgia, an eighth grader from Lawrenceville, Georgia, had been cheerleading since kindergarten. Her mother enrolled her partly to help with difficulties involving speech and fine motor skills. Over the years, the sport helped her develop confidence, make friends and find her voice.

But during the summer of 2026, her eight-member squad began shrinking. Some girls lost interest. Others left because of personal circumstances. By September, Jorgia was the only one remaining.

She could join a younger squad or miss her final competition. Instead, she chose to finish what she had started.

Her coach, Kenya Barbour, helped her prepare a two-minute routine. They practiced together every day, knowing Jorgia would have to perform every cheer, movement and crowd chant herself.

On October 25, Jorgia stepped onto the competition floor. Before she began, organizers asked the audience to remain silent so she could hear her music and cues.

Then came the crowd participation portion, when cheerleaders must persuade spectators to repeat their chants. Most teams rely on several voices. Jorgia had only hers.

She called out to the crowd.

All 1,500 people responded.

The arena erupted as spectators clapped and cheered along with the girl standing alone on the floor.

When the results were announced, Jorgia had won first place. Her coach said she finally began crying when she heard the news.

A video of the performance soon spread online, attracting attention far beyond Georgia.

Jorgia had entered the competition without a single teammate beside her. By the end of her routine, she had persuaded an entire arena to cheer with her.

text:
🚆 TRAIN REVIEW: Special Express No. 43 (Bangkok to Ban Krut)

If you’re heading south from Bangkok for a few days by the sea, Special Express No. 43 is one train worth considering. It’s a daytime diesel railcar to Surat Thani, with stops at Hua Hin, Prachuap Khiri Khan, Ban Krut, Bang Saphan Yai and Chumphon. We took it as far as Ban Krut today. I’ll write about the trip itself later, but a few things are worth knowing about the train, especially if you’re counting on lunch!

We left Krung Thep Aphiwat at 07:30 and arrived at Ban Krut at 12:24. That’s just under five hours, and the fare was 392 baht.

💺 What’s it like on board?

There are three carriages. The seats are reversible, so everyone faces the direction of travel. Mine reclined and had a footrest, a fold-down table and a net pocket. Even when the passenger in front reclined, I still had enough legroom. There are curtains for the bright sunshine and hooks for a jacket or bag, though my jacket spent more time on me than on the hook. The carriage averaged about 20°C. Blankets are sometimes available if you ask.

A carry-on suitcase fits easily on the overhead rack. I saw a couple of cases up there that looked about 28 inches, though there’s also space for larger bags at the ends of the carriages. There are no power sockets at the seats, so bring a power bank if you’ll need to charge your phone.

Each carriage has two toilets, one of which may be a squat toilet. The ones I checked were clean and had toilet paper and a handheld bidet spray. Outside were washbasins, soap and a mirror.

🍜 Can you get food on board?

There’s no dining car, but shortly after we left Bangkok, the conductors came through taking orders for food from stations along the way. Everything was announced verbally in Thai, so if you don’t speak the language, it’s easy to miss your chance.

There were two rounds of orders. The first was for dry noodles from Ratchaburi (20 baht) and a Thai dessert from Phetchaburi (100 baht). Later, we were offered a choice of rice dishes for 50 baht each. These would come on board at Bang Saphan, just after our stop at Ban Krut. Too late for our lunch, but worth knowing if you’re staying on to Chumphon or Surat Thani.

The cleaner also came through offering bottled water, hot coffee, Ovaltine and Mama instant noodles for 10 to 30 baht. I’d still bring a packed meal, drinks and a few snacks. What you can get depends partly on where you get off.

🎟️ A few booking tips

From Bangkok, it’s 300 baht to Hua Hin or 392 baht to Ban Krut. Both journeys can be booked up to 30 days ahead. If you want to buy tickets further ahead for Ban Krut, booking through to Chumphon costs just 37 baht more and gives you a 90-day booking window. You can still get off at Ban Krut.

Tomorrow we’re catching No. 43 again from Ban Krut to Chumphon. For a short hop like this, tickets only go on sale one day ahead. We bought ours at Krung Thep Aphiwat this morning, though we could have booked online from midnight last night. For Sunday night’s sleeper back to Bangkok, we booked from Surat Thani to get the longer booking window and plan to join the train at Chumphon. More about that later. 

Would I take No. 43 again? For Ban Krut, I like being there by lunchtime. If you’d rather save money, Ordinary No. 255 is a lot cheaper and gets in about two hours later. It also goes on to Chumphon, so that was our backup for tomorrow if No. 43 had been full.

🚆 Have you taken Special Express No. 43? How was your journey, and what’s one tip you’d give someone taking it for the first time?

text:
Sunshine Through the Rain, currently airing on MGTV, is receiving positive feedback for its grounded portrayal of youth, highlighting the struggles that often remain hidden behind the seemingly carefree image of campus life. 

Rather than following the usual formula of a lighthearted campus romance, the youth drama explores financial pressure, family misfortune, emotional wounds, and the importance of having someone to lean on.

Director Mao De Shu, known for When I Fly Toward You and Love Between Lines, brings a distinct visual style to the series. Rain-slicked streets, muted colors, and soft lighting create a quiet melancholy, letting romantic tension build through understated moments rather than grand, exaggerated gestures.

The show marks the first collaboration between #YangChaoyue and #DongSicheng. Yang plays Zheng Yu, a proud, financially struggling biology student who is determined to handle her problems without burdening others. Her subtle expressions bring out the character's vulnerability. 

Dong plays Chen Yanzhou, a student still grieving the loss of his brother. Their relationship begins with friction/rivalry when Chen returns from a year-long leave and wins the scholarship Zheng Yu needs to help cover her mother's hospital expenses.

The series gives particular attention to the small details of hardship. Zheng Yu refuses presents she cannot repay, hides expired rice balls from her roommates, and only begins opening up about her circumstances in Episode 12.

The drama ultimately stands out as a sincere coming-of-age story that values emotional truth over idealized romance. By showing how shared vulnerability can ease the weight of personal struggles, #SunshineThroughtheRain continues to offer a thoughtful look at resilience, empathy, and quiet companionship.

text:
Myrah Zeigler was 19 years old, a college student from Fort Pierce, and on the night of May 19, 2025, she did everything people are told to do when they are in danger. She found the police. She told them she was scared. She asked them to walk with her. Then she walked anyway, alone, and three minutes later the same officers' body cameras recorded the gunshots that killed her.

Here is the timeline, and it is all on the department's own cameras. Zeigler was at a party at a duplex Airbnb in Fort Lauderdale's River Oaks when a fight broke out. She was pepper-sprayed and robbed. People who were not guests had taken her group's car keys and were waiting at a park nearby. A neighbor called 911 at about 4:30 in the morning after hearing mace, screaming, glass breaking, and a voice saying "I'm going to shoot you." She called her mother on FaceTime. And at about 4:35, crying, she stood in front of a Fort Lauderdale officer and asked for an escort to go get her keys from the park.

Her mother, Alacia Ford-Barron, released that bodycam footage on November 2, and what it shows is the ask. What it does not show is an officer going with her. The family says one officer appeared to offer, and then nobody went. The party was cleared, the officers left, and Zeigler walked toward Gore Betz Park with a friend instead. At about 4:38, the bodycam audio picks up roughly eight gunshots. At 4:44, officers found her in the roadway, shot twice. She died at Broward Health Medical Center.

Sit with the math on that, because the math is the whole case. Four thirty-five, she is standing in front of armed officers asking for help. Four thirty-eight, shots. Four forty-four, she is on the ground. Nine minutes from asking to dying, inside the response window of the very call that brought police to that street.

The man charged with pulling the trigger is Larry Lamar Smith, 19, of Lauderhill, arrested July 6, 2025, on a murder warrant and charged with second-degree murder with a firearm. He has pleaded not guilty, and that case is his to answer in a Broward courtroom. But the criminal case is only half of what this family is fighting. Ford-Barron has filed a wrongful death lawsuit over the escort that never happened, and the family's reviewer, retired Miami assistant police chief Craig McQueen, watched the footage and said it plainly: after appearing to promise an escort, letting her walk alone was unwise, and officers should have waited for backup and gone with her.

Fort Lauderdale police declined to comment, citing the active investigation. In the department's statement shown this week, it pointed to the lead detective staying in contact with the family and invited them to raise concerns through formal channels. Read that carefully. Contact with a detective about the murder case is not an answer about the nine minutes. The family is not asking whether the detective calls. They are asking why a scared 19-year-old who begged for a walk got a cleared scene and an empty street instead.

"My daughter was scared," her mother said. "No one listened to her. They neglected my baby." The bodycam is public now. Watch the ask. Then count the minutes.

text:
Vickie is 27 and weighs 98 pounds. She shoots a speedball up to 18 times a day and stays awake for 48 to 72 hours. She went to a hospital for an infected finger and someone there jabbed her with a dirty needle, did it, and never came back.

She's from Tennessee. She lost herself in Overtown, Miami.

Ask her what she's on and she corrects you twice. "Fentanyl they call it Molly. But it's not Molly. It's closer to bath salt." She speedballs it. Mixes it with more fentanyl. Then she shoots.

How many times a day? "Five, six, seven." But days aren't days out here. "It's 48, 72 hours. You're up the whole time. That's a good 18 shots."

She started shooting at 20. She's 27 now. Seven years.

She used to shoot into her own neck "for fun," when she felt like it. Now her body is breaking. Five foot two. Ninety-eight pounds. She can't close her hand a fracture, or an infection, she's not sure which.

The finger got infected. She went to a hospital. Someone there stuck her with a dirty needle, did it, and never came back. It's still infected. There's blood on her hand.

She thought about wiping it off before the camera started. Then didn't. "Let's be honest. That's my path. What I'm good at is being honest."

Some will say she does this to herself 18 times a day, by her own hand. Others will say a 27-year-old at 98 pounds, husband in prison, kid gone, isn't choosing anything. She's just still breathing.

Minutes before this, a stranger offered to drive her to rehab. She said yes. The waitlist is a month.

Do you think she's still here in a month?

On March 25, he was indicted on charges of second-degree murder.

Lopez-Gomez then fled the scene, and Babcock later succumbed to his injuries. Babcock leaves behind a wife, two stepchildren, and a sister. After being located and taken into custody, USCIS confirmed that Lopez-Gomez is an illegal alien who entered the country at an unknown time and place. He remains in custody.
(WFIN, March 2026; Fox News, March 2026)

The suspects allegedly set up staged armed robberies, so the store clerks would be able to apply for a U visa. USCIS may grant U visas to “victims of certain crimes who have suffered mental or physical abuse and are helpful to law enforcement or government officials in the investigation or prosecution of criminal activity.” These allow the holder to get a work permit, and, under certain conditions, visa holders may be eligible for permanent residence after a few years. The eleven suspects, all surnamed “Patel”, are accused of allegedly arranging a robbery or paying for themselves or a family member to be a “victim.”

One of the suspects, Rambhai Patel, was previously charged and convicted in New York in December 2023 for conspiracy to commit visa fraud. According to court documents, Rambhai and his co-conspirators set up and carried out staged armed robberies at convenience stores and fast-food restaurants across a few states. All of this was done in front of security cameras, so when the victims called the police, they could offer their help and qualify for a U-visa. The U-Visa Program has been rife with fraud since its inception in 2000, and police agencies have been bombarded with fraudulent applications or reports of fake crimes.
(Breitbart, March 2026; USAO, March 2026; USAO, December 2023; USCIS)
Samir Ousman Alsheikh (March 16, 2026)
On March 16, a federal jury in Los Angeles, California, convicted Syrian national Samir Ousman Alsheikh, who was the former head of Syria’s largest civil prison, Adra Prison, under the rule of President Bashar al-Assad. Alsheikh was convicted of torture and lying to U.S. immigration officials about his background to fraudulently obtain a green card and attempting to naturalize as a U.S. citizen. According to evidence from his victims, from 2005 to 2008, Alsheikh inflicted severe mental and physical pain and suffering on prisoners. A form of torture that he was accused of carrying out on prisoners was known as the “magic carpet.” An inmate would be strapped to two wooden panels with hinges in the middle. The guards would then bend the inmate in half, and sometimes stomp on the device, which resulted in serious injury, including broken spines. After his tenure at Adra Prison, Alsheikh briefly served as Governor of Deir Es-Zour, a critical oil-rich region on the Syria-Iraq border, and where he was also accused of brutal crackdowns on dissidents.

It is believed that Alsheikh entered the United States and settled in Los Angeles, California at some point in 2020. Shortly after, he applied for U.S. citizenship. In 2022, the Syrian Emergency Task Force alerted the United States that Alsheikh was in the country, and in July 2024, a complaint was filed that Alsheikh lied on his visa and citizenship applications about having never persecuted any person on any basis and having never been involved in killing or trying to kill someone. He was then taken into custody. After a two-week federal jury trial, he was convicted and is now awaiting sentencing. 
(OPA, March 2026; Courthouse News Service, March 2026; PBS, March 2026)
Christopher Leon Bailey (March 16, 2026)
On March 16, ICE agents arrested Jamaican national Christopher Leon Bailey in connection with a January road rage incident that took place in Ridley Township, Pennsylvania. On January 23, Bailey was arrested by local police after he allegedly pulled a knife on and attempted to stab an individual following a near collision. He then returned to his vehicle to chase down and run over the victim. ICE reported that Bailey had overstayed his tourist visa in 2009, and he was previously arrested by ICE in Philadelphia in 2023 for violating immigration laws. On April 9, ICE announced the arrest of Mexican national Cristobal Felipe-Sarmiento in Salem, Oregon. Felipe-Sarmiento was convicted of raping and sodomizing an incapacitated woman in Marion County, Oregon, in December 2016. He was sentenced to twelve years of post-prison supervision and was required to register as a sex offender. He was also convicted of driving under the influence in 2014.
(DHS, April 2026; Statesman Journal, December 2016)
Luis Alfonzo Marcano-Marcano (April 12, 2026)
On April 12, police responded to a medical center in Mint Hill, North Carolina, after a pregnant woman who suffered a gunshot wound to her stomach was admitted. The victim’s unborn child was pronounced dead shortly after. According to investigators, Venezuelan national Luis Alfonzo Marcano-Marcano dropped his wife off at the medical center and then sped away. He was later arrested in the lobby, and investigators pieced together details of the story. According to Marcano-Marcano, the incident occurred at their house following a birthday party. He and his girlfriend were standing on the porch arguing when he grabbed his pistol and shot the ground next to her feet. He then left the gun on the railing and left. His girlfriend picked up the gun and tried putting it into her pocket but accidentally pulled the trigger and shot herself in the stomach. Marcano-Marcano admitted that the reason why he left the hospital was to go home and throw the pistol into the woods. Once in custody, ICE lodged a detainer against him.
(ABC 7, April 2026; WCNC, April 2026; WXII 12, April 2026)
Eri Otoniel Roblero-Perez (April 12, 2026)
On April 12, illegal alien Eri Otoniel Roblero-Perez was allegedly driving under the influence and killed two boys on their bicycles in Spartanburg County, South Carolina. The two victims, 12-year-old Dereon Robinson and 9-year-old Mikhail-Lee Smith, were riding their bikes on the sidewalk when Perez jumped the curb, ran them over, ultimately killed them. Robinson’s mother watched the whole scene unfold and immediately performed CPR on them. When state troopers arrived at the scene, Roblero-Perez was so intoxicated that he was unable to do a sobriety test. Roblero-Perez was charged with two counts of felony DUI, open container, and driving without a license. He was also placed under a detainer from ICE.
(Fox Carolina, April 2026; WSPA 7, April 2026; WTOC 11, April 2026; NBC 4, April 2026)
Josue Abraham Chirino-Leonice (April 12, 2026)

On April 20, ICE lodged a detainer against Chirino-Leonice and revealed that he entered the country as an unaccompanied minor in November 2023 and was apprehended by Border Patrol. However, he was released into the country by the Biden administration.

Luis Antonio Angel Orduno (April 15, 2026)

After receiving treatment for his injuries, Orduno was detained and charged with Vehicular Homicide, DUI 1st Degree, No Operator’s License, No Insurance, and Criminal Mischief 1st Degree. He has an immigration detainer hold, and it is unknown when and where he entered the country illegally.
(Kentucky State Police, April 2026; Madison Courier, April 2026)

However, this is not Ahmed’s first contact with U.S. officials. In March 2012, he and nine other armed pirates were encountered and fingerprinted by the U.S. Navy after taking an Indian ship hostage. Ahmed then entered the United States illegally in September 2022 and was detained by ICE officials in 2024. He was extradited in April 2025.
(DHS, April 2026; Fox 11, April 2026)
Roman Ceron Amatitla (April 14, 2026)
On April 14, ICE lodged a detainer against Mexican national Roman Ceron Amatitla, who is accused of randomly setting a building on fire on March 16 that killed four people in New York City, New York. According to the Queens District Attorney, Amatitla entered and exited the building several times before the incident, then went to a nearby gas station where he bought a beer and grabbed a pack of matches. He returned to the building, lit a piece of paper on fire, and placed it in the stairwell trash can. Afterward, as the building went up into flames, Amatitla drank his beer as he watched the building go up into flames and residents struggled to evacuate. Among his victims is a 3-year-old child. Following their detainer, the New York City Police Department told ICE that it would refuse to cooperate due to its sanctuary policies.
(AOL, April 2026; Fox News, April 2026)
Dipakkumar Ghelani (April 16, 2026)
On April 16, Indian national Dipakkumar Ghelani was arrested by the Florida Highway Patrol for allegedly trafficking cannabis with a street value of over $13 million in Jacksonville, Florida. Once in custody, ICE took custody of Ghelani thanks to the Florida Highway Patrol’s 287(g) law enforcement partnership with ICE. ICE reported that Ghelani entered the United States on a B-2 visa in March 2016 and overstayed when it expired. During his interview with immigration officers, he was unable to provide documentation proving his legal presence.
(ICE, April 2026; Action News JAX, April 2026)
Atharva Vyas (April 18, 2026)
On April 18, Indian national Atharva Vyas assaulted a mother and her three-year-old daughter in a park in San Antonio, Texas. Vyas allegedly appeared out of the woods while the victims were fishing and began randomly attacking them. After he punched the mother and yanked her by the hair, he turned his attention to the three-year-old girl, whom he attempted to push in her eyes with his thumbs before he began biting her face. The little girl lost two teeth in the attack. Vyas was then restrained by several bystanders until police arrived and he was taken to jail. Once in custody, ICE lodged a detainer against Vyas, revealing that his F-1 visa had been revoked in April 2025 by the Trump administration due to a 2023 arrest for felony assault. Josue Ortiz-Villeda & Faustino Ruiz-Juarez (April 19, 2026)
On April 19, Honduran national Josue Ortiz-Villeda and Mexican national Faustino Ruiz-Juarez were arrested after police found fifteen kilograms of cocaine and a loaded handgun during a traffic stop in Lowell, North Carolina. According to local police, after the vehicle was pulled over, a police K-9 alerted officers to the presence of narcotics. The two suspects were taken into custody following the search and charged with trafficking cocaine, and Ruiz-Juarez was charged with carrying a concealed weapon. Denisa Ghiocel & Dorel Ghiocel (April 22, 2026)
On April 22, Loudoun County Sheriff deputies arrested Romanian nationals Denisa Ghiocel and Dorel Ghiocel for alleged attempted robbery of jewelry in Ashburn, Virginia. Following an investigation into several similar incidents in the area, deputies identified a vehicle linked to the robberies. The couple is accused of using distraction techniques to remove jewelry from the victims. The Sheriff’s Office announced that the Ghiocels have active ICE detainers; however, there is no information on when or where they entered the country illegally.
Loudoun County Sheriff’s Office, April 2026; Fox 5, April 2026)
Roni Mendez-Escobar (April 22, 2026)

However, on October 27, Fairfax County politicians released him from custody without notifying ICE. (DHS, April 2026; ABC 7, April 2026)

Samuel Antonio Maldonado-Erazo (March 4, 2026)

Maldonado-Erazo brought the child to work with him and ignored the child’s signs of distress throughout the day. Eventually, first responders were called, finding the victim in cardiac arrest and taking him to the hospital. Unfortunately, the three-year-old died. According to the Escambia County Sheriff, the child had extensive bruising across his body, several burn marks, several broken ribs – one of which was detached from the backbone – a broken collarbone, and a transected pancreas, which raised concerns of possible sexual abuse. Maldonado-Erazo was then taken into custody and charged with negligent manslaughter, but his charges may be upgraded. According to ICE, he entered the country illegally with his daughter in August 2021, but they were later released due to the Biden administration’s catch-and-release policies.

Conrrado Ahuexoteco Atrisco (Incident Feb. 25, arrested March 5, 2026)
On March 5, Mexican national Conrrado Ahuexoteco Atrisco was arrested for allegedly sexually assaulting a 14-year-old high school student in Park City, Utah. The incident was reported to the Park City High School resource officer on February 25. According to the victim, she was at her friend’s house, lying in her bed and playing on her phone, when the friend’s ex-boyfriend, Atrisco, asked if he could join her. Atrisco then got onto the bed and tried cuddling with her, then pulled down her pants and sexually assaulted her. Following the report, the Park City Police Department obtained a search warrant for Atrisco’s DNA and began attempting to locate him. (DHS, March 2026; ABC 4, March 2026; VOZ, March 2026)
Franquin Inestroza-Martinez & Gerzon Jose Chirinos-Munguia (Incident Jan. 7, arrested March 5, 2026)
On March 5, Sunnyvale Department of Public Safety detectives arrested Honduran nationals Franquin Inestroza-Martinez and Gerzon Jose Chirinos-Munguia for the alleged shooting and murder of 24-year-old Kembery Chirinos-Flores. ICE lodged detainers against both suspects, but Santa Clara County refused to honor them. ICE reports that Inestroza-Martinez illegally entered the country three times (caught and removed in June 2013, caught and removed in January 2018, and most recently entered illegally at an unknown date and time). Chirinos-Munguia illegally entered the country in May 2015 and was later removed.  He reentered a second time at an unknown date and time and has been living in the country illegally. (DHS, March 2026, City of Sunnyvale, March 2026)
Sukhdev Singh (March 6, 2026)
On March 6, Indian national Sukhdev Singh allegedly struck a 65-year-old pedestrian, who remains in critical condition, with his semi-truck in Indianapolis, Indiana. When police responded to the scene, they arrested him after discovering that Singh had a non-domiciled CDL which was issued in January 2026 by New York. Later that day, Sukhdev Singh was released and immediately taken into ICE custody, where he remains. It is still unclear when or where he entered the country illegally.

His victims, 31-year-old John Rodriguez and 83-year-old Richard Williams, survived at the scene; however, a few days later, Williams, an Air Force veteran, passed away from his injuries. On March 10, Posada-Hernandez was arrested for attempted murder and had an ICE detainer lodged against him. Prior to this, he had racked up fifteen charges, including domestic violence and aggravated assault. In a press release, ICE revealed that Posada-Hernandez has been deported four different times – most recently in 2020 – and it is unknown when or where he reentered for the fifth time. On March 25, he was indicted on charges of second-degree murder.

Erasto Lopez-Gomez (March 11, 2026)
On March 11, Mexican national Erasto Lopez-Gomez allegedly killed a 62-year-old man in a fatal hit-and-run in Pitt County, North Carolina. The victim, Christopher Babcock, was riding his motorcycle towards Greenville, North Carolina, when Lopez-Gomez turned left in front of him and caused a collision. Lopez-Gomez then fled the scene, and Babcock later succumbed to his injuries. Babcock leaves behind a wife, two stepchildren, and a sister. After being located and taken into custody, USCIS confirmed that Lopez-Gomez is an illegal alien who entered the country at an unknown time and place. He remains in custody.

Patel Visa Fraud (March 13, 2026)
On March 13, the U.S. Attorney’s Office announced that eleven Indian nationals in Kentucky, Massachusetts, and Ohio were arrested and charged with conspiracy to commit visa fraud. The suspects allegedly set up staged armed robberies, so the store clerks would be able to apply for a U visa. USCIS may grant U visas to “victims of certain crimes who have suffered mental or physical abuse and are helpful to law enforcement or government officials in the investigation or prosecution of criminal activity.” These allow the holder to get a work permit, and, under certain conditions, visa holders may be eligible for permanent residence after a few years. The eleven suspects, all surnamed “Patel”, are accused of allegedly arranging a robbery or paying for themselves or a family member to be a “victim.”

One of the suspects, Rambhai Patel, was previously charged and convicted in New York in December 2023 for conspiracy to commit visa fraud. According to court documents, Rambhai and his co-conspirators set up and carried out staged armed robberies at convenience stores and fast-food restaurants across a few states. All of this was done in front of security cameras, so when the victims called the police, they could offer their help and qualify for a U-visa. The U-Visa Program has been rife with fraud since its inception in 2000, and police agencies have been bombarded with fraudulent applications or reports of fake crimes.
(Breitbart, March 2026; USAO, March 2026; USAO, December 2023; USCIS)
Samir Ousman Alsheikh (March 16, 2026)
On March 16, a federal jury in Los Angeles, California, convicted Syrian national Samir Ousman Alsheikh, who was the former head of Syria’s largest civil prison, Adra Prison, under the rule of President Bashar al-Assad. Alsheikh was convicted of torture and lying to U.S. immigration officials about his background to fraudulently obtain a green card and attempting to naturalize as a U.S. citizen. According to evidence from his victims, from 2005 to 2008, Alsheikh inflicted severe mental and physical pain and suffering on prisoners. A form of torture that he was accused of carrying out on prisoners was known as the “magic carpet.” An inmate would be strapped to two wooden panels with hinges in the middle. The guards would then bend the inmate in half, and sometimes stomp on the device, which resulted in serious injury, including broken spines. After his tenure at Adra Prison, Alsheikh briefly served as Governor of Deir Es-Zour, a critical oil-rich region on the Syria-Iraq border, and where he was also accused of brutal crackdowns on dissidents.

It is believed that Alsheikh entered the United States and settled in Los Angeles, California at some point in 2020. Shortly after, he applied for U.S. citizenship. In 2022, the Syrian Emergency Task Force alerted the United States that Alsheikh was in the country, and in July 2024, a complaint was filed that Alsheikh lied on his visa and citizenship applications about having never persecuted any person on any basis and having never been involved in killing or trying to kill someone. He was then taken into custody. After a two-week federal jury trial, he was convicted and is now awaiting sentencing. 
(OPA, March 2026; Courthouse News Service, March 2026; PBS, March 2026)
Christopher Leon Bailey (March 16, 2026)
On March 16, ICE agents arrested Jamaican national Christopher Leon Bailey in connection with a January road rage incident that took place in Ridley Township, Pennsylvania. He then returned to his vehicle to chase down and run over the victim. ICE reported that Bailey had overstayed his tourist visa in 2009, and he was previously arrested by ICE in Philadelphia in 2023 for violating immigration laws. text:
Margaret Qualley trained her whole childhood to be a professional ballerina. At 16 she finally got offered the job, and she quit.

Now the ballet she walked away from is a big reason Kalshi has her at 48% to be the next Bond girl.

She left home at 14 to board at the North Carolina School of the Arts. By 16 she was in New York for American Ballet Theatre's summer program, dancing eight hours a day, six days a week. Then North Carolina Dance Theatre offered her an apprenticeship, which is basically the first rung of a pro career, and she turned it down. She's said she just knew it wasn't going to be good for her head or her heart.

So she stayed in New York, hated a short stint of modeling, and started acting.

The dancing kept sneaking back in anyway.

Spike Jonze cast her in a Kenzo perfume ad in 2016. It's the one where she's sulking at a fancy gala in a green dress and then totally loses it in the ballroom. She made up a lot of those moves on the spot from her ballet training, and she's said that ad was huge for her because she'd quit dancing at 16. A few years later she got her first Emmy nomination playing Ann Reinking in Fosse/Verdon. Reinking was a dancer she used to watch on video in the back of a minivan on the way to class.

Then came the Oscars in March 2025. Halle Berry introduced a Bond tribute, and the first person out was Qualley in a long red gown, dancing to the James Bond Theme with a line of guys in tuxedos. Almost 20 million people were watching. Within a week, bookmakers had her at even money for Bond girl.

That clip is doing a lot of work, by the way. Nobody's been cast yet, and the handful of people who'll actually decide aren't talking. So everyone betting on this is going off whatever they can see. Sydney Sweeney led Kalshi back in May with Qualley at 17%. Anya Taylor-Joy shot up to 65% in August. Qualley keeps climbing back to the top anyway, because she's the only one in the race who's already done the job on live TV in front of all of Hollywood.

They probably won't cast the women until Villeneuve picks his Bond. But I love that the thing she gave up at 16 keeps getting her into the biggest rooms of her career.
